Not "Run a single manual quality check before the initial launch.": A one-time check does not catch regressions introduced by later model or prompt changes. Not "Rely on end-user complaints to surface quality problems.": Waiting for complaints is reactive and lets defects reach users undetected. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A security team is hardening a Bedrock workload according to the Security pillar of the Generative AI Lens. Which TWO practices should they adopt? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Send prompts to a public endpoint without TLS to reduce overhead.
Embed long-lived IAM access keys in the application package.
Encrypt data at rest with AWS KMS and reach Bedrock through VPC endpoints to keep traffic on the AWS network.
Apply least-privilege IAM with condition keys (for example, requiring a specific bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier) for model access.
Disable all logging to minimize the data footprint.

explanation: Customer-managed encryption and private connectivity protect data confidentiality and reduce exposure of prompts and outputs. Least-privilege identity-based policies with condition keys restrict who can call models and can enforce that guardrails are applied. Not "Send prompts to a public endpoint without TLS to reduce o…": Unencrypted transport exposes sensitive prompt and response data. Not "Embed long-lived IAM access keys in the application package.": Long-lived embedded keys are a major security risk and violate credential best practices. Not "Disable all logging to minimize the data footprint.": Disabling logging removes the audit trail needed for security monitoring and compliance. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A company must classify tens of millions of archived documents with a foundation model. Results are consumed by an analytics team the next day, so real-time latency is unnecessary. Which approach best satisfies the Cost Optimization and Sustainability pillars?

options.text: Provision dedicated throughput and keep it running 24/7.
Use Amazon Bedrock batch inference with a right-sized model.
Invoke the model in real time, one document per request, as fast as possible.
Use the largest available model for every document in real time.

explanation: Batch inference processes large datasets asynchronously at lower cost, and a right-sized model avoids over-provisioning compute for a latency-tolerant job. Not "Provision dedicated throughput and keep it running 24/7.": A continuously provisioned endpoint wastes capacity for a once-daily, latency-tolerant job. Not "Invoke the model in real time, one document per request, …": High-volume real-time invocation is more expensive and unnecessary when results are needed only the next day. Not "Use the largest available model for every document in rea…": This maximizes cost and energy use with no benefit for a non-interactive workload. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A data scientist must clean, transform, and engineer features from large tabular datasets before training, and wants a mostly visual, low-code flow that exports prepared data to Amazon S3. Which service fits best?

options.text: Amazon QuickSight.
Amazon Kendra.
Amazon Athena.
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.

explanation: Data Wrangler offers a visual, low-code interface for importing, cleaning, transforming, and exporting tabular data for ML, reducing custom preprocessing code. Not "Amazon QuickSight.": QuickSight is for business-intelligence dashboards, not ML data preparation. Not "Amazon Kendra.": Kendra is an enterprise search service, not a data-prep tool. Not "Amazon Athena.": Athena queries data in S3 with SQL but is not a guided data-preparation and feature-engineering tool. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A real-time chat router must classify incoming text messages into a small set of intents. The task is simple, but volume is very high and the team wants the lowest latency at very low cost. Which Amazon Nova model is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Nova 2 Sonic.
Amazon Nova Lite.
Amazon Nova Pro.
Amazon Nova Micro.

explanation: Nova Micro is the text-only Nova model that delivers the lowest-latency responses at very low cost, well suited to high-volume, simple text tasks such as intent classification. Not "Amazon Nova 2 Sonic.": Nova 2 Sonic is a speech model for voice-enabled applications, not a text classifier. Not "Amazon Nova Lite.": Nova Lite is the very-low-cost multimodal model for image, video and text inputs; for a text-only task Nova Micro is the lowest-latency choice. Not "Amazon Nova Pro.": Nova Pro is a highly capable multimodal model, more than a simple classification task requires. Status note: Nova Reel and Nova Canvas, which older versions of this kind of question use as distractors, reached end-of-life on September 30, 2026, and Nova Premier on September 14, 2026. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/nova/latest/userguide/what-is-nova.html

prompt: An assistant must answer using internal documents that change frequently, and answers must always reflect the latest content. Which approach meets this with the LOWEST ongoing maintenance?

options.text: Paste all documents into every prompt.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation with a knowledge base over the documents.
Fine-tune the model nightly on the latest documents.
Use continued pre-training whenever documents change.

explanation: RAG retrieves the current documents at query time, so updated content is reflected immediately without retraining the model. Not "Paste all documents into every prompt.": Stuffing all documents into the prompt is costly, hits context limits, and does not scale as the corpus grows. Not "Fine-tune the model nightly on the latest documents.": Repeated fine-tuning is costly and operationally heavy and still lags behind document changes between runs. Not "Use continued pre-training whenever documents change.": Continued pre-training is even heavier than fine-tuning and is not how you keep answers current. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Prompt engineering has not reliably produced a company's required brand voice and a strict, consistent output format. The underlying domain knowledge is stable and does not change often. Which customization approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Add a knowledge base and use RAG.
Increase the temperature parameter.
Fine-tune the model on labeled examples that demonstrate the desired tone and format.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput.

explanation: Fine-tuning teaches consistent style and formatting from examples and is appropriate when the behavior, not freshness of facts, is the gap. Not "Add a knowledge base and use RAG.": RAG supplies fresh facts but does not reliably enforce tone and output formatting. Not "Increase the temperature parameter.": Higher temperature increases variability, working against a consistent voice and format. Not "Purchase Provisioned Throughput.": Provisioned Throughput affects capacity and cost, not the model's style or formatting behavior. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A startup's Bedrock usage is spiky and unpredictable, with long idle periods between bursts. They want to pay only for what they use and avoid paying for idle capacity. Which pricing/inference choice is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Batch inference for all traffic.
On-demand inference.
Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment.
A dedicated SageMaker endpoint kept always on.

explanation: On-demand pricing charges per request with no commitment, which is most cost-effective for spiky, unpredictable, low-utilization traffic. Not "Batch inference for all traffic.": Batch is offline and cannot serve interactive, bursty requests. Not "Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment.": A commitment pays for reserved capacity that sits idle during the long quiet periods. Not "A dedicated SageMaker endpoint kept always on.": An always-on endpoint incurs cost during idle periods, defeating the goal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: An application already calls Amazon Nova Pro through a US cross-Region inference profile, a configuration that supports latency-optimized inference. The team wants to reduce token-generation latency with the smallest possible application change. Which option should they evaluate first?

options.text: Switch to a larger, more capable model.
Move the workload to batch inference.
Enable latency-optimized inference for the supported model.
Add more retries to the client.

explanation: Latency-optimized inference reduces response latency for supported models with one request parameter and no application rewrite or model fine-tuning. Status note: latency-optimized inference is still labelled preview and covers only Amazon Nova Pro, Claude 3.5 Haiku and Llama 3.1 70B/405B through cross-Region inference in a few US Regions (`performanceConfig` with `latency` set to `optimized`). For other models, the Priority service tier gives the fastest response times at a price premium by setting `service_tier` to `priority`. Not "Switch to a larger, more capable model.": A larger model typically increases latency rather than reducing it. Not "Move the workload to batch inference.": Batch inference is asynchronous and increases, not decreases, time-to-response. Not "Add more retries to the client.": Retries handle failures; they do not lower per-request latency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/latency-optimized-inference.html

prompt: A team is creating an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base and wants a fully managed vector store that integrates natively with Bedrock, supports frequent low-latency similarity queries, and requires no cluster sizing or management. Which option fits best?

options.text: Amazon S3 with objects named by embedding.
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless as the vector store.
A self-managed Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster you size and patch.
Amazon DynamoDB with a custom similarity function.

explanation: OpenSearch Serverless is a natively integrated, fully managed vector store for Bedrock knowledge bases that scales automatically for frequent low-latency queries. Not "Amazon S3 with objects named by embedding.": Plain S3 has no vector index or similarity search capability. Not "A self-managed Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster you size…": A provisioned cluster requires capacity planning, scaling, and maintenance, adding operational overhead. Not "Amazon DynamoDB with a custom similarity function.": DynamoDB is not one of the vector stores Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports, and a hand-written similarity function is extra code to maintain. (DynamoDB has had native vector search since August 2026, but outside Knowledge Bases.) Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A knowledge base serves several departments, and each user must only retrieve documents tagged for their department. The team wants to enforce this at retrieval time without maintaining separate copies of the corpus. Which capability should they use?

options.text: Raise the temperature so the model is less literal.
Retrieve everything and truncate the results in the client.
Apply metadata filtering on the Retrieve call using the document's department attribute.
Add an instruction in the prompt asking the model to ignore other departments.

explanation: Bedrock knowledge bases support metadata attributes and filter expressions so retrieval returns only chunks matching the user's department. Not "Raise the temperature so the model is less literal.": Temperature has nothing to do with which documents are retrieved. Not "Retrieve everything and truncate the results in the client.": Truncation does not enforce department-level access and may still expose other departments' content. Not "Add an instruction in the prompt asking the model to igno…": Prompt instructions cannot reliably prevent irrelevant or unauthorized chunks from being retrieved and used. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: An application must show end users the exact source passages that support each generated answer, with the least custom development. Which Amazon Bedrock approach provides this?

options.text: Use InvokeModel with the whole corpus pasted into the prompt.
Use the RetrieveAndGenerate API, which returns generated answers with citations to the source chunks.
Enable model invocation logging and show users the logs.
Increase max tokens so the model lists its sources.

explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate produces a grounded answer and returns citations identifying the retrieved passages used, with no custom attribution code. Not "Use InvokeModel with the whole corpus pasted into the pro…": Stuffing the corpus into the prompt does not produce reliable citations and does not scale. Not "Enable model invocation logging and show users the logs.": Invocation logs are for operators and do not provide user-facing source citations. Not "Increase max tokens so the model lists its sources.": Asking the model to self-report sources is unreliable; max tokens does not create verifiable citations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A developer wants to fetch the most relevant chunks from a Bedrock knowledge base, post-process them in their own code, and send them with a custom prompt to a model hosted outside Amazon Bedrock. Which API is appropriate?

options.text: The RetrieveAndGenerate API exclusively.
The CreateModelCustomizationJob API.
The StartIngestionJob API.
The Retrieve API, which returns ranked chunks for the developer to use in a custom generation step.

explanation: Retrieve returns the relevant passages only, letting the developer control the post-processing, the prompt and the generation model themselves. Not "The RetrieveAndGenerate API exclusively.": RetrieveAndGenerate does accept a custom prompt template (`promptTemplate.textPromptTemplate`) and a model of your choice as `modelArn`, but it always runs the generation step itself inside Amazon Bedrock, so it cannot hand the chunks to your own code or to a model the knowledge base cannot call. Not "The CreateModelCustomizationJob API.": That API runs fine-tuning, unrelated to retrieving chunks. Not "The StartIngestionJob API.": StartIngestionJob ingests data into the knowledge base; it does not retrieve chunks for a query. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A RAG assistant occasionally produces answers that are not supported by the retrieved passages. The team wants a managed way to detect and block responses that are not grounded in the source context. Which capability helps MOST?

options.text: Increase the model temperature.
Remove the retrieved context from the prompt.
Enable the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding check.
Switch to on-demand pricing.

explanation: The contextual grounding (and relevance) check scores whether a response is grounded in the provided source and can block ungrounded answers. Not "Increase the model temperature.": Higher temperature increases variability and tends to worsen, not reduce, ungrounded output. Not "Remove the retrieved context from the prompt.": Removing context guarantees the answer cannot be grounded, the opposite of the goal. Not "Switch to on-demand pricing.": Pricing mode has no effect on grounding. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: An analyst tool must answer questions that require reasoning over relationships among connected entities (people, companies, and the links between them), not just similarity to text passages. Which Amazon Bedrock knowledge base option is designed for this?

options.text: Amazon Athena queries over CSV files.
An Amazon DynamoDB table of entities.
A standard vector-only knowledge base.
A knowledge base using GraphRAG with Amazon Neptune Analytics.

explanation: GraphRAG with Neptune Analytics builds a graph of entities and relationships, enabling retrieval that reasons over connections rather than only vector similarity. Not "Amazon Athena queries over CSV files.": Athena runs SQL over files and is not a graph-aware retrieval system for RAG. Not "An Amazon DynamoDB table of entities.": DynamoDB stores items but provides no graph reasoning or managed RAG integration. Not "A standard vector-only knowledge base.": Pure vector similarity does not capture explicit relationships among connected entities. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Business users want to ask natural-language analytical questions (sums, trends, comparisons) over data in an Amazon Redshift warehouse, and have the system generate and run the appropriate queries. Which Amazon Bedrock capability fits?

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to read the question.
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with structured data retrieval, which generates SQL from natural language.
Fine-tune a model on the warehouse schema.
Embed every table row as a vector and do similarity search.

explanation: Structured-data knowledge bases translate natural-language questions into SQL against the connected warehouse, returning accurate analytical results. Not "Use Amazon Comprehend to read the question.": Comprehend analyzes text but does not generate SQL or query a warehouse. Not "Fine-tune a model on the warehouse schema.": Fine-tuning does not give live, accurate query results over changing data the way text-to-SQL retrieval does. Not "Embed every table row as a vector and do similarity search.": Vector similarity over rows cannot perform aggregations or precise analytical queries. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A company keeps 200 million archived document embeddings that are queried only a few times per month for occasional investigations. They want the lowest-cost durable vector storage with no capacity to manage. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: A provisioned OpenSearch Service cluster sized for the full corpus.
OpenSearch Serverless kept warm at all times.
Amazon S3 Vectors.
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector.

explanation: S3 Vectors offers cost-optimized vector storage and search with no infrastructure to provision and pay-for-what-you-use pricing, ideal for large corpora queried infrequently. Not "A provisioned OpenSearch Service cluster sized for the fu…": A continuously provisioned cluster is expensive for data queried only a few times a month. Not "OpenSearch Serverless kept warm at all times.": Keeping search capacity running all the time is more expensive than needed for rare queries. Next-generation OpenSearch Serverless (May 2026) can scale to zero when idle, but S3 Vectors remains the cost-optimized store for rarely queried vectors. Not "Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector.": RDS requires running instances and is not the lowest-cost option for rarely queried, very large vector sets. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/s3-vectors.html

prompt: A team has standardized on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL for its application data and wants to store and query embeddings alongside related relational records using familiar tooling, while keeping the vector store as a managed Bedrock knowledge base option. Which choice fits best?

options.text: Use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension as the knowledge base vector store.
Store vectors in Amazon DynamoDB.
Adopt a brand-new self-managed search cluster instead.
Keep embeddings only in application memory.

explanation: Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector is a supported Bedrock vector store and lets the team keep vectors next to relational data using PostgreSQL tooling. Not "Store vectors in Amazon DynamoDB.": DynamoDB is not a supported Bedrock Knowledge Bases vector store, and it would move the vectors away from the relational records in Aurora. Not "Adopt a brand-new self-managed search cluster instead.": Introducing a separate self-managed system adds operational overhead the team is trying to avoid. Not "Keep embeddings only in application memory.": In-memory storage is not durable and cannot serve as a knowledge base vector store. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: Source content lives in Amazon S3, Confluence, and a SharePoint site. The team wants to ingest all of it into one Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with the LEAST custom code. What should they do?

options.text: Use the knowledge base's native data source connectors for S3, Confluence, and SharePoint.
Manually export everything to S3 on a schedule.
Write custom crawlers for each system and push to S3 only.
Fine-tune the model on each source instead of ingesting.

explanation: A Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base has native connectors for S3, SharePoint, Confluence, Web Crawler, Google Drive, OneDrive and custom sources, avoiding custom ingestion code. Status note: starting September 30, 2026, new Confluence, Microsoft SharePoint, Salesforce and Web Crawler connectors can no longer be created on customer-managed knowledge bases (existing ones keep working); AWS points applications that need these connectors to a Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, whose native connectors are S3, SharePoint, Confluence, Web Crawler, Google Drive, OneDrive and Custom. Not "Manually export everything to S3 on a schedule.": Manual exports are brittle and lag behind source changes compared with managed connectors. Not "Write custom crawlers for each system and push to S3 only.": Custom crawlers add development and maintenance overhead that the built-in connectors remove. Not "Fine-tune the model on each source instead of ingesting.": Fine-tuning is not how you ingest changing documents for retrieval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/data-source-connectors.html

prompt: A chat experience built on RetrieveAndGenerate must keep context across follow-up questions in a conversation with the least custom state management. Which approach should the developer use?

options.text: Increase the model context window only.
Re-embed the entire chat history into the vector store each turn.
Pass a session identifier to RetrieveAndGenerate so Bedrock maintains the conversation context.
Store every message in DynamoDB and rebuild the prompt manually each turn.

explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate supports a session ID that preserves multi-turn context without the developer building custom conversation state. Not "Increase the model context window only.": A larger window does not automatically carry prior turns into each RetrieveAndGenerate call. Not "Re-embed the entire chat history into the vector store ea…": Re-embedding the conversation each turn is unnecessary and costly and is not how session context is maintained. Not "Store every message in DynamoDB and rebuild the prompt ma…": Manual state assembly adds development overhead compared with built-in session support. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team wants to add retrieval-augmented answers over their documents but does not want to build and operate an embedding pipeline, a vector database, and custom retrieval code. Which option provides managed RAG with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which manages embedding, storage, and retrieval as a service.
Fine-tune a model on the documents instead of retrieving.
Paste documents into prompts at request time.
Build a custom pipeline with Lambda, a self-managed vector database, and bespoke retrieval code.

explanation: Knowledge Bases provide fully managed RAG, handling chunking, embeddings, the vector store, and retrieval so the team avoids building the pipeline. Not "Fine-tune a model on the documents instead of retrieving.": Fine-tuning does not keep answers current as documents change and is not managed RAG. Not "Paste documents into prompts at request time.": Prompt stuffing does not scale and is not a managed retrieval solution. Not "Build a custom pipeline with Lambda, a self-managed vecto…": A hand-built pipeline maximizes operational overhead, which the team is trying to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Long policy documents have distinct topical sections. With the default fixed-size chunking, related ideas are split across chunks and retrieval quality suffers. Which chunking strategy is MOST likely to improve relevance?

options.text: Use larger fixed-size chunks only.
Increase the model temperature.
Disable chunking and embed each whole document as one vector.
Semantic chunking, which splits on semantic boundaries so each chunk holds a coherent idea.

explanation: Semantic chunking groups text by meaning rather than a fixed token count, keeping related content together and improving retrieval relevance. Not "Use larger fixed-size chunks only.": Bigger fixed chunks still ignore topic boundaries and can mix unrelated content. Not "Increase the model temperature.": Temperature affects generation, not how documents are chunked or retrieved. Not "Disable chunking and embed each whole document as one vec…": Embedding an entire long document dilutes the vector and harms precise retrieval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team needs precise matching on small text units but also wants the language model to receive surrounding context when a small unit matches. Which chunking approach provides both?

options.text: A single fixed chunk size for everything.
Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking.
No chunking at all.
Switching to a larger embedding dimension.

explanation: Hierarchical chunking matches on small child chunks for precision and supplies the larger parent chunk as context for generation. Not "A single fixed chunk size for everything.": One fixed size cannot simultaneously optimize for precise matching and broad context. Not "No chunking at all.": Treating each document as one chunk loses the precision of small-unit matching. Not "Switching to a larger embedding dimension.": Dimension size does not provide the parent-context behavior hierarchical chunking gives. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team decides to upgrade to a newer embedding model for better retrieval. What must they do to keep retrieval working correctly?

options.text: Lower the temperature on the generation model.
Do nothing; existing vectors remain compatible.
Re-embed (re-index) the entire document corpus with the new model so document and query vectors share the same space.
Re-embed only the queries, not the documents.

explanation: Query and document embeddings must come from the same model; changing the model requires re-embedding the whole corpus to avoid vector-space mismatch. Not "Lower the temperature on the generation model.": Temperature is unrelated to embedding compatibility. Not "Do nothing; existing vectors remain compatible.": Vectors from a different model live in a different space and will not match new query embeddings. Not "Re-embed only the queries, not the documents.": Mismatched query and document embeddings produce poor or empty retrieval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A vector store is becoming expensive as the corpus grows. The team wants to cut storage and query cost while keeping acceptable retrieval accuracy. Which embedding choice helps MOST?

options.text: Store each chunk twice for redundancy.
Always use the maximum available embedding dimension.
Raise the generation temperature.
Use an embedding model that supports smaller output dimensions (for example, Titan Text Embeddings V2) and select a smaller dimension.

explanation: Smaller-dimension embeddings reduce index size and query cost, and V2 lets you trade some accuracy for substantial storage savings. Not "Store each chunk twice for redundancy.": Duplicating vectors increases cost without improving accuracy. Not "Always use the maximum available embedding dimension.": Maximum dimensions increase storage and cost, the opposite of the goal. Not "Raise the generation temperature.": Temperature does not affect embedding storage or cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: An application must retrieve relevant items from a combined catalog of product images and text descriptions using a single query that may be text or an image. Which embedding approach supports this?

options.text: Use Amazon Rekognition labels as the only index.
Store images as base64 strings and embed the strings as text.
Use a multimodal embedding model (such as Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings) so images and text share one vector space.
Use a text-only embedding model for everything.

explanation: Multimodal embeddings place images and text in a shared space, enabling cross-modal similarity search from either input type. Not "Use Amazon Rekognition labels as the only index.": Label detection is not a shared embedding space for semantic text-and-image retrieval. Not "Store images as base64 strings and embed the strings as t…": Embedding raw base64 as text does not capture visual semantics for retrieval. Not "Use a text-only embedding model for everything.": A text-only model cannot embed images for similarity search. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Developers want inline, context-aware code suggestions and the ability to generate functions from natural-language comments directly inside their IDE to speed up routine coding. Which capability provides this?

options.text: Amazon Kendra.
Amazon Q Developer in-IDE code suggestions and generation.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon QuickSight Q.

explanation: Amazon Q Developer integrates with the IDE to provide real-time inline completions and generate code from natural-language prompts. Not "Amazon Kendra.": Kendra is enterprise search, not an IDE coding assistant. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend is an NLP analysis service, not a coding assistant. Not "Amazon QuickSight Q.": QuickSight Q answers natural-language questions about BI data, not IDE code generation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: An application intermittently receives throttling errors from Amazon Bedrock, and operators want to be alerted automatically when throttling rises. What should they configure?

options.text: Nothing; throttling cannot be monitored.
Lower the temperature to reduce throttling.
A CloudWatch alarm on the Bedrock throttling metric for the model.
Increase max tokens to avoid throttling.

explanation: Bedrock publishes CloudWatch metrics (including throttling), so an alarm on the throttle metric notifies operators when throttling increases. Not "Nothing; throttling cannot be monitored.": Throttling is observable through CloudWatch metrics and can be alarmed on. Not "Lower the temperature to reduce throttling.": Temperature has no effect on throttling or its monitoring. Not "Increase max tokens to avoid throttling.": Output length does not address request-rate throttling or provide alerting. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A production Bedrock workload has steady, high, predictable demand for 12 business hours and near-zero traffic overnight. The team must guarantee dedicated capacity during business hours (no throttling) at the lowest total cost, keeping the same model and API. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Use Provisioned Throughput without a long-term commitment, creating model units for business hours and deleting them overnight.
Use on-demand inference for all traffic.
Use Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment sized for peak.
Use cross-Region inference to add capacity during business hours.

explanation: No-commitment Provisioned Throughput can be deleted at any time and is billed hourly until it is deleted, so creating it for business hours and deleting it overnight gives dedicated capacity without paying for the idle period. Status note: Provisioned Throughput can be purchased only for the models on its supported list (Amazon Nova, older Anthropic models up to Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2, Llama 3.1/3.2 and some embedding models). Bedrock also offers a Reserved service tier, which reserves input and output tokens-per-minute capacity for 1 or 3 months at a fixed price. The Reserved tier has no hourly on/off option, so this pattern applies to models that still support Provisioned Throughput. Not "Use on-demand inference for all traffic.": On-demand has no idle cost but cannot guarantee dedicated capacity during peak hours, so it fails the no-throttling requirement. Not "Use Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment size…": A committed term has the most discounted hourly price, but it cannot be deleted until the term ends, so you pay for the units overnight too. Not "Use cross-Region inference to add capacity during busines…": Cross-Region inference routes on-demand traffic across Regions for throughput but does not reserve guaranteed capacity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: A synchronous, customer-facing Bedrock feature must become more resilient to transient errors and to a single-Region impairment, per the Reliability pillar. Which TWO measures are MOST effective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Increase maxTokens so fewer requests are needed.
Place a single-Region Amazon SQS queue in front of the model call.
Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter for throttling and transient 5xx errors.
Use cross-Region inference (or multi-Region failover) so requests can be served if one Region is impaired.
Lower the temperature for more consistent outputs.

explanation: Backoff with jitter recovers from transient throttling/5xx without synchronized retry storms, directly improving reliability. Spreading or failing over across Regions keeps the feature available during a regional impairment. Not "Increase maxTokens so fewer requests are needed.": Output length has no effect on resilience to errors or regional failure. Not "Place a single-Region Amazon SQS queue in front of the mo…": A queue in one Region is itself a regional single point of failure and adds latency to a synchronous, user-facing path, so it does not address regional resilience here. Not "Lower the temperature for more consistent outputs.": Temperature controls randomness, not reliability. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: An interactive assistant must reduce the latency users perceive on long answers, WITHOUT changing which model is used and without a training step. Which choice is BEST?

options.text: Enable response streaming and, where the model supports it, latency-optimized inference.
Buy Provisioned Throughput at high model units.
Distill to a smaller student model.
Switch to a model with a larger context window.

explanation: Streaming shows tokens as they are generated (cutting perceived latency), and latency-optimized inference speeds generation for the models that support it, both without changing the model or training anything. Status note: latency-optimized inference is still labelled preview and covers only Amazon Nova Pro, Claude 3.5 Haiku and Llama 3.1 70B/405B through cross-Region inference in a few US Regions (`performanceConfig` with `latency` set to `optimized`). For other models, the Priority service tier gives the fastest response times at a price premium by setting `service_tier` to `priority`. Not "Buy Provisioned Throughput at high model units.": Provisioned Throughput reduces throttling/queueing but does not lower the per-token generation time that dominates perceived latency on long answers. Not "Distill to a smaller student model.": Distillation reduces latency but changes the model and requires a training step, which the scenario forbids. Not "Switch to a model with a larger context window.": A bigger context window does not reduce generation latency and can increase it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/latency-optimized-inference.html

prompt: A team must roll out a new prompt version to production with the ability to revert instantly if quality regresses, measure both versions, and avoid redeploying application code. Which approach best fits Operational Excellence?

options.text: Manage the prompt as versions in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, keep the version ARN the application invokes in AWS AppConfig, evaluate both versions, and switch or revert by changing that configuration value.
Hard-code the new prompt behind an application feature flag.
Raise the temperature so the new prompt is more robust.
Deploy two Lambda functions, each hard-coding one prompt, and split traffic.

explanation: A Prompt Management version is a snapshot of the prompt, and the application invokes a specific version by passing the prompt ARN with its version number as the `modelId`. Prompt Management documents no alias or "active version" pointer, so the version identifier should live outside the code, for example in AWS AppConfig, which changes application behaviour in production without redeploying code. Rolling out or reverting is then a configuration change, and both versions can be run and compared. Not "Hard-code the new prompt behind an application feature flag.": A feature flag enables reverting but still requires a code deploy to ship the prompt and provides no managed versioning or evaluation. Not "Raise the temperature so the new prompt is more robust.": Temperature does not provide rollout control, measurement, or rollback. Not "Deploy two Lambda functions, each hard-coding one prompt,…": This is custom, requires code deploys, and lacks managed prompt versioning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-deploy.html

prompt: A workload classifies tens of millions of documents per day in rolling waves; each wave's results are needed by the next business day (not real time). Cost must be minimized. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput sized for the wave peaks.
On-demand real-time invocation for each document.
Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference.
Amazon Bedrock batch inference jobs.

explanation: The work is high-volume and latency-tolerant (next business day), which is exactly what Bedrock batch inference is priced and designed for. Batch jobs run asynchronously, write their results to S3 and are priced 50% below on-demand for supported models. Their timeout cannot be set below 24 hours, so batch fits next-day deadlines rather than a deadline of an hour or two; for latency-tolerant work that still needs an answer per request, the Flex service tier offers discounted on-demand inference in exchange for longer processing times. Not "Provisioned Throughput sized for the wave peaks.": Reserved capacity guarantees throughput but costs more than batch for latency-tolerant bulk work. Not "On-demand real-time invocation for each document.": Per-document real-time calls work but cost more than batch at this volume and are unnecessary given the next-day tolerance. Not "Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference.": Asynchronous inference serves SageMaker-hosted models, not Bedrock foundation models, so it does not apply. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_CreateModelInvocationJob.html

prompt: A team building a Bedrock RAG application wants AWS prescriptive best practices created specifically for generative AI concerns such as RAG accuracy, responsible AI, and model selection. Which resource is the BEST fit?

options.text: The AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens.
The AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens.
The AWS Well-Architected Machine Learning Lens.
The six core Well-Architected pillars alone.

explanation: The Generative AI Lens provides design principles and best practices tailored to generative AI workloads, including RAG and responsible AI. Not "The AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens.": The SaaS Lens targets SaaS business/architecture concerns, not generative AI design. Not "The AWS Well-Architected Machine Learning Lens.": The ML Lens covers the traditional ML lifecycle and is not focused on generative-AI-specific concerns like RAG accuracy and responsible AI for FMs. Not "The six core Well-Architected pillars alone.": The core pillars are general guidance; the GenAI-specific practices live in the Generative AI Lens. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A RAG chatbot includes a 6,000-token static policy preamble in every request. The team wants to cut the cost and latency of that repeated context with minimal change and using the SAME model. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Enable prompt caching for the static preamble so the repeated prefix is reused across requests.
Store the preamble in a knowledge base and retrieve it each call.
Fine-tune the model so the policy is implicit and can be dropped from prompts.
Reduce maxTokens on the response.

explanation: Prompt caching reuses the unchanging prefix, reducing both billed tokens and latency for the repeated context with no model change. Not "Store the preamble in a knowledge base and retrieve it ea…": Retrieval still injects the preamble tokens every call and adds a retrieval step, so it does not cut the repeated-token cost. Not "Fine-tune the model so the policy is implicit and can be …": Fine-tuning changes the model, adds maintenance, and is not a minimal change; it also makes policy updates harder. Not "Reduce maxTokens on the response.": Lowering output length does not reduce the cost of the repeated input preamble. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A customer-facing RAG assistant occasionally produces confident but unsupported answers. The team wants to reduce hallucinations while keeping a good user experience, aligned with the GenAI Lens responsible-AI guidance. Which combination is BEST?

options.text: Add a Guardrails contextual grounding check and instruct the model to answer only from the retrieved context and to say it does not know when the answer is absent.
Switch to a larger model.
Set temperature to 0.
Add a denied-topics policy for the subject area.

explanation: Combining a grounding check with an explicit grounding/abstention instruction is defense-in-depth that targets ungrounded answers directly. Not "Switch to a larger model.": A larger model still hallucinates without grounding controls; size is not a grounding mechanism. Not "Set temperature to 0.": Lower randomness alone does not make an answer grounded in the sources; the model can still confidently fabricate. Not "Add a denied-topics policy for the subject area.": Denied topics block whole subjects; they do not detect or prevent ungrounded answers within an allowed subject. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A bank's assistant must always cite the LATEST internal regulations (which change weekly) AND must CONSISTENTLY emit a strict report template. Which approach meets BOTH with the least ongoing effort?

options.text: Fine-tune the model every week on both the regulations and the template.
Use RAG only, relying on a detailed prompt to enforce the template.
Use continued pre-training on the regulations and a prompt for the template.
Use RAG for the frequently changing regulations and fine-tune the model for the fixed report template/style.

explanation: RAG keeps regulatory content current without retraining, while fine-tuning reliably enforces a rigid output format; each technique handles the part it is best at. Not "Fine-tune the model every week on both the regulations an…": Weekly fine-tuning is operationally heavy and still lags between runs; RAG handles freshness far more cheaply. Not "Use RAG only, relying on a detailed prompt to enforce the…": RAG fixes freshness, but prompt-only formatting is not reliably consistent, which the scenario explicitly requires. Not "Use continued pre-training on the regulations and a promp…": Continued pre-training is for absorbing domain language from large corpora, is heavy, and does not keep weekly content current. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team has a very large corpus of UNLABELED specialized legal text and wants the base model to internalize the domain's vocabulary and patterns. Which customization method is appropriate?

options.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
Continued pre-training on the unlabeled corpus.
Supervised fine-tuning.
Model distillation.

explanation: Continued pre-training adapts a model to domain language using large volumes of unlabeled text. Status note: the Amazon Bedrock user guide now lists supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement fine-tuning and distillation as its customization methods. Continued pre-training was offered in Bedrock for Amazon Titan Text models and `CreateModelCustomizationJob` still accepts `CONTINUED_PRE_TRAINING`, so treat it as a technique the exam can still name rather than a current Bedrock console option. Not "Retrieval-Augmented Generation.": RAG retrieves text at inference time but does not make the model internalize domain language. Not "Supervised fine-tuning.": Fine-tuning requires labeled prompt/response pairs; the corpus is unlabeled, so it does not apply. Not "Model distillation.": Distillation transfers knowledge from a larger teacher model to a smaller student; it is not a method for absorbing a domain corpus. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/custom-models.html

prompt: Latency and cost of a large model are too high, but the team must KEEP its accuracy on their specific task and can accept an upfront training step. Which option BEST fits?

options.text: Enable latency-optimized inference on the large model.
Lower top-k to make the large model cheaper.
Model distillation, training a smaller student from the large teacher on the task.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the large model.

explanation: Distillation produces a smaller, cheaper, faster model that retains much of the teacher's task accuracy, and it explicitly involves an upfront training step. Not "Enable latency-optimized inference on the large model.": Latency-optimized inference speeds responses but does not meaningfully cut the large model's cost and involves no training step. Not "Lower top-k to make the large model cheaper.": Sampling parameters do not change model cost or latency materially. Not "Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the large model.": Provisioned Throughput stabilizes capacity but does not reduce the per-call cost or size of the large model. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Throughput must increase for a steady, predictable, high baseline load running 24/7, at the lowest per-token cost, using the same model and API. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput with a committed term.
On-demand inference with client retries.
Bedrock batch inference.
Cross-Region inference.

explanation: Provisioned Throughput provisions a fixed level of throughput for a model at a fixed hourly price, and the longer the commitment (1 month or 6 months) the more discounted that price, which suits a steady 24/7 load. Status note: Provisioned Throughput can be purchased only for the models on its supported list (Amazon Nova, older Anthropic models up to Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2, Llama 3.1/3.2 and some embedding models). Bedrock also offers a Reserved service tier, which reserves input and output tokens-per-minute capacity for 1 or 3 months at a fixed price. Not "On-demand inference with client retries.": On-demand provisions no capacity, so constant high volume risks throttling, and retries do not add throughput. Not "Bedrock batch inference.": Batch inference is asynchronous and writes results to S3; it cannot serve steady real-time throughput. Not "Cross-Region inference.": Cross-Region inference routes on-demand requests across Regions; it reserves no capacity, and inference profiles do not support Provisioned Throughput. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: To make a model's outputs as deterministic as possible for snapshot tests, which inference setting is the PRIMARY lever?

options.text: Set temperature to 0.
Add several stop sequences.
Use a high temperature with a low maxTokens.
Increase top-k substantially.

explanation: A lower temperature steepens the next-token probability distribution and leads to more deterministic responses, so the minimum value of 0 is the main lever. Lowering top-p (or top-k) is an alternative lever, not an addition: the guidance for Anthropic models on Bedrock is to modify either `temperature` or `top_p`, not both, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5 accept only one of the two in a request. Not "Add several stop sequences.": Stop sequences control where generation ends, not how deterministic the tokens are. Not "Use a high temperature with a low maxTokens.": A higher temperature leads to more random responses; capping length does not make content deterministic. Not "Increase top-k substantially.": A larger top-k widens the candidate pool and allows less likely tokens. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-parameters.html

prompt: A pipeline expects the model to stop generating exactly when it produces the marker END_JSON, and that marker must not appear in the output to keep downstream parsing clean. Which solution is BEST?

options.text: Configure END_JSON as a stop sequence in the inference request.
Set maxTokens to an estimated length.
Instruct the model in the prompt to stop after END_JSON.
Lower the temperature.

explanation: A stop sequence halts generation when the phrase is produced and the stop text itself is not included in the returned output, which keeps parsing clean. Not "Set maxTokens to an estimated length.": A length guess does not stop at the marker and risks cutting content or leaving the marker in. Not "Instruct the model in the prompt to stop after END_JSON.": Prompt instructions are not a reliable stopping mechanism and would leave the marker in the text. Not "Lower the temperature.": Temperature does not control stopping at a specific phrase. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A high-volume pipeline must caption product IMAGES with short text at the lowest cost and latency while still supporting vision. Which Amazon Nova model is BEST?

options.text: Amazon Nova Pro.
Amazon Nova Micro.
Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings.
Amazon Nova Lite.

explanation: Nova Lite is the very-low-cost multimodal Nova model with fast processing for image, video and text inputs, so it is the cheapest fit that still understands images. Not "Amazon Nova Pro.": Nova Pro also understands images but is the highly capable tier, more than short, high-volume captions need. Not "Amazon Nova Micro.": Nova Micro is text-only and cannot process images. Not "Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings.": It accepts images but outputs embeddings for semantic search and similarity matching, not caption text. Status note: Nova Canvas, an image generation model that older versions of this question use as a distractor, reached end-of-life on September 30, 2026. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/nova/latest/userguide/what-is-nova.html

prompt: A team must cut vector-storage cost for a TEXT-ONLY semantic search while keeping good recall, with minimal re-architecture. Which choice is BEST?

options.text: Use Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and select a smaller output dimension.
Increase the embedding dimension to improve accuracy.
Use a text-generation model to produce the embeddings.
Switch to Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings.

explanation: Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports configurable, smaller dimensions that cut index size and cost while keeping acceptable recall, with no architecture change. Not "Increase the embedding dimension to improve accuracy.": Larger dimensions increase storage and cost, the opposite of the goal. Not "Use a text-generation model to produce the embeddings.": Generative models are not embedding models and would not provide a proper vector index. Not "Switch to Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings.": Multimodal embeddings target image+text retrieval and do not reduce storage for a text-only search. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team must compare two models on SUMMARY quality (coherence and relevance) over thousands of documents, automatically, with NO human raters and NO reference summaries available. Which evaluation approach fits?

options.text: Compare the two models' CloudWatch latency metrics.
A human evaluation workflow.
Amazon Bedrock model evaluation with an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator.
Bedrock evaluation using reference-based metrics such as BERTScore or exact match.

explanation: LLM-as-a-judge scores open-ended quality dimensions at scale without humans and without needing reference answers. Not "Compare the two models' CloudWatch latency metrics.": Latency does not measure summary coherence or relevance. Not "A human evaluation workflow.": Human evaluation is excluded by the no-human-raters constraint. Not "Bedrock evaluation using reference-based metrics such as …": Reference-based metrics require ground-truth reference summaries, which are not available here. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team must build ONE codebase that does multi-turn chat WITH tool calling across both Anthropic Claude and Amazon Nova models, minimizing model-specific request/response code. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Build a custom abstraction layer over each model's API.
Use InvokeModelWithResponseStream per model.
Call InvokeModel with each model's native JSON body.
Use the Amazon Bedrock Converse API.

explanation: Converse provides a unified, model-agnostic interface for multi-turn messages and tool use across supported models, minimizing per-model code. Not "Build a custom abstraction layer over each model's API.": A custom layer reinvents what Converse already standardizes. Not "Use InvokeModelWithResponseStream per model.": This still needs model-specific bodies and only adds streaming, not unification. Not "Call InvokeModel with each model's native JSON body.": InvokeModel requires model-specific payloads and parsing, which is exactly the per-model code to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A company fine-tuned open-weights Llama models OUTSIDE AWS (a supported architecture) and wants them callable through the Amazon Bedrock runtime API, on demand, with no servers to run. Which option is correct?

options.text: Buy Provisioned Throughput on a Bedrock base model.
Deploy the weights to a SageMaker real-time endpoint.
Run continued pre-training in Bedrock.
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import.

explanation: Custom Model Import brings supported external weights into Bedrock, where they are invoked through `InvokeModel` with on-demand throughput and no infrastructure for you to run. Not "Buy Provisioned Throughput on a Bedrock base model.": Provisioned Throughput on a base model serves that base model; it does not serve your own imported weights. Not "Deploy the weights to a SageMaker real-time endpoint.": A SageMaker endpoint can serve the model but is not the Bedrock runtime API and requires managing the endpoint. Not "Run continued pre-training in Bedrock.": Continued pre-training further trains a base model on unlabeled data (and is no longer among the customization methods the Bedrock user guide lists); it does not import your externally trained weights. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-import-model.html

prompt: A team wants to grow throughput using cross-Region inference, but compliance requires that all inference data remain within one approved Region. What is the CORRECT stance?

options.text: Enable cross-Region inference; it always keeps data within the source Region's country.
Enable cross-Region inference; the data never leaves the source Region.
Do not use a cross-Region profile that can route outside the approved Region; stay on in-Region on-demand or Provisioned Throughput.
Switch to batch inference to keep data in Region.

explanation: Cross-Region inference can route requests to other Regions in the geography, which would violate single-Region data residency, so it must be avoided for this requirement. Not "Enable cross-Region inference; it always keeps data withi…": Routing targets depend on the profile's geography and are not guaranteed to stay in one country/Region. Not "Enable cross-Region inference; the data never leaves the …": Cross-Region inference can process requests in other Regions, so this statement is incorrect. Not "Switch to batch inference to keep data in Region.": Batch versus real-time is unrelated to the residency guarantee and does not address the throughput requirement correctly. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Users upload SCREENSHOTS OF CHARTS and ask analytical questions about the trends shown. Which approach BEST answers them?

options.text: Use Amazon Textract to extract the chart.
Use Amazon Rekognition to analyze the image.
Send the image to a Bedrock multimodal foundation model via the Converse API.
Use Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings.

explanation: A multimodal FM can interpret the chart's visuals and answer natural-language analytical questions about the trends. Not "Use Amazon Textract to extract the chart.": Textract extracts text and tables from documents but does not reason about a chart's visual trends. Not "Use Amazon Rekognition to analyze the image.": Rekognition returns labels/objects, not analytical answers about chart trends. Not "Use Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings.": Multimodal embeddings support retrieval/similarity, not question answering about an image. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A Bedrock foundation model must process a very large OFFLINE job over millions of prompts at the lowest cost; getting the results within a day is fine. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput.
Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference.
Amazon Bedrock batch inference (a model invocation job).
A loop of on-demand InvokeModel calls.

explanation: Batch inference is purpose-built for large, latency-tolerant offline workloads on Bedrock FMs at the lowest cost. Batch jobs run asynchronously, write their results to S3 and are priced 50% below on-demand for supported models. Their timeout cannot be set below 24 hours, so batch fits next-day deadlines rather than a deadline of an hour or two; for latency-tolerant work that still needs an answer per request, the Flex service tier offers discounted on-demand inference in exchange for longer processing times. Not "Provisioned Throughput.": Reserved online capacity is not the cheapest way to run a one-off offline bulk job. Not "Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference.": Asynchronous inference serves SageMaker-hosted models, not Bedrock foundation models, so it does not apply. Not "A loop of on-demand InvokeModel calls.": Real-time calls in a loop cost more than a batch job for millions of prompts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_CreateModelInvocationJob.html

prompt: A team has only about 30 examples of a desired behavior and needs better adherence quickly; collecting thousands of labeled examples is not feasible. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Use few-shot prompting that includes the example demonstrations.
Distill the model.
Run continued pre-training.
Fine-tune the model on the 30 examples.

explanation: Few-shot prompting leverages a handful of examples immediately and is the right tool when labeled data is scarce. Not "Distill the model.": Distillation addresses cost/latency, not teaching a behavior from a few examples. Not "Run continued pre-training.": Continued pre-training needs a large unlabeled corpus, not 30 examples. Not "Fine-tune the model on the 30 examples.": Roughly 30 examples are generally too few to fine-tune effectively and risk overfitting with little gain. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A summarizer sometimes truncates mid-sentence, but the team also wants to prevent runaway, overly long outputs. Which TWO settings TOGETHER best address both? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a stop sequence at the natural end-of-answer marker.
Lower the temperature.
Increase maxTokens enough to fit a complete answer.
Increase top-k.
Enlarge the model's context window.

explanation: A stop sequence ends generation cleanly at the intended boundary, preventing runaway length. Mid-sentence truncation means the output is hitting the token cap, so raising maxTokens to a sufficient size lets answers complete. Not "Lower the temperature.": Temperature affects randomness, not truncation or maximum length. Not "Increase top-k.": Top-k changes token diversity, not output length. Not "Enlarge the model's context window.": The context window governs input size, not how long the output may be. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: Before fine-tuning on customer chat transcripts, a team must programmatically REMOVE PII from the free text of a large set of transcript files in Amazon S3, as a batch job. Which service is the right tool?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails sensitive-information filter.
Amazon Comprehend PII detection and redaction.
Amazon Macie.
Amazon Textract.

explanation: Comprehend can run an asynchronous batch job over a collection of documents and return a copy of the text with each PII entity redacted, producing sanitized transcripts for training. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails sensitive-information filter.": Guardrails can mask PII, and the `ApplyGuardrail` API works on any text without invoking a model, but it assesses only the text sent in each call. It is not a batch job over files in S3, so the team would have to build that pipeline around it. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data across S3 but does not redact PII inside text for downstream training. Not "Amazon Textract.": Textract extracts text from documents; it does not detect or redact PII. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/how-pii.html

prompt: A governance team must INVENTORY where PII resides across 500 Amazon S3 buckets before deciding how to process it. Which service fits BEST?

options.text: Amazon Macie.
Amazon Comprehend.
Amazon S3 Inventory.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

explanation: Macie is built to discover and classify sensitive data and PII across S3 at scale, producing the inventory the team needs. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend analyzes and redacts PII within individual text inputs but is not a bucket-scale discovery/classification inventory tool. Not "Amazon S3 Inventory.": S3 Inventory lists objects and metadata but does not classify which contain PII. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.": Guardrails govern model I/O at inference; they do not scan storage for sensitive data. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team needs human-labeled instruction/response pairs with a managed workforce option and built-in quality controls (annotation consolidation). Which service is BEST?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend custom classification.
Raw Amazon Mechanical Turk tasks.
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth.

explanation: Ground Truth provides managed labeling workflows, workforce options, and quality features such as annotation consolidation. Not "Amazon Comprehend custom classification.": Comprehend automates classification; it is not a human-labeling service for creating new pairs. Not "Raw Amazon Mechanical Turk tasks.": Mechanical Turk supplies a crowd but lacks the managed labeling workflow, templates, and consolidation that Ground Truth adds. Not "Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.": Data Wrangler transforms tabular data; it does not run human annotation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Millions of raw JSON documents must be cleaned, normalized, and partitioned every night as a repeatable, serverless production pipeline with the least operational overhead. Which service is BEST?

options.text: An Amazon EMR Spark cluster.
AWS Glue serverless ETL jobs.
One AWS Lambda invocation per file.
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.

explanation: Glue runs scheduled, serverless Spark ETL for large-scale cleaning/partitioning with no clusters to manage. Not "An Amazon EMR Spark cluster.": EMR is capable but requires provisioning and managing cluster capacity. Not "One AWS Lambda invocation per file.": Per-file Lambda processing is hard to orchestrate at this scale and hits timeout limits. Not "Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.": Data Wrangler is an interactive, notebook-oriented prep tool, not a hands-off serverless nightly production pipeline at this scale. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A developer must provide a SUPERVISED fine-tuning dataset to Amazon Bedrock. What is the correct format and location?

options.text: An Amazon DynamoDB table of examples.
A JSONL file of prompt/completion (or messages) examples in Amazon S3 matching the model's schema.
A CSV export of raw documents in S3.
A folder of PDFs in S3.

explanation: Bedrock customization reads labeled examples as JSONL records from S3 in the required schema. Not "An Amazon DynamoDB table of examples.": Fine-tuning reads from S3 in the required file format, not from DynamoDB. Not "A CSV export of raw documents in S3.": Raw documents are not labeled prompt/response pairs; this is not a supervised fine-tuning dataset. Not "A folder of PDFs in S3.": An unstructured PDF corpus suits RAG ingestion, not supervised fine-tuning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team must measure representation imbalance in the TRAINING DATASET before any training begins. Which capability is correct?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.
Amazon SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics.
Amazon SageMaker Clarify post-training bias metrics.
Amazon Comprehend.

explanation: Clarify computes pre-training bias metrics directly on the dataset before training. Not "Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.": Model Monitor detects drift on a deployed endpoint, not dataset bias before training. Not "Amazon SageMaker Clarify post-training bias metrics.": Post-training metrics evaluate a trained model's predictions, not the dataset before training. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend performs NLP tasks, not dataset bias measurement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A governance team must publish a standardized, human-readable record of each model's intended use, training data, evaluation, and risk rating for audits. Which feature is BEST?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards.
AWS CloudTrail.
Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking.
AWS Config.

explanation: Model Cards capture intended use, training details, evaluation, and risk in a standardized, versioned, auditable document. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail logs API activity, not model governance documentation. Not "Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking.": Lineage tracking records artifact/step graphs automatically; it is not the human-readable governance document of intended use and risk. Not "AWS Config.": Config tracks resource configuration compliance, not model documentation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team must AUTOMATICALLY track which dataset version and which processing job produced a given model artifact, as a queryable lineage graph. Which capability is correct?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Amazon SageMaker Model Cards.
Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking.
AWS CloudTrail.

explanation: ML Lineage Tracking automatically records the entities and relationships (datasets, jobs, models) as a queryable lineage graph. Not "AWS Glue Data Catalog.": The Data Catalog inventories data sources; it does not track model-artifact lineage. Not "Amazon SageMaker Model Cards.": Model Cards are a manually authored governance document, not an automatic artifact-lineage graph. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API calls, not a model-artifact lineage graph. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team is preparing a fine-tuning dataset and wants to minimize overfitting and train/test leakage. Which TWO steps best support this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Include the evaluation questions in the training set for coverage.
Increase the number of training epochs.
Deduplicate near-duplicate examples.
Create a held-out test split that does not overlap the training data.
Oversample the majority class to grow the dataset.

explanation: Removing duplicates prevents the model from overweighting repeated samples and reduces overfitting. A non-overlapping evaluation split prevents leakage and gives an honest generalization estimate. Not "Include the evaluation questions in the training set for …": Putting test items into training is textbook data leakage. Not "Increase the number of training epochs.": Epoch count is a training hyperparameter, not a data-preparation step, and more epochs can overfit. Not "Oversample the majority class to grow the dataset.": Oversampling the majority worsens imbalance and encourages overfitting. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A Bedrock knowledge base needs a fully managed vector store for HIGH query-per-second, LOW-latency similarity search with no capacity planning. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.
Amazon Neptune Analytics.
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.
Amazon S3 Vectors.

explanation: OpenSearch Serverless is the natively integrated, auto-scaling managed vector store suited to frequent, low-latency queries without capacity planning. Not "Amazon Neptune Analytics.": Neptune Analytics powers GraphRAG over relationships, not general high-QPS vector search. Not "Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.": Aurora pgvector is supported but you size and manage the database instance; it is not the auto-scaling serverless choice for high QPS. Not "Amazon S3 Vectors.": S3 Vectors optimizes cost for infrequent queries at huge scale, not high-QPS low-latency search. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A corpus of billions of embeddings is queried only a few times per month for occasional investigations. The team wants the lowest-cost durable vector storage with no capacity to manage. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.
Amazon DynamoDB.
Amazon S3 Vectors.
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.

explanation: S3 Vectors gives cost-optimized, pay-for-what-you-use vector storage and search (up to 2 billion vectors per index, many indexes per vector bucket) and is ideal for workloads where queries are infrequent. Not "Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.": OpenSearch Serverless targets high query rates and low-latency search; for a large corpus that is rarely queried, S3 Vectors is the cost-optimized store. (Next-generation OpenSearch Serverless, announced May 28, 2026, can scale to zero when idle, so the older argument about paying for idle capacity applies only to Classic collections.) Not "Amazon DynamoDB.": DynamoDB has native vector search since August 2026, but it is built for real-time, single-digit-millisecond lookups; S3 Vectors is the store AWS positions for lowest-cost, rarely queried vectors. Not "Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.": Aurora requires running instances and is not the lowest-cost option for rarely queried, very large vector sets. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/s3-vectors.html

prompt: Embeddings must live ALONGSIDE existing relational records in the SAME managed PostgreSQL database for transactional consistency, with minimal new technology. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.
Amazon Neptune Analytics.
Amazon S3 Vectors.
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension.

explanation: Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector keeps vectors next to relational data in one transactional database with familiar tooling. Not "Amazon OpenSearch Serverless.": OpenSearch Serverless is excellent for vectors but is a separate system with no transactional co-location with the relational data. Not "Amazon Neptune Analytics.": Neptune is a graph store, not a relational+vector database. Not "Amazon S3 Vectors.": S3 Vectors is a separate, non-transactional store and cannot co-locate with relational records. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Answering a question requires MULTI-HOP reasoning over relationships among connected entities, not just similarity to text. Which knowledge base option is BEST?

options.text: A vector-only knowledge base with more results returned.
A structured-data (text-to-SQL) knowledge base.
A knowledge base using GraphRAG with Amazon Neptune Analytics.
Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.

explanation: GraphRAG builds an entity-relationship graph that supports multi-hop reasoning over connections. Not "A vector-only knowledge base with more results returned.": Returning more similar chunks does not provide explicit multi-hop relationship traversal. Not "A structured-data (text-to-SQL) knowledge base.": Structured-data retrieval handles tabular aggregation, not entity-to-entity multi-hop reasoning. Not "Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector.": pgvector does similarity search, not graph multi-hop reasoning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Business users ask natural-language questions that require SUMS and aggregations over an Amazon Redshift warehouse, and the assistant should generate and run the queries. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Dashboards in Amazon Quick Sight (formerly Amazon QuickSight).
A GraphRAG knowledge base on Neptune Analytics.
Embed each table row as a vector and use similarity search.
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with structured data retrieval (text-to-SQL).

explanation: A knowledge base connected to a structured data store converts the natural-language question into a SQL query, runs it to retrieve the data, and can generate a response from the result, so aggregations are computed by the warehouse. Not "Dashboards in Amazon Quick Sight (formerly Amazon QuickSight).": Quick Sight is the business intelligence feature of Amazon Quick for data visualization and dashboards; it is not the knowledge base path that turns the assistant's questions into SQL. Not "A GraphRAG knowledge base on Neptune Analytics.": GraphRAG reasons over relationships, not tabular aggregation. Not "Embed each table row as a vector and use similarity search.": Vector similarity over rows cannot compute sums or precise aggregations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-build-structured.html

prompt: A developer must fetch the top relevant chunks and then run them through their OWN prompt and a model NOT wired into the knowledge base. Which API is correct?

options.text: The RetrieveAndGenerate API.
The Retrieve API.
The RetrieveAndGenerateStream API.
The StartIngestionJob API.

explanation: Retrieve returns ranked chunks only, leaving the prompt and generation model fully under the developer's control. Not "The RetrieveAndGenerate API.": RetrieveAndGenerate does accept a custom prompt template (`promptTemplate.textPromptTemplate`) and a model of your choice as `modelArn`, but it always runs the generation step itself inside Amazon Bedrock, so it cannot hand the chunks to your own code or to a model the knowledge base cannot call. Not "The RetrieveAndGenerateStream API.": This is the streaming form of RetrieveAndGenerate, so it also performs the generation itself. Not "The StartIngestionJob API.": StartIngestionJob ingests data; it does not retrieve chunks for a query. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: An app must show end users the exact source passages behind each answer with the LEAST custom development. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Ask the model in the prompt to list its sources.
Use Retrieve, then build custom generation and citation-mapping code.
Use RetrieveAndGenerate, which returns the answer with citations to the source chunks.
Enable model invocation logging and surface the logs.

explanation: RetrieveAndGenerate produces a grounded answer plus citations with no custom attribution code. Not "Ask the model in the prompt to list its sources.": Self-reported sources are unreliable and not verifiable citations. Not "Use Retrieve, then build custom generation and citation-m…": This works but adds the custom generation and citation code the requirement wants to avoid. Not "Enable model invocation logging and surface the logs.": Invocation logs are operator data, not user-facing citations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS uses one shared knowledge base and must GUARANTEE that a tenant can never retrieve another tenant's documents. Which design is the most secure and reliable?

options.text: Pass the tenant filter from the client and trust it.
Rely on relevance ranking to keep tenants separate.
Instruct the model in the system prompt to stay within the tenant.
Tag documents with tenant ID and apply a metadata filter derived from the authenticated tenant on every Retrieve call (or use a separate knowledge base per tenant).

explanation: A server-side filter bound to the verified identity (or full per-tenant isolation) reliably prevents cross-tenant retrieval. Not "Pass the tenant filter from the client and trust it.": A client-supplied, untrusted filter can be tampered with to reach other tenants' data. Not "Rely on relevance ranking to keep tenants separate.": Ranking can still surface another tenant's documents; it is not an isolation control.
