Tracing across service boundaries is the documented approach for observability in composed GenAI applications. Not "CloudWatch alarms on the p99 latency of each individual service...": per-service alarms tell you a service is slow in aggregate, not that it caused this request's latency. Not "Model invocation logging...Athena query...": that covers only the Bedrock call and says nothing about the other four hops. Not "A CloudWatch dashboard showing each service's average latency...": averages hide the tail, and visual comparison does not correlate hops within one request. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring.html

prompt: A team runs a RAG evaluation and finds a high rate of unsupported claims in generated answers. They want the system itself to block such answers at runtime, with a tunable sensitivity they can set from the evaluation data. What should they configure?

options.text: A Guardrails denied topics policy, listing the subject areas in which unsupported claims were observed during evaluation.
A Guardrails word filter, populated with the specific phrases that appeared in the unsupported claims during evaluation.
A Guardrails contextual grounding policy, with grounding and relevance thresholds tuned against the evaluation results.
A Guardrails sensitive information filter, configured to block responses containing entities absent from the source documents.

explanation: Contextual grounding checks compare the model's response against the retrieved source material and the user's query, and block responses whose grounding or relevance scores fall below configurable thresholds. Evaluation data is exactly what you use to pick those thresholds. Not "A Guardrails denied topics policy...": denied topics blocks subject areas regardless of whether a claim is supported; unsupported claims are a grounding problem, not a topic problem. Not "A Guardrails sensitive information filter...": that detects and redacts PII and similar sensitive entities, not ungrounded assertions. Not "A Guardrails word filter...": blocklists catch known strings; hallucinated claims are novel text by nature. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html

prompt: A downstream system requires strictly valid JSON matching a fixed schema. Parsing currently fails on a small percentage of responses because the model wraps the JSON in prose or omits a field. Which approach most reliably enforces the contract?

options.text: Post-process with a regular expression that extracts the first JSON object found anywhere in the response body.
Use Amazon Bedrock structured outputs: supply the JSON schema in the request (Converse `outputConfig.textFormat`), or define the output as a tool marked `strict: true`.
Use a Guardrails policy that blocks any response which fails JSON schema validation before returning it to the caller.
Append "Return only valid JSON and nothing else" to the system prompt and set the temperature to 0 for all calls.

explanation: Structured outputs ensure the model response conforms to the JSON schema you supply (`outputConfig.textFormat` in Converse), and `strict: true` on a tool definition makes tool calls follow the tool input schema. That turns a formatting request into an enforced contract; a tool definition without `strict` only describes the schema. Not "...to the system prompt and set the temperature to 0 for all calls": prompt instructions plus greedy decoding reduce the failure rate but guarantee nothing, which is the situation the team is already in. Not "Post-process with a regular expression...": extraction may recover the wrapped-in-prose case, but it cannot supply a field the model omitted. Not "Use a Guardrails policy that blocks any response which fails JSON schema validation...": Guardrails evaluates content safety policies; it does not perform JSON schema validation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/structured-output.html

prompt: An evaluation of an agent must report how often it finishes the user's task, not merely whether each individual model call returned successfully. Which measurement framework is appropriate?

options.text: Mean tokens consumed per session, tracked over time and compared against the baseline recorded before the change.
Task completion rate over a suite of representative goals, combined with tool-usage correctness along each trajectory.
The ratio of successful HTTP responses to total invocations across the agent's action group Lambda functions.
The proportion of sessions in which the agent produced a final response before reaching its configured iteration limit.

explanation: Agent quality is an end-to-end property. Task completion rate over representative goals measures whether the agent achieved what the user wanted, and examining the trajectory tells you whether it selected and used the right tools to get there - the pair of measures the exam guide names for agent performance frameworks. Not "The ratio of successful HTTP responses...": every tool call can return HTTP 200 while the agent still fails the task. Not "Mean tokens consumed per session...": an efficiency metric that says nothing about correctness. Not "The proportion of sessions in which the agent produced a final response before reaching its configured iteration limit": not hitting the ceiling is not the same as succeeding. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-test.html

prompt: A team maintains several prompt versions in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management and needs to know which version a given production response came from when investigating a quality complaint. What should they do?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail so that each prompt invocation records the full prompt text used for that particular request.
Store every prompt version in Amazon S3 with versioning enabled and reconcile against response timestamps afterwards.
Invoke a specific prompt version by its identifier and record that identifier alongside each response in application logs.
Invoke the prompt by name so the latest draft is always used, and rely on the Prompt Management change history for attribution.

explanation: Prompt Management versions prompts so a specific, immutable version can be invoked by identifier. Logging that identifier with each response gives you exact attribution at investigation time - the basis for prompt version comparison and regression analysis. Not "Invoke the prompt by name so the latest draft is always used...": if production always follows the moving draft, you cannot reconstruct what a past response actually used. Not "Store every prompt version in Amazon S3...reconcile against response timestamps": timestamp reconciliation is fragile and breaks around deployments, which is when you need it most. Not "Enable CloudTrail so that each prompt invocation records the full prompt text...": CloudTrail records API activity, never prompt payloads. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Six months after launch, a RAG assistant's retrieval quality has degraded on newer queries, though no code or configuration changed. The corpus has grown and now uses product names and terminology that did not exist at launch. What is the most likely cause and the right investigation?

options.text: Vector index fragmentation caused by continual incremental ingestion; rebuild the index from scratch and re-run the retrieval tests.
Gradual expiry of cached embeddings for older documents; re-ingest the full corpus so all embeddings are regenerated.
Query and content drift against a fixed embedding space; re-measure retrieval on a refreshed golden query set and reassess the embedding model.
Silent model deprecation of the generator model; pin an explicit model version and re-run the retrieval evaluation.

explanation: The corpus and the query distribution have both moved while the embedding space stayed fixed - the standard drift failure mode. The disciplined response is to measure it: refresh the golden query set with current terminology, re-run retrieval evaluation, and decide from the numbers whether the embedding model still fits the domain. Not "Vector index fragmentation...": index maintenance can affect latency; it does not make semantically correct matches stop matching. Not "Gradual expiry of cached embeddings...": stored embeddings do not expire. Not "Silent model deprecation of the generator model...": the symptom is in retrieval, which happens before the generator is involved. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A product team already runs offline evaluation and automated LLM-as-a-judge scoring on a sample of production traffic. They now want direct feedback from end users on real responses, in a form that lets them trace a poor rating back to its cause and prioritize fixes. Which mechanism should they build?

options.text: A second automated LLM-as-a-judge job scoring a larger random daily sample of production responses, with no human input in the loop.
A per-response rating and comment interface, with ratings stored alongside the request identifier, prompt version and retrieved sources.
A CloudWatch alarm on the assistant's error rate, so degradations in quality surface as operational alerts to the team.
A monthly survey emailed to active users asking them to rate the assistant's overall helpfulness on a five-point scale.

explanation: Inline per-response feedback captured with the context that produced the response - request identifier, prompt version, retrieved sources - is what lets you trace a bad rating back to a cause and prioritize the fix. That linkage is the point; a rating with no context is not actionable. Not "A monthly survey emailed to active users...": aggregate periodic sentiment cannot be attributed to specific responses or changes. Not "A CloudWatch alarm on the assistant's error rate...": errors and quality are different failure classes; a confidently wrong answer is not an error. Not "An automated LLM-as-a-judge job...with no human input in the loop": automated scoring is already in place; more of it adds no direct end-user feedback. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-human.html

prompt: A nightly deployment pipeline updates the model version behind a customer-facing assistant. The team wants automated validation that catches GenAI-specific regressions before traffic shifts, beyond checking that the endpoint returns HTTP 200. Which validation should gate the rollout?

options.text: Synthetic user workflows whose outputs are scored for hallucination rate and consistency against a reference set, gating promotion.
A canary that shifts 10% of traffic to the new version and rolls back automatically if the 5xx error rate exceeds a threshold.
A smoke test asserting that the new model version returns a non-empty response for one representative prompt.
A load test that confirms the new model version sustains the expected requests per second at the target p99 latency.

explanation: The regressions that matter here are semantic - hallucination rate, response drift, inconsistency - and none of them show up as an error code. Running synthetic workflows and scoring their outputs against a reference set is the AI-specific deployment validation the exam guide describes, and it is the only option that can fail a build for being wrong rather than broken. Not "A load test...": performance validation, orthogonal to output quality. Not "A smoke test asserting...a non-empty response...": a non-empty wrong answer passes. Not "A canary that shifts 10% of traffic to the new version...if the 5xx error rate exceeds a threshold": canarying is good practice, but a 5xx-based trigger is blind to a model that answers fluently and incorrectly. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html

prompt: Which TWO findings from a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation would specifically indicate that the problem lies in generation rather than retrieval? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Low faithfulness scores, indicating the response asserts information that is not present in the retrieved context.
Low context relevance scores, indicating the retrieved passages do not address the intent of the query.
High retrieval latency at p95, indicating the vector search is returning candidates more slowly than the target.
Low completeness scores while the retrieved context demonstrably contains all the information the question required.
Low context coverage scores, indicating the retrieved passages omit much of the expected ground truth material.

explanation: Faithfulness and completeness are both properties of the generated response given its context. Low faithfulness means the generator went beyond its context; low completeness with demonstrably sufficient context means the generator failed to use what it was given. Both indict generation. Not "Low context relevance scores...": that is a retrieval precision problem. Not "Low context coverage scores...": that is a retrieval recall problem. Not "High retrieval latency at p95...": a performance symptom in the retrieval path, unrelated to output quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A team must evaluate a RAG system that runs entirely outside AWS, using their own retriever and their own self-hosted model, but they want Amazon Bedrock's scored RAG metrics and report. Is this possible, and how?

options.text: Yes: point the RAG evaluation job at the external retriever's endpoint, and Bedrock will call it directly during the job.
Yes: bring your own inference response data into a RAG evaluation job, and Bedrock scores the supplied retrievals and responses.
No: RAG evaluation jobs can only score an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base, so the corpus would first have to be ingested into one.
No: external systems must be evaluated with an LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation job, which has no RAG-specific metrics.

explanation: RAG evaluation jobs accept your own inference response data from an external RAG source, in both retrieve-only and retrieve-and-generate modes. Bedrock skips the invocation step and scores the data you supply, so the metrics and report are available without moving the system onto AWS. Not "No: RAG evaluation jobs can only score an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base...": external RAG sources are explicitly supported. Not "Yes: point the RAG evaluation job at the external retriever's endpoint...": Bedrock does not call arbitrary external retrievers; you supply the data. Not "No: external systems must be evaluated with an LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation job...": judge-based model evaluation also accepts bring-your-own response data, so the premise is wrong twice over. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A team needs a metric that specifically detects whether a model declines to answer prompts it should be able to handle, after a Guardrails configuration change appeared to make the assistant overly cautious. Which built-in LLM-as-a-judge metric targets this?

options.text: Builtin.Refusal, which determines whether the response declines to answer or rejects the request with reasons.
Builtin.FollowingInstructions, which measures how closely the response respects the directions given in the prompt.
Builtin.Helpfulness, which measures how useful the response is, including coherence and anticipation of user needs.
Builtin.Harmfulness, which evaluates whether the response contains content that could be considered harmful.

explanation: Builtin.Refusal is defined precisely as detecting responses that decline to answer or reject the request - the direct measure of over-refusal after a safety configuration change. Not "Builtin.Harmfulness...": it scores harmful content in the output, the opposite failure from over-caution. Not "Builtin.FollowingInstructions...": a refusal can be scored as instruction-following if the instructions permit declining, so it does not isolate the behavior. Not "Builtin.Helpfulness...": a refusal would drag helpfulness down, but so would a dozen other defects, making it a lagging and non-specific signal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-metrics.html

prompt: An LLM-as-a-judge evaluation must score responses against a company-specific rubric - adherence to an internal style guide and correct use of regulated product terminology - that no built-in metric covers. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Run a human evaluation job, because judge-model evaluations support only the built-in metric set that Bedrock provides.
Define a custom metric with your own judge prompt and rating scale, and run the evaluation job with a supported evaluator model.
Run the job with Builtin.ProfessionalStyleAndTone, which can be parameterized with the company's own style guide as input.
Fine-tune the evaluator model on the style guide first, then run a standard built-in-metric evaluation against it.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock supports custom metrics for judge-based evaluations: you author the prompt that instructs the evaluator model and define the rating scale, then run the job with one of the evaluator models that supports custom metrics. That is the supported path for a bespoke rubric. Not "Run the job with Builtin.ProfessionalStyleAndTone...parameterized with the company's own style guide": built-in metrics use fixed prompts and take no rubric parameter. Not "Run a human evaluation job, because judge-model evaluations support only the built-in metric set": the premise is false - custom metrics exist. Not "Fine-tune the evaluator model on the style guide first...": evaluation jobs do not require or expect a fine-tuned judge, and this is far more effort than authoring a metric prompt. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-custom-metrics-create-job.html

prompt: A knowledge base ingestion job reports partial success: most documents ingest, a subset consistently fails, and the team needs to know which documents failed and why. Where should they look?

options.text: The Amazon S3 server access logs for the data source bucket, which show which objects the service failed to read.
The CloudTrail event for the StartIngestionJob call, which includes the list of documents that the job was unable to process.
The knowledge base ingestion job's CloudWatch logs, which record per-document failure reasons for the data source sync.
The Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs, which record the embedding calls that failed during the ingestion job.

explanation: Knowledge base data source sync emits per-document ingestion results to CloudWatch Logs, including the reason a given document failed - unsupported format, size limit, parsing error. That is the designed troubleshooting surface for partial ingestion failures. Not "The CloudTrail event for the StartIngestionJob call...": CloudTrail records that the job was started and by whom, not per-document outcomes. Not "The Amazon S3 server access logs...": those show request-level access to objects, which does not explain a parsing or format rejection after a successful read. Not "The Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs...": ingestion embedding calls are not what invocation logging surfaces for this purpose, and a format rejection never reaches the embedding step. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-ingestion-monitoring.html

prompt: Which TWO practices best isolate whether a quality regression after a release came from the prompt change or the model version change, when both shipped together? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Re-run the golden dataset with the previous prompt against the new model version, holding everything else constant.
Increase the golden dataset size so that the combined effect of both changes is measured with tighter confidence intervals.
Compare the p95 latency of the new release against the previous release across the same production traffic mix.
Re-run the golden dataset with the new prompt against the previous model version, holding everything else constant.
Re-run the golden dataset with the new prompt and new model at temperature 0 to remove sampling as a variable.

explanation: Isolating a confounded change means varying one factor at a time. Running new prompt with old model, and old prompt with new model, against the same golden dataset attributes the regression to whichever cell reproduces it - the standard controlled comparison. Not "...new prompt and new model at temperature 0...": reducing sampling variance is good hygiene but still measures both changes together. Not "Compare the p95 latency...": latency is not the regression being investigated. Not "Increase the golden dataset size...": a tighter estimate of the combined effect still does not decompose it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html

prompt: A team must monitor a production assistant for a rise in hallucination rate over time, and be alerted when it degrades, without a human reading every response. Which approach is workable at production volume?

options.text: Route every production response through a human review queue, and alarm when reviewers flag more responses than the baseline rate.
Score a continuous random sample of production traffic with an automated grounding or faithfulness check, and alarm on the trend.
Alarm on the rate of change in average output token count, which rises when the model begins fabricating extra detail.
Alarm on the count of Guardrails interventions, which rises in proportion to the rate of hallucinated content in responses.

explanation: Continuous sampling with an automated grounding or faithfulness scorer, trended over time and alarmed on, is the production-scale way to watch hallucination rate - it costs a fraction of full coverage while still detecting a shift in the population. Not "Route every production response through a human review queue...": full human review does not scale to production volume and adds unacceptable latency. Not "Alarm on the count of Guardrails interventions...": interventions count blocked policy violations, which is a different population from ungrounded claims - unless contextual grounding is configured to block, and even then it measures blocks rather than rate. Not "Alarm on the rate of change in average output token count...": output length is not a hallucination signal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html

prompt: An agent deployed on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore must be debugged in production: the team needs per-session traces of the agent's execution path, plus token usage and error rates, and wants the data in their existing OpenTelemetry-based monitoring stack. What should they rely on?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging, which records each agent session's spans and token counts into Amazon S3.
AWS X-Ray active tracing configured on the AgentCore runtime, which is the only supported way to capture agent spans.
AgentCore Observability, which emits OTEL-compatible telemetry and stores spans, metrics and logs in Amazon CloudWatch.
AWS CloudTrail with data events enabled for AgentCore, which records each agent step as an auditable API event.

explanation: AgentCore Observability provides built-in metrics, spans and logs for agent, gateway and memory resources, stores them in CloudWatch, and emits them in standardized OpenTelemetry-compatible format specifically so they can be consumed by an existing observability stack. Session count, latency, duration, token usage and error rates are among the built-in metrics. Not "AWS CloudTrail with data events enabled for AgentCore...": CloudTrail is an audit record of API activity, not an execution-path trace. Not "Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging...records each agent session's spans...": invocation logging captures model request and response payloads; it does not produce spans. Not "AWS X-Ray active tracing...the only supported way to capture agent spans": AgentCore emits its own telemetry natively, so X-Ray is not required and is certainly not the only path. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability.html

prompt: A German health insurer is designing a claims-summarisation service in eu-central-1 on Amazon Bedrock. The chosen model can be invoked from eu-central-1 only through an inference profile. Regulators require that prompts and responses are processed only in AWS Regions inside the EU. Traffic is unpredictable, and the company wants to pay per token. The organisation's service control policy (SCP) denies every action whose aws:RequestedRegion is not eu-central-1, and the security team will not let any other service be used outside eu-central-1. Which combination of design decisions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Call the model through its global inference profile so that requests can draw on capacity in every supported commercial Region.
Call the model through its EU geographic inference profile, and allow the role to invoke the profile and the model in each destination Region.
Extend the list of allowed Regions in the SCP so that it includes every destination Region that the inference profile can route requests to from eu-central-1.
Add an exception to the Region deny in the SCP that applies only when bedrock:InferenceProfileArn matches the chosen inference profile.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model in eu-central-1, and invoke the provisioned model ARN instead of an inference profile.

explanation: A geographic inference profile keeps processing inside its geography, so the EU profile satisfies the residency rule while still spreading unpredictable traffic over several Regions at on-demand, per-token prices. The role needs bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile in the source Region and on the foundation model in the source and every destination Region. Because the SCP allows only eu-central-1, routing to the other EU Regions would be denied; AWS documents that bedrock:InferenceProfileArn is populated on the foundation-model evaluations, so a Region-deny SCP can exempt cross-Region routing for that profile without opening those Regions to other services. The option to use the "global inference profile" fails the residency rule, because requests can be processed in any supported commercial Region worldwide. The option to "extend the list of allowed Regions" would make inference work, but it also lets every other service run in those Regions, which the security team forbids. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput" fails twice: the model is reachable here only through an inference profile, and inference profiles do not support Provisioned Throughput; it is also billed hourly rather than per token. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/geographic-cross-region-inference.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cross-region-inference.html

prompt: A logistics company has three weeks to run a proof of concept for three generative AI use cases: shipment-delay emails, customs-form extraction and a driver FAQ. All three call the same Amazon Bedrock model with on-demand inference from one AWS account in us-east-1, at a few hundred requests a day. Before funding a full build, the finance team wants to see the model spend of each use case separately in AWS Cost Explorer, and the engineering lead wants usage metrics per use case. The company wants to keep paying only for the tokens it uses and does not want to change its account structure. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Purchase a no-commitment Provisioned Throughput for each use case, tag each provisioned model, and delete all three when the proof of concept ends.
Create one member account per use case in AWS Organizations, and run each use case in its own account so that costs group by linked account.
Create one application inference profile per use case from the model, tag each profile, and invoke the model with the profile ARN as the model ID.
Enable model invocation logging, pass the use-case name in requestMetadata, and compute the spend per use case with a scheduled Logs Insights query.

explanation: An application inference profile is a user-created profile whose purpose is tracking cost and usage. Each profile is created from the foundation model (or from a cross-Region profile), carries its own tags, and is used by passing its ARN as the model ID in InvokeModel or Converse. Once the tag is activated as a cost allocation tag, on-demand spend appears per use case in Cost Explorer, and usage metrics can be viewed per profile. Pricing stays on-demand, and nothing about the account changes. "Purchase a no-commitment Provisioned Throughput" is billed by the hour for every model unit whether or not requests arrive, so it abandons pay-per-token for a workload of a few hundred requests a day. "Create one member account per use case" would separate the costs, but it changes the account structure, which the company ruled out. "Enable model invocation logging" with requestMetadata does give per-use-case token counts, but the spend is then a number the team calculates and maintains itself; it does not show up as cost in Cost Explorer, which is what finance asked for. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles-create.html

prompt: A platform team supports 40 product teams that each build generative AI workloads on Amazon Bedrock in their own AWS accounts. Architecture reviews are done in slide decks today, and every team interprets best practices differently. The platform team wants every workload reviewed against AWS best practices for generative AI and against 14 internal questions (for example, whether the company's mandatory guardrail is attached). Each review must produce a list of risks with an improvement plan, must be repeatable in every account, and must show progress between quarterly reviews. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST custom development?

options.text: In the AWS Well-Architected Tool, apply the Generative AI Lens from the Lens Catalog, add the internal questions as a shared custom lens, and save milestones.
In the AWS Well-Architected Tool, edit the Generative AI Lens in the Lens Catalog to add the 14 internal questions, and apply the edited lens at each quarterly review.
Publish an approved reference architecture as an AWS Service Catalog product, and treat a successful launch of the product in a team account as the completed review.
In the AWS Well-Architected Tool, apply only the default Framework lens to each workload, and record the generative AI and internal answers in the notes fields.

explanation: The AWS Well-Architected Tool applies lenses to a workload, and each lens has its own questions, best practices and improvement plan. The Generative AI Lens is an official lens in the Lens Catalog, available to every account with nothing to install. Company-specific questions belong in a custom lens, which has its own pillars, questions and improvement plan and can be shared with other accounts, and milestones record the state of a workload so that progress is visible from one review to the next. That covers all four requirements with no code. The option to "edit the Generative AI Lens in the Lens Catalog" relies on something the tool does not offer: catalog lenses are created and maintained by AWS, and user-defined content goes in custom lenses. "Publish an approved reference architecture as an AWS Service Catalog product" standardises what is deployed, but a successful launch is not a review and produces no risks or improvement plan. Applying "only the default Framework lens" and using notes leaves out the generative AI questions altogether, and free-text notes have no risk rating or improvement plan. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/lenses.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/lenses-custom.html

prompt: A travel company wants an assistant that answers employee questions about its expense and travel policies. The policies total about 9,000 pages (roughly 5 million tokens) and are revised every week. Answers must reflect the current revision and must point to the source passage. The team has four application developers, no ML engineers and no labelled question-and-answer data. A developer proposes to fine-tune a model on the policy text every week. The architect reviews the proposal against the guidance in the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens on when to customise models. Which design is MOST consistent with that guidance and meets the requirements?

options.text: Fine-tune a small model each week on question-and-answer pairs that a larger model generates from the newly revised policy text.
Run a continued pre-training job on the full policy corpus after each weekly revision, and serve the resulting custom model.
Place the full policy corpus in the system prompt of a large-context model, and enable prompt caching for that prompt.
Start with prompt engineering on a base model, and add retrieval from a knowledge base that is re-synchronised after each revision.

explanation: The lens best practice on learning when to customise models (GENOPS05-BP01) says to prioritise prompt engineering and RAG before model customisation, starting with the least resource-intensive option and moving on only if needed. Retrieval also fits the requirements directly: a knowledge base that is synchronised after each revision serves the current text, returns the retrieved passages so that answers can cite their source, and needs neither labelled data nor ML engineers. "Fine-tune a small model each week" bakes the policy into weights that are out of date at the next revision, cannot point to a source passage, and adds a weekly training and evaluation cycle for a team with no ML engineers. "Run a continued pre-training job" has the same staleness and citation problems, and it skips the cheaper steps that the lens puts first; continued pre-training is also no longer listed among the current Amazon Bedrock customisation methods. "Place the full policy corpus in the system prompt" cannot work at this size, because about 5 million tokens is several times larger than even a 1-million-token context window, and each weekly revision would invalidate the cached prefix anyway. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/genops05-bp01.html

prompt: A legal-tech company fine-tuned an open-weight Llama 3.1 8B model on its own GPU cluster. The weights are in Amazon S3 in us-east-1 in Hugging Face safetensors format, together with the config and tokenizer files (16 GB in total). The company's application already calls Amazon Bedrock models through InvokeModel on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. Traffic for the new model is interactive and spiky, and the three-person team does not want to operate inference endpoints, instances or scaling policies. The existing weights must be reused as they are. Which deployment design meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on GPU instances with auto scaling, and change the application to call InvokeEndpoint.
Submit an Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import job that points to the S3 location, and call the imported model through InvokeModel.
Run an Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning job on a Llama base model with the original training data, and call the resulting custom model.
Register the weights as a model package in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry, and pass the model package ARN as the model ID in InvokeModel.

explanation: Custom Model Import brings a model that was customised elsewhere into Amazon Bedrock. The Llama 3.1 architecture is supported, the files must be Hugging Face safetensors weights with config and tokenizer files in S3, us-east-1 is a supported Region, and 16 GB is far below the 200 GB limit for text models. The imported model runs with on-demand throughput and is called with InvokeModel or InvokeModelWithResponseStream, so the application keeps its existing integration and the team operates no endpoints. "Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint" reuses the weights, but the team would own instances, scaling policies and a new invocation path, which is exactly what it wants to avoid. "Run an Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning job" creates a different model from scratch on a Bedrock base model; it does not reuse the existing weights. "Register the weights as a model package" depends on a capability that does not exist: Model Registry catalogues and versions models for SageMaker AI deployment, and InvokeModel does not accept a model package ARN. Note that Custom Model Import cannot be used with batch inference or AWS CloudFormation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-import-model.html

prompt: A Dutch insurer must choose between three Amazon Bedrock models for summarising insurance-law case files that are written in Dutch. Public leaderboards rank the three models differently. The team has 600 anonymised case files with reference summaries written by its lawyers, five lawyers who can each spare two hours, and one week. The decision must rest on evidence from the insurer's own documents, must include the lawyers' judgement of legal tone, and must not require the team to build its own test harness. Which combination of steps should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs that use a judge model, with the 600 case files and reference summaries as a custom prompt dataset.
Run programmatic model evaluation jobs for the text summarisation task type with the built-in prompt datasets that Amazon Bedrock provides.
Run a model evaluation job that uses human workers, with the lawyers as the work team rating a sample of outputs from the two leading models.
Rank the three models by the benchmark scores on their model cards and on public leaderboards, and choose the model with the best rank.
Fine-tune each of the three models on the 600 case files, and choose the model that reaches the lowest validation loss at the end of training.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock evaluations provide the harness. A judge-model job takes a custom prompt dataset in JSON Lines on Amazon S3 (up to 1,000 prompts per job, each with an optional referenceResponse), invokes each candidate and scores metrics such as correctness and completeness against the lawyers' reference summaries, so all 600 files can be used for all three models within the week. A job that uses human workers lets a work team of the company's own experts rate responses, which is how the lawyers' view of legal tone enters the decision; such a job compares up to two models, so it is run on a sample from the two leaders. "Run programmatic model evaluation jobs" with built-in datasets measures general summarisation, not Dutch insurance-law documents, so it is not evidence from the insurer's own data. "Rank the three models by the benchmark scores" has the same weakness, and the leaderboards already disagree. "Fine-tune each of the three models" answers a different question: validation loss measures fit to the training data, not summary quality or tone, it uses up the only labelled data, and customisation comes after model selection. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-prompt-datasets-judge.html

prompt: A retailer runs two workloads on the same Amazon Bedrock model. A customer-facing chat assistant is busy only from 09:00 to 18:00 on weekdays, peaks at about 30,000 input tokens per minute, and has missed its latency target in busy hours on standard on-demand inference. A nightly agentic job enriches product records by calling tools through the Converse API in a multi-turn loop; it may take several hours, and nobody waits for it. The company will not sign a capacity reservation or a term commitment, and it wants the nightly job to cost as little as possible. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move the chat assistant to the Reserved service tier, with the reservation sized for the weekday peak.
Keep the chat assistant on on-demand inference, and set the service tier of its requests to priority.
Convert the nightly job to an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job that reads JSONL records from Amazon S3.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a 1-month commitment for the chat assistant's weekday peak.
Keep the nightly job on the Converse API, and set the service tier of its requests to flex.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock has four service tiers, chosen per request. Priority gives the fastest responses at a price premium and needs no reservation; AWS describes it for customer-facing workloads that do not warrant a 24x7 capacity reservation, which is the chat assistant. Flex gives a discount to workloads that tolerate longer processing times, and AWS lists agentic workflows as an example. Flex requests are ordinary synchronous Converse calls, so the tool loop keeps working. "Move the chat assistant to the Reserved service tier" breaks the no-commitment rule: Reserved is a 1-month or 3-month reservation arranged through the account team, with a minimum of 100,000 input tokens per minute, more than three times this peak. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a 1-month commitment" is also a term commitment and is billed every hour, including nights and weekends when chat is idle. "Convert the nightly job to an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job" looks cheapest, but batch inference does not support tool calling: each record is processed independently with no multi-turn exchange. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/batch-inference.html

prompt: A media company serves article tagging from a custom model that it fine-tuned in January 2026 on an Amazon Bedrock base model in us-east-1. The custom model is served through an on-demand custom model deployment. AWS has notified the company that the base model has entered the Legacy state and has announced its end-of-life (EOL) date. The team expects a traffic peak next month, wants better accuracy from 20,000 new labelled examples, and must keep the tagging service running after the EOL date. Which plan is consistent with how Amazon Bedrock handles models in the Legacy state?

options.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the custom model to cover the peak, and fine-tune the same base model again with the new examples before the EOL date.
Keep the current deployment, fine-tune the same base model again with the new examples, and let Amazon Bedrock move the deployment to the successor at EOL.
Keep serving the custom model from on-demand deployments, fine-tune an Active base model with the examples, and switch before the EOL date.
Keep the current deployment unchanged, request a higher quota for the peak, and continue with the same custom model after the EOL date of the base model.

explanation: When a base model enters the Legacy state, a model that was customised earlier can still be used: the company can keep its existing on-demand deployments and can even create a new custom model deployment for on-demand inference. What stops is anything new on the Legacy base: no new fine-tuning jobs and no new Provisioned Throughput. After the EOL date the model is removed and requests fail, and AWS states that migration does not happen automatically. The workable plan is therefore to keep serving as is, customise an Active base model with the old and new examples, evaluate the result, and cut over before EOL. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the custom model" fails on both halves, because new Provisioned Throughput and new fine-tuning jobs are not allowed on a Legacy model. The plan to "let Amazon Bedrock move the deployment to the successor" also needs a new fine-tuning job on the Legacy base and assumes an automatic migration that does not exist. "Keep the current deployment unchanged" ignores that requests fail after EOL, and AWS does not grant quota increases for Legacy models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-lifecycle.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-lifecycle-legacy.html

prompt: A SaaS company exposes a text-generation API through Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. The model ID and inference parameters are hard-coded, so every model change needs a code release. Product managers want to change the model for each customer tier without a code deployment. A change must be checked against a list of approved model IDs before it takes effect, must reach traffic gradually, and must roll back automatically if a CloudWatch alarm on the function's error rate goes into alarm. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Keep the tier-to-model mapping in an AWS AppConfig configuration profile with a validator, and deploy changes with a strategy that monitors the alarm.
Keep the tier-to-model mapping in Lambda environment variables, and have a pipeline update the function configuration when product managers approve a change.
Keep the tier-to-model mapping in a Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter with an allowed-pattern check, and have the function read it on every invocation.
Publish one Lambda function version for each model, and select the version to invoke through an API Gateway stage variable that product managers can edit.

explanation: AWS AppConfig is built for changing application behaviour without redeploying code. A free-form configuration profile holds the tier-to-model mapping and inference parameters; a Lambda validator (or a JSON Schema) runs before a deployment starts, so a model ID that is not on the approved list never goes live; a deployment strategy rolls the new version out in steps over a set time; and if an associated CloudWatch alarm goes into alarm during the deployment or bake time, AppConfig rolls back to the previous version. The function reads the configuration through the AppConfig Agent Lambda extension, which caches it locally. "Lambda environment variables" change for all traffic at once when the function configuration is updated, with no validation step and no alarm-driven rollback. A "Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter" can be changed without a release, but the new value applies to every invocation immediately, so there is no gradual exposure and no automatic rollback. "Publish one Lambda function version for each model" still needs a function deployment for each new model, and a stage variable switches the whole stage at once rather than one customer tier. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appconfig/latest/userguide/what-is-appconfig.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appconfig/latest/userguide/monitoring-deployments.html

prompt: A bank's AWS Step Functions workflow calls a large Amazon Bedrock model to draft replies to customer complaints. The model is already invoked through a geographic cross-Region inference profile. During two hours of model-side degradation, every execution waited for the task timeout and then retried four times before it failed, and the backlog grew to thousands of executions. The bank wants executions to stop calling the degraded model for a cool-down period after repeated failures, to produce a shorter draft from a smaller model during that period, and to return to the large model automatically once it recovers. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Raise MaxAttempts in the Retry block of the model task, and add a higher BackoffRate with jitter so that the retries are spread over a longer period of time.
Add a Catch for States.ALL to the model task so that an execution moves on to a task that invokes the smaller model after all of the retries are exhausted.
Put an Amazon SQS queue with a dead-letter queue in front of the workflow, and limit how many executions can start at the same time.
After repeated failures, write an item with an expiry time to a DynamoDB table; each execution reads it first and uses the smaller model until it expires.

explanation: This is the circuit breaker pattern, which AWS Prescriptive Guidance implements with Step Functions and a DynamoDB table that stores circuit status. After the bounded retries fail, the workflow writes a record for the callee with an expiry timestamp. Every execution reads that record first: while it is unexpired the circuit is open and a Choice state skips the large model, here routing to the smaller model for a shorter draft (graceful degradation). When the record expires, removed by DynamoDB TTL, executions try the large model again, so recovery is automatic. "Raise MaxAttempts in the Retry block" is the retry-with-backoff pattern, which suits transient errors; in a two-hour degradation it keeps calling the model and makes each execution wait longer. "Add a Catch for States.ALL" does provide a fallback, but there is no shared state, so every execution still calls the degraded model and waits for the timeout and all retries before falling back. "Put an Amazon SQS queue" in front smooths the backlog, but executions still call the degraded model and customers get no draft at all. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/circuit-breaker.html

prompt: A company calls an Amazon Bedrock model from us-east-1. To lower its token cost, it changes the model ID from the us. geographic inference profile to the global. inference profile of the same model. The role's IAM policy allows bedrock:InvokeModel on the global inference profile ARN in us-east-1, on the foundation-model ARN in us-east-1, and on the foundation-model ARN that has no Region and no account ID. Requests through the us. profile still succeed. Requests through the global. profile fail with an AccessDeniedException that cites an explicit deny in a service control policy. The SCP denies all actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not us-east-1, us-east-2 or us-west-2. Data residency is not a concern. What should the company change?

options.text: Add every commercial Region that the global inference profile can route to into the list of allowed Regions in the SCP.
Exempt requests whose bedrock:InferenceProfileArn matches the global inference profile from the Region deny in the SCP.
Enable the opt-in Regions that the global inference profile can route to in the Region settings of the AWS account.
Add the foundation-model ARN of every destination Region of the global inference profile to the IAM policy of the role.

explanation: For a global inference profile, Amazon Bedrock authorises three resources: the profile in the source Region, the foundation model in the source Region, and a Region-agnostic foundation-model ARN. For that last evaluation the service sets aws:RequestedRegion to the literal value unspecified, not to a destination Region. An SCP that denies everything outside a list of Region names therefore denies it. AWS documents two fixes: add unspecified to the allowed values, or keep the Region list as it is and add an exception that uses bedrock:InferenceProfileArn, which is populated on the foundation-model evaluations. The exception leaves the Region restriction intact for every other service. "Add every commercial Region" does not help, because no Region name equals unspecified; it would also remove the Region control for all services. "Enable the opt-in Regions" is not needed, since cross-Region inference routes to Regions that are not enabled in the account, and it does not change the SCP result. "Add the foundation-model ARN of every destination Region" cannot work, because an IAM allow never overrides an SCP deny and the global profile is authorised through the Region-less ARN the role already has. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/global-cross-region-inference.html

prompt: A team load-tests a contract-review feature on Amazon Bedrock with on-demand inference. No other workload uses the model in this account. The model's quotas are 2,000,000 tokens per minute and 1,000 requests per minute. At 60 requests per minute the test starts to return ThrottlingException (HTTP 429). Each request has about 4,000 input tokens and returns about 300 output tokens, and prompt caching is not used. Every request sets max_tokens to 32,000 'to be safe'. During the test, the CloudWatch metrics InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount for the model add up to about 260,000 tokens per minute. What is the MOST likely cause of the throttling?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock deducts input tokens plus max_tokens from the quota when a request starts, so 60 requests reserve more than the quota.
The output tokens of this model count several times toward the quota, so the 300-token responses use up the quota for one minute.
The Region is short of capacity for this model during the test, so Amazon Bedrock rejects a share of the requests that it receives from the account.
The AWS SDK retries each failed call automatically, so the real request rate is higher than the requests-per-minute quota allows.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock deducts total input tokens plus max_tokens from the tokens-per-minute quota at the start of each request, and throttles if that exceeds the quota. Only at the end is the deduction corrected to the real usage and the unused part returned. Here each request reserves about 36,000 tokens (4,000 + 32,000), so 60 requests in a minute reserve about 2,160,000 tokens, above the 2,000,000 quota, even though real consumption is a fraction of that. The fix AWS recommends is to set max_tokens close to the real completion size. The option that output tokens "count several times toward the quota" describes the burndown rate, which is real for some models, but even at the highest documented rate of 15x, 300 output tokens add 4,500, giving about 510,000 tokens per minute for 60 requests. "The Region is short of capacity" would surface as a 503 ServiceUnavailable error; AWS states that 503 is unrelated to account quotas, which return 429. "The AWS SDK retries each failed call" describes a consequence of throttling, not its cause, and 60 requests per minute is far below the 1,000 request quota. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-api-error-codes.html

prompt: A SaaS vendor hosts an open-weight 7-billion-parameter model on Amazon SageMaker AI and has trained one LoRA adapter of about 150 MB for each of 30 enterprise customers. Each request must be answered with the calling customer's adapter. The vendor wants all customers to share one GPU fleet, wants to add or replace one customer's adapter without redeploying the base model or affecting other customers, and wants the base weights to be stored and loaded only once. Which deployment meets these requirements?

options.text: Merge each adapter into the base weights, and deploy 30 real-time endpoints, one for each customer, each with its own auto scaling policy.
Merge each adapter into the base weights, and bring the 30 merged models into Amazon Bedrock with Custom Model Import, one for each customer.
Deploy the base model as an inference component on one endpoint, and create an adapter inference component for each customer that references it.
Deploy one endpoint whose container loads all 30 adapters from Amazon S3 when it starts, and redeploy the endpoint when an adapter changes.

explanation: SageMaker AI supports LoRA adapters as adapter inference components. The base model is deployed once as a base inference component on an endpoint. Each adapter inference component names that base component and the S3 location of the adapter artifacts; it has no compute requirements of its own because it uses the compute of the base component. A request selects the customer's adapter by passing its InferenceComponentName to InvokeEndpoint, and SageMaker AI combines the adapter with the base model. Adding or replacing one customer's adapter is a change to that one component. "Deploy 30 real-time endpoints" gives each customer a separate fleet and 30 copies of the base weights. "Custom Model Import" also needs 30 full merged copies, replacing an adapter means merging and importing a whole model again, and it leaves the shared SageMaker AI fleet. "Deploy one endpoint whose container loads all 30 adapters" shares the fleet and the base weights, but every adapter change is an endpoint redeployment that touches all customers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/realtime-endpoints-adapt.html

prompt: An ML platform team retrains a domain-specific fine-tuned model every month and serves it from an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Today an engineer copies the new model artifact over the old one in Amazon S3 and recreates the endpoint by hand. The team needs each trained version catalogued with its evaluation metrics, a reviewer's approval before deployment, automatic deployment once a version is approved, and an automatic return to the previous model if error-rate or latency alarms fire while the new version takes traffic. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Register each trained model as a version in a SageMaker Model Registry model group, and start the deployment pipeline when its status changes to Approved.
Enable S3 Versioning on the artifact bucket, and overwrite the artifact after each training run so that the endpoint serves the newest object version from then on.
Add each new model to the endpoint as a second production variant with 10 percent of the traffic, and have an engineer raise the weight after checking the dashboards.
Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that uses canary traffic shifting, a baking period, and CloudWatch alarms in the auto-rollback configuration.
Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that shifts all traffic at once with no baking period, to shorten the time during which two fleets are running.

explanation: SageMaker Model Registry catalogues models as versions in a model group, associates metadata such as evaluation metrics with each version, and manages approval status. A version registered as PendingManualApproval waits for the reviewer, and changing the status to Approved can initiate CI/CD deployment. For the rollout, deployment guardrails update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment: canary shifting sends a small share of traffic to the new fleet, and if any of the specified CloudWatch alarms trips during the baking period, SageMaker AI rolls all traffic back to the old fleet automatically. "Enable S3 Versioning" changes nothing on a running endpoint, which does not reload an overwritten artifact, and it provides no metrics catalogue or approval. "Add each new model to the endpoint as a second production variant" limits exposure, but the weight changes and any rollback are done by an engineer, not automatically. The deployment that "shifts all traffic at once with no baking period" exposes every request to the new model and has no monitoring window in which alarms could trigger a rollback. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/model-registry-approve.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deployment-guardrails-blue-green.html

prompt: A fintech company classifies and summarises support tickets with a large Amazon Bedrock model. Quality is good, but the cost for each ticket is three times the budget and latency is too high. The company has 12,000 representative production prompts in Amazon S3 but did not keep the responses. It has no labelled examples, and no engineer has time to design and validate a scoring function for model outputs. The company wants every ticket served by a smaller, cheaper model on Amazon Bedrock whose quality on this task is as close as possible to the large model. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a supervised fine-tuning job for a smaller model, and provide the 12,000 production prompts as the training dataset.
Create a model distillation job with the large model as teacher, a smaller model as student, and the 12,000 prompts as input.
Create a reinforcement fine-tuning job for a smaller model with the 12,000 prompts and a reward function in AWS Lambda.
Create a prompt router that uses intelligent prompt routing between the large model and a smaller model of the same family.

explanation: Model distillation transfers the behaviour of a larger teacher model to a smaller student. The input is a set of use-case prompts in JSONL; Amazon Bedrock generates the teacher's responses for them, may add synthetic data, and fine-tunes the student on the result. Labelled pairs are optional, so 12,000 prompts without responses are enough, and the outcome is a smaller custom model that serves every ticket. "Create a supervised fine-tuning job" needs labelled examples, meaning prompts paired with the desired outputs, which the company does not have. "Create a reinforcement fine-tuning job" replaces labels with a reward function that scores each response, either Lambda code or a model-as-judge grader; designing and validating that scoring is the work the company cannot staff, and the method optimises for the reward rather than for matching the teacher. "Create a prompt router" trains nothing: it sends each request to one of the models in the same family, so some tickets would still go to the large model, which conflicts with serving every ticket from the smaller one. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-distillation.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/custom-models.html

prompt: A company fine-tuned Amazon Nova Lite on Amazon Bedrock in us-east-1 in March 2026 to rewrite product descriptions in its brand voice. The custom model is served from a no-commitment Provisioned Throughput of two model units that has run continuously since launch. Amazon CloudWatch shows that an internal tool invokes the model in short interactive bursts for about two hours on each working day, and that the model is idle otherwise. The fine-tuned behaviour passed a formal brand review and must not change. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to serve this model?

options.text: Replace the current Provisioned Throughput with a Provisioned Throughput of one model unit that has a 1-month commitment term.
Submit each day's requests as Amazon Bedrock batch inference jobs that run against the provisioned model during working hours.
Delete the custom model, and add few-shot examples of the brand voice to prompts that call the base model with on-demand inference.
Create a custom model deployment for on-demand inference, use the deployment ARN as the model ID, and delete the Provisioned Throughput.

explanation: A custom model no longer has to be served from Provisioned Throughput. A custom model deployment (the CreateCustomModelDeployment operation) makes the model available for on-demand inference; the deployment ARN is passed as the model ID, and the company pays only for what it uses. The prerequisites are met: the Region is us-east-1, the model was customised after 16 July 2025, and Amazon Nova Lite is a supported base model. For a model that is busy two hours a day, paying per request is cheaper than paying for every hour, and the model itself is unchanged. "A Provisioned Throughput of one model unit that has a 1-month commitment term" lowers the hourly rate but is still billed for every hour of the month. "Amazon Bedrock batch inference jobs" fail twice: batch inference is not supported for provisioned models, and an asynchronous job does not suit an interactive tool. "Delete the custom model" and prompt the base model replaces the reviewed behaviour with something different, which the brand review rules out. One page of the Bedrock guide still says a customised model must use Provisioned Throughput; the on-demand deployment page is the newer one. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/deploy-custom-model-on-demand.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: A retailer's nightly AWS Glue ETL job copies product records from a JDBC database to a curated Amazon S3 prefix. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base is synchronised from that prefix each morning. Records with an empty description, a duplicate SKU or a description shorter than 20 characters have been reaching the knowledge base and producing poor answers. The data team wants failing records kept out of the curated prefix and written to a quarantine prefix for data stewards, wants valid records to keep flowing every night, and wants a notification when the nightly quality score drops. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Schedule an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset to run against the Data Catalog table of the curated prefix after each nightly load.
In the ETL job, set the data quality action so that the job fails without loading the target when the ruleset fails.
Add an Evaluate Data Quality transform before the S3 target with IsComplete, IsUnique and ColumnLength rules, and route rows by row-level outcome.
Add an Evaluate Data Quality transform before the S3 target with RowCount and CustomSql rules that encode the three checks, and route rows by row-level outcome.
Publish the data quality results from the ETL job to Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon EventBridge, and notify the team from an alarm or rule.

explanation: AWS Glue Data Quality has two entry points. In an ETL job it evaluates data in transit, which lets a pipeline filter bad data before it is loaded. The Evaluate Data Quality transform can output the original data with added columns (rules passed, rules failed, and a row-level Passed or Failed result), so the job can write passed rows to the curated prefix and failed rows to quarantine. IsComplete, IsUnique and ColumnLength are evaluated for each row. The job can also publish results to CloudWatch, and the same metrics go to EventBridge, which covers the notification. Running a ruleset "against the Data Catalog table of the curated prefix" checks data at rest after the bad records have already been loaded, and may be ingested the next morning. Setting the action so that "the job fails without loading the target" keeps bad records out but stops the valid ones too. The transform with "RowCount and CustomSql rules" cannot separate records, because AWS lists both among the rules that apply at dataset level and cannot identify error records. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/tutorial-data-quality.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/glue-data-quality.html

prompt: A contact centre stores 20,000 recorded calls a day in Amazon S3 as single-channel audio. Each call has one agent and one customer and is in either US English or US Spanish; the language of each call is recorded in the IVR metadata. A foundation model will summarise each call. The summariser needs to know who said what, product names such as 'Zentrix Q7' must be transcribed correctly, and card numbers and personal names must be removed before any transcript is stored or sent to a model. Which Amazon Transcribe batch configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable automatic language identification, speaker partitioning, PII redaction with redacted-only output, and a custom vocabulary on each job.
Set the language code from the metadata, and enable channel identification, PII redaction with redacted-only output, and a custom vocabulary.
Set the language code from the metadata, and enable speaker partitioning, PII redaction with redacted-only output, and a custom vocabulary.
Set the language code from the metadata, enable speaker partitioning and a custom vocabulary, and mask PII with a guardrail at inference time.

explanation: Each requirement maps to a Transcribe feature. Speaker partitioning (diarization) labels each speaker in single-channel audio, which gives the summariser who said what. A custom vocabulary improves recognition of domain terms such as product names; it must be created in the same Region as the job, and its entries must use the character set of the language. PII redaction replaces detected PII with [PII] in the transcript, is available for both en-US and es-US in batch jobs, and with the output set to redacted Transcribe creates only the redacted transcript, so nothing unredacted is stored. Setting the language code explicitly matters, because AWS states that redaction is not compatible with language identification; that is why the option with "automatic language identification" fails, and the IVR metadata makes it unnecessary. "Channel identification" separates speakers only when the audio has two channels with one speaker on each, and these recordings have one channel. The option to "mask PII with a guardrail at inference time" leaves an unredacted transcript in S3, which breaks the rule that PII is removed before any transcript is stored. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/pii-redaction-batch.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/diarization.html

prompt: An insurer receives 15,000 scanned claim forms a day as PDFs that mix printed text, tables and handwriting. Downstream, a foundation model drafts a settlement letter from a fixed set of 40 fields. The fields must arrive in a consistent form (dates as YYYY-MM-DD, amounts as numbers), and any field that was extracted with low certainty must go to a human reviewer before the model uses it. The two-person team wants to avoid training models and to avoid orchestrating separate OCR, classification and normalisation steps. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project with a blueprint whose field descriptions state the formats, and route fields by confidence score.
Send each PDF to a multimodal model as a document block in the Converse API with a prompt that asks for the 40 fields as JSON in the required formats.
Extract forms and tables with Amazon Textract, normalise the values in AWS Lambda functions, and orchestrate the steps with AWS Step Functions.
Train an Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognizer on annotated claim forms, and run an entity detection job on each day's PDFs.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Data Automation is designed to remove the orchestration of classification, extraction, normalisation and validation in document processing. A blueprint lists the fields to extract, the type of each (string, number, boolean and so on) and a natural-language description that can state normalisation rules such as a date format. For documents the output includes a confidence score for each field, which gives the pipeline a simple rule for sending uncertain fields to a reviewer. Forty fields fit within the limit of 100 fields for a blueprint used with the asynchronous API. "Send each PDF to a multimodal model" can return JSON in the right formats, but the model gives no per-field confidence score to drive human review, and each document block is limited to 4.5 MB. "Extract forms and tables with Amazon Textract" works technically, but it is the multi-step pipeline of separate services that the team wants to avoid building and running. "Train an Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognizer" requires annotated training documents and a model to maintain, and it does not normalise the values it finds. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/bda.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/bda-blueprint-info.html

prompt: A developer uses the AWS SDK for Python to call the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with a model that supports document input. The request has a system field with one text block, an inferenceConfig, and one message with the role user. The content array of that message holds a single block: a document with the format pdf, the name claims_2026.q3-final, and the raw bytes of a 3.9 MB file in source.bytes. The call is rejected with a validation error before the model runs. Which changes are required to make the request valid? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Encode the file's bytes as a base64 string in the application code before passing them to the SDK in source.bytes.
Add a text block that contains the instruction for the model to the same content array as the document block.
Rename the document so that the name contains only letters, digits, single spaces, hyphens, parentheses and square brackets.
Reduce the size of the PDF to less than 3.75 MB, which is the largest file that a single content block can carry.
Move the system instruction into an assistant message before the user message, because system cannot be combined with documents.

explanation: The Converse API has two rules for document blocks that this request breaks. First, a message that includes a document must also include a text block, in the same content array, with a prompt related to the document. Second, the document name may contain only alphanumeric characters, whitespace characters (no more than one in a row), hyphens, parentheses and square brackets; the underscore and the period in claims_2026.q3-final are not allowed. AWS also recommends a neutral name, because the name is exposed to the model and is vulnerable to prompt injection. "Encode the file's bytes as a base64 string" is unnecessary with an AWS SDK, which does the encoding itself; doing it again would corrupt the document. "Reduce the size of the PDF to less than 3.75 MB" confuses two limits: 3.75 MB is the limit for an image, and a document can be up to 4.5 MB, so 3.9 MB is acceptable. "Move the system instruction into an assistant message" is wrong because the system field is the correct place for system prompts and works with documents; documents and images are allowed only in user messages. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/conversation-inference.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Message.html

prompt: A developer builds an order-status assistant with the Amazon Bedrock Converse API and client-side tool use. The first request contains the user's question and a toolConfig that defines the tool get_order_status. The response has the stopReason tool_use and an assistant message with a toolUse block whose toolUseId is tooluse_7Kp and whose input is the order ID A-1182. The developer's code calls the order system and receives the status 'shipped'. Every candidate for the next request repeats the same toolConfig. Which messages array is formatted correctly so that the model can write the final answer?

options.text: The original user message, followed by a user message whose content has a toolResult block with the toolUseId tooluse_7Kp and the status.
The original user message, the assistant message with the toolUse block, and an assistant message with a toolResult block for tooluse_7Kp.
The original user message, the assistant message with the toolUse block, and a user message with a toolResult block whose toolUseId is get_order_status.
The original user message, the assistant message with the toolUse block, and a user message with a toolResult block whose toolUseId is tooluse_7Kp.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock keeps no conversation state, so every Converse request must carry the whole exchange. With client-side tool use the application appends the assistant message that the model returned, including its toolUse block, and then appends a message with the role user whose content holds a toolResult block. The toolResult carries the toolUseId of the request it answers (here tooluse_7Kp) and the result as json or text content, optionally with a status of error if the tool failed. The model then produces the final answer. The array that goes from the original user message straight to a toolResult drops the assistant turn, so the result refers to a tool request that is not in the conversation. The array with "an assistant message with a toolResult block" puts the result in the wrong role: the model issues toolUse as assistant, and the application returns toolResult as user. The array "whose toolUseId is get_order_status" confuses the tool name with the request identifier; toolUseId must be the ID of the specific tool request, which is how results are matched when a model asks for several tools in one turn. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/tool-use-client-side.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_ToolResultBlock.html

prompt: An airline maintenance team feeds 50,000 free-text technician notes a night into a foundation model that drafts reliability reports. The notes refer to the airline's own part codes in many spellings ('PN 44-871A', 'pn44871a', 'part 44871-A'), and the model treats the variants as different parts. The team has a master list of 6,000 part codes and a large archive of notes, but no annotated documents. It wants the part codes identified in every note, including misspelt ones, and passed to the model in one canonical form, without losing any notes. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Train an Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognizer from an entity list of the part codes and the archive, and run it as a nightly asynchronous job.
Run Amazon Comprehend built-in entity detection as a nightly asynchronous job, and treat every COMMERCIAL_ITEM entity as a part code.
Attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a sensitive information filter that uses a regular expression for part codes to each model call.
Add an AWS Glue Data Quality rule to the nightly job that rejects every note whose part codes do not match the canonical pattern.
Add an AWS Lambda function that maps each detected part code to its master-list form before the prompt for the model is assembled.

explanation: The task has two parts: find the company-specific entity, then normalise it before the model sees it. Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognition identifies entity types that are not in the preset list, such as product codes. It can be trained from an entity list plus unannotated documents that contain those entities, which is what the team has, and the trained model runs in asynchronous entity detection jobs. AWS notes that a custom model learns context and can detect entities with typos, which string matching cannot. A Lambda function then maps each detected span to its master-list form, so every variant reaches the model as one code. Built-in detection with "COMMERCIAL_ITEM" relies on a preset type that means a branded product; it is not trained on the airline's codes, so it would miss codes and mislabel other items. "A sensitive information filter" in a guardrail blocks or masks what its pattern matches, which removes part codes from the prompt instead of standardising them.
