"An AWS Glue Data Quality rule" that rejects notes validates rather than repairs, and discarding non-canonical notes conflicts with keeping every note. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/custom-entity-recognition.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/how-entities.html

prompt: A law firm is building a research assistant over 90 million archived case memos stored in Amazon S3. Paralegals run about 200 questions per day, mostly in two short bursts, and a response within two seconds is acceptable. The memos are short plain-text files, queries are conceptual (no exact-term matching is needed), and retrieval is filtered only by an exact `practice_area` value. The firm embeds with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and wants an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with no cluster to size, patch or keep running between bursts. Which vector store design is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: An OpenSearch Service managed domain with memory-optimized data nodes, a faiss HNSW index of float32 vectors, default chunking, and `practice_area` as a keyword field.
An S3 vector index that stores binary embeddings from Titan Text Embeddings V2 with Hamming distance, and default chunking.
An S3 vector index that stores float32 embeddings with cosine distance, default chunking, and `practice_area` as filterable metadata.
An S3 vector index that stores float32 embeddings, and hierarchical chunking with 8,000-token parents and 1,500-token children.

explanation: Amazon S3 Vectors is described by AWS as best suited for infrequent query workloads: it stores large vector datasets without provisioned infrastructure and answers in under a second, which fits 200 queries a day and a two-second target. The workload needs only semantic search and an equality filter, both of which S3 Vectors supports through a knowledge base, so float32 vectors with cosine distance and a filterable `practice_area` key satisfy every constraint. The option with 'memory-optimized data nodes' works technically, but a managed domain is a cluster that the firm must size and patch and that runs between the bursts, which the stem rules out and which costs more for this query volume. The option with 'binary embeddings' and 'Hamming distance' relies on a capability the store does not have: S3 Vectors supports only floating-point embeddings, and binary vectors are limited to OpenSearch Serverless and OpenSearch managed clusters. The option with '8,000-token parents' uses hierarchical chunking, which is not recommended with an S3 vector bucket because parent-child context is stored as non-filterable metadata and a combined size above 8,000 tokens can exceed the metadata limit and fail ingestion; short memos do not need it anyway. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A manufacturer runs its order and parts systems on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and has a platform team of experienced PostgreSQL administrators. It is adding an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over 3 million maintenance bulletins. Technicians search with exact part numbers such as `PN-88417-C` mixed with natural-language symptoms, so retrieval must combine keyword matching with semantic matching. Newly synced bulletins must be queryable as soon as the sync finishes, and the team wants to reuse its existing database skills and tooling instead of learning a new engine. Which vector store should the team choose?

options.text: Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, using an HNSW index on the embedding column and a GIN index on the text column.
Amazon S3 Vectors with a float32 vector index, and `HYBRID` set as the override search type in each query.
An OpenSearch Service managed domain deployed inside the company VPC, with a faiss k-NN vector index.
An Amazon Neptune Analytics graph with a vector search index, populated through the GraphRAG option.

explanation: Hybrid search in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is supported for Amazon RDS (Aurora), OpenSearch Serverless and MongoDB vector stores that have a filterable text field. Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector therefore gives keyword plus semantic matching (the GIN index on the text column serves the keyword side), reuses the team's PostgreSQL skills, and is the one store for which the documentation does not warn of a few minutes' delay before newly ingested embeddings become queryable. The option that sets '`HYBRID`' on 'Amazon S3 Vectors' fails because S3 Vectors is not one of the stores that support hybrid search; the request silently falls back to semantic search and part numbers would still be missed. The option with a managed domain 'deployed inside the company VPC' relies on something Knowledge Bases does not support: an OpenSearch managed cluster must use public network access, and it would also be a new engine for the team. The 'Neptune Analytics graph' option solves a different problem, connecting entities across documents; it is not listed for hybrid search and adds a graph engine the team does not know. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A SaaS company uses one Amazon Bedrock knowledge base backed by Aurora PostgreSQL (pgvector 0.8.0) for 600 customers. Each chunk carries a `tenant_id` in the `custom_metadata` JSONB column, which has a GIN index, and every `Retrieve` call applies an `equals` filter on `tenant_id` with `numberOfResults` set to 10. Large tenants get 10 results. Small tenants, which each own under 0.1% of the rows but still have hundreds of relevant chunks, usually get one or two results and sometimes none. No errors are logged and latency is normal. What is the MOST likely cause, and what should the team do?

options.text: The GIN index cannot serve equality on a JSONB key, so matching rows are skipped; add an expression index on `tenant_id`.
Semantic search does not apply metadata filters to vectors; set the override search type to `HYBRID` instead.
The HNSW graph was built with low `m` and `ef_construction` values; rebuild the index with higher values.
The filter is applied after the HNSW index scan, so few rows survive; enable `hnsw.iterative_scan` on the database.

explanation: With pgvector, the HNSW index scan returns a limited candidate set and the metadata filter is applied afterwards. When a filter is very selective, as it is for a tenant that owns a tiny share of the rows, most candidates are discarded and fewer results than requested come back, with no error. AWS recommends enabling HNSW iterative index scans (pgvector 0.8.0 or later, for example `hnsw.iterative_scan = 'relaxed_order'`) when metadata filtering is used, so that the scan keeps going until enough filtered rows are found. That matches the symptom exactly: large tenants are fine, small tenants are starved. The option claiming the 'GIN index cannot serve equality' is wrong; GIN on JSONB is what AWS prescribes for key-value metadata filtering, and an expression index is a performance aid for range filters that would not change how many rows are returned. The option that switches to '`HYBRID`' misreads the problem: filters are applied in semantic search too, and hybrid search adds keyword matching, not filter behaviour. The option that rebuilds the graph with higher '`m` and `ef_construction`' improves recall of nearest neighbours in general, but the neighbours are being found and then filtered out, so the shortfall for selective filters would remain. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A legal-tech SaaS provider hosts contract documents for 400 customers in one S3 bucket, organised by a prefix per customer, and indexes them in a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on OpenSearch Serverless. Users sign in through Amazon Cognito, and the chat backend runs on AWS Lambda behind Amazon API Gateway. An audit requires that a user can never receive chunks from another customer's documents, even if the user tampers with the request body or writes a manipulative prompt. The provider does not want to operate one knowledge base per customer. Which combination of actions meets the requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add an instruction to the generation prompt template that tells the model to use only search results from the user's company.
Upload a `.metadata.json` sidecar file with each document that sets a `tenant_id` attribute, and then sync the data source.
Configure `implicitFilterConfiguration` with a `tenant_id` schema so that the model derives the tenant filter from each query.
Have the browser client add a `tenant_id` filter to the request body, which the Lambda function forwards to `Retrieve`.
Have Lambda read the tenant from the verified Cognito token claims and set an `equals` filter on `tenant_id` in every query.

explanation: Tenant isolation in a shared knowledge base needs two things: every chunk must carry the tenant attribute, and the filter must be set by trusted code from a verified identity. For an S3 data source the attribute comes from a `fileName.extension.metadata.json` sidecar stored next to each document, which becomes filterable metadata after a sync. The Lambda function then takes the tenant from the validated Cognito token, never from user input, and adds an `equals` filter in `vectorSearchConfiguration`, so chunks from other tenants are excluded before anything reaches the model. The option that adds 'an instruction to the generation prompt template' is not an access control: other tenants' chunks would still be retrieved and placed in context, and a manipulative prompt could surface them. The option using '`implicitFilterConfiguration`' lets a model generate the filter from the query text, which is useful for relevance but means the user's wording decides the tenant. The option in which 'the browser client' supplies the filter fails the tampering requirement, because the caller controls the request body. Note that anyone with `bedrock:Retrieve` permission on the knowledge base can read all synced data, so only the backend role should hold it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/s3-data-source-connector.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A media company runs its own RAG retrieval layer on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain with six data nodes. A new k-NN index for article embeddings is expected to hold about 200 GiB including indexing overhead, with little growth, and the workload is read-heavy with a strict search latency objective. The team created the index with the service default of five primary shards and now sees uneven shard distribution across the nodes and slow queries. Because the primary shard count of an existing index cannot easily be changed, they plan to reindex once into a new index. Which shard configuration follows AWS sizing guidance for this index?

options.text: 1 primary shard with 5 replicas, so that every data node holds a complete copy of the index.
12 primary shards with 1 replica, which gives shards of about 17 GiB spread evenly over the nodes.
5 primary shards with 2 replicas, which keeps the current layout and adds read capacity.
120 primary shards with 1 replica, which gives shards of under 2 GiB each for fast parallel search.

explanation: AWS guidance is to keep shards between 10 and 30 GiB when search latency is the key objective (30 to 50 GiB is for write-heavy workloads such as logs), and to make the primary shard count a multiple of the data node count so that shards distribute evenly and no node runs hot. For 200 GiB on six nodes, 12 primaries gives roughly 17 GiB per shard, inside the range, and two primaries per node; one replica provides the recommended second copy. The option with '1 primary shard' creates a 200 GiB shard, far above the range, which makes each search scan one very large shard and slows recovery. The option that keeps '5 primary shards' leaves 40 GiB shards, above the search range, and five is not a multiple of six, which is the uneven distribution the team already sees; extra replicas add copies but do not fix shard size. The option with '120 primary shards' goes too far the other way: each search query touches one copy (primary or replica) of every shard of the index, and many tiny shards consume CPU and memory for no benefit, which AWS warns can cause performance problems. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/bp-sharding.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/bp.html

prompt: An engineering firm keeps design standards in a third-party document management system (DMS) that has no native Amazon Bedrock connector. The DMS calls a webhook when a document is published, revised or withdrawn, and exposes an API that returns document text and attributes. Withdrawn standards must stop appearing in the RAG assistant within 5 minutes, and revisions must be searchable within the same window. The team wants Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to keep doing the chunking, embedding and retrieval, and does not want to operate a staging bucket or sync jobs. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Export the DMS content to an S3 bucket every night, and run `StartIngestionJob` on an Amazon EventBridge schedule after each export.
Have a webhook Lambda function chunk and embed each document itself, and write the vectors straight into the knowledge base's vector index.
Create a custom data source, and have a webhook Lambda function call `IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments` or `DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments`.
Create an S3 data source, have a webhook Lambda function copy each document into the bucket, and call `StartIngestionJob` after each copy.

explanation: A custom data source exists for sources without a connector. Documents are added, updated or deleted with the KnowledgeBaseDocuments API operations (`IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments`, `DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments`), text and metadata can be supplied inline, and no sync is needed: the change becomes part of both the data source and the knowledge base in one step. A small Lambda function behind the webhook therefore meets the 5-minute window for revisions and withdrawals, while Bedrock still performs chunking, embedding and retrieval. The option that exports 'every night' misses the 5-minute requirement and needs the staging bucket the team wants to avoid. The option in which the function will 'chunk and embed each document itself' abandons the managed ingestion the team asked to keep, and vectors written behind the service's back lack the metadata that Bedrock manages for source attribution. The option that copies each document into a bucket and calls '`StartIngestionJob` after each copy' can work, because sync is incremental and removes deleted documents, but it requires a staging bucket and a stream of sync jobs that must be started and monitored for every event, which is exactly the overhead the stem excludes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-direct-ingestion.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/custom-data-source-connector.html

prompt: A bank indexes 1.8 million PDF policy documents from S3 in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Each PDF has a `.metadata.json` sidecar file, and the data source uses fixed-size chunking together with a custom transformation Lambda function that adds a `section_owner` attribute to every chunk. Each quarter a job rewrites only the sidecar files to update a `review_status` attribute and then starts a sync. The team expected the sync to merge the new metadata into the existing vectors, but the embedding model's invocation count shows that every document is embedded again each quarter. What is the MOST likely reason?

options.text: The metadata-only update path is not used when a data source has a custom transformation Lambda function.
A sync always re-ingests every document in the data source, whether or not it changed since the last sync.
The data deletion policy is `DELETE`, so each sync removes the data source's vectors and then rebuilds them.
PDF files, like CSV files, are always ingested again in full whenever their metadata files are modified.

explanation: Sync is incremental: unchanged documents are skipped and changed ones are re-parsed, re-chunked, re-embedded and re-indexed. For a change to metadata alone, Bedrock can fetch the existing vectors, merge the new metadata and write them back without calling the embedding model, but only when three conditions all hold: only `metadata.json` files changed, the content files are not CSV, and the data source does not use a custom transformation Lambda function. This data source has such a function, so each changed sidecar triggers full re-ingestion of its PDF, and because the quarterly job touches every sidecar, every document is embedded again. Moving the chunk attribute out of the Lambda function, or limiting the job to sidecars whose status really changed, would cut the cost. The option stating that a sync 're-ingests every document' contradicts incremental sync; unchanged documents are skipped. The option blaming the 'data deletion policy' confuses two things: that policy governs what happens to vectors when the data source or knowledge base is deleted, not what a sync does. The option claiming 'PDF files, like CSV files' are always re-ingested extends a rule that applies only to CSV, whose metadata file carries column structure. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-data-source-sync-ingest.html

prompt: An insurer wants its claims assistant to answer questions that require connecting facts across documents, such as which repair shops appear in claims handled by adjusters who also worked on a flagged policy. Standard chunk retrieval returns each fact separately and misses the links between them. The 6,500 claim files are in one S3 prefix and are embedded with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 at 1,024 dimensions. The team decides to create an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that uses Amazon Neptune Analytics (GraphRAG). Which considerations must the team plan for? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The vector search index, with 1,024 dimensions, has to be defined at the time the Neptune Analytics graph is created.
The graph needs a public endpoint or a private graph endpoint in the team's VPC before Amazon Bedrock can connect to it.
Graph capacity scales automatically with ingestion volume, so no m-NCU value has to be chosen when creating the graph.
The files must be split across folders or data sources, or a limit increase requested, as a data source takes 1,000 files by default.
With hierarchical chunking, GraphRAG returns parent chunks in place of the matched child chunks, as other vector stores do.

explanation: GraphRAG fits the requirement because it identifies entities and relationships across ingested documents and traverses the graph after the initial vector search. Two documented constraints affect this plan. First, the Neptune Analytics graph must be created empty with a vector search index, the index can only be created when the graph is created, and its dimension must match the embedding model, here 1,024. Second, each GraphRAG data source can hold up to 1,000 files by default (raisable on request to 10,000), or the S3 bucket can be partitioned into folders of up to 1,000 files, so 6,500 files in one prefix need reorganising or a quota increase. The option requiring 'a public endpoint or a private graph endpoint' is wrong: Bedrock creates the network connection to the graph, and the default connectivity settings can be left alone. The option saying capacity 'scales automatically' is wrong because autoscaling is not supported for Neptune Analytics graphs; the team allocates m-NCUs and resizes manually. The option about 'parent chunks' reverses the documented behaviour: with hierarchical chunking GraphRAG retrieves only child chunks and does not replace them with parents. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-build-graphs.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A retailer stores sales, returns and inventory tables in Amazon Redshift Serverless. Regional managers want to ask questions such as 'which five stores had the highest return rate last quarter' in a chat assistant. Answers must be computed from current table data, not from a periodic export. A data governance rule requires every generated SQL statement to pass an in-house policy checker, which blocks access to salary and customer columns, before the statement runs. The team wants to write and maintain as little text-to-SQL logic as possible. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Unload the tables to CSV files in S3 each night, index them in a vector knowledge base, and answer with `RetrieveAndGenerate`.
Create a knowledge base with a structured data store on Redshift, and call `RetrieveAndGenerate` to generate and run the SQL.
Write a Lambda function that sends the table schemas to the Converse API to produce SQL, runs the checker, and executes the SQL.
Create a knowledge base with a structured data store on Redshift, call `GenerateQuery`, run the checker, and execute the SQL.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can connect to a structured data store with Amazon Redshift (Serverless or provisioned) as the query engine and convert natural-language questions into SQL using the table metadata, optional descriptions and curated example queries. The `GenerateQuery` operation decouples query conversion from retrieval: it returns the SQL without running it, so the application can pass the statement through the policy checker and only then execute it against live tables. That satisfies current data, the pre-execution check, and minimal custom text-to-SQL logic. The option that will 'unload the tables to CSV files' answers from a nightly export, which the stem forbids, and vector retrieval of rows cannot compute a ranking of return rates. The option that calls '`RetrieveAndGenerate` to generate and run the SQL' uses the right knowledge base type, but generation and execution happen inside one call, leaving no point at which the checker can inspect the statement first. The option with a Lambda function that 'sends the table schemas to the Converse API' can satisfy the governance rule, but the team would own prompt design, schema handling and example management, which is the logic they want to avoid. AWS also recommends restricted, read-only roles for any text-to-SQL workload. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-generate-query.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-prereq-structured.html

prompt: An aircraft maintenance provider indexes 12,000 service manuals in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on OpenSearch Serverless. Each manual has deeply nested sections in which a short procedure step only makes sense together with the warnings and prerequisites in the surrounding section. With default chunking, retrieval finds the right step, but the generated answers omit the related warnings. The team wants embeddings to stay small and precise for matching, wants the model to receive the broader surrounding passage, and does not want to pay for foundation model invocations during chunking. Which chunking strategy should the team configure?

options.text: Fixed-size chunking with 2,000-token chunks and 20% overlap, so each chunk spans a whole section.
Hierarchical chunking with small child chunks for matching and larger parent chunks for context.
Semantic chunking with a larger buffer size and a higher breakpoint percentile threshold.
No chunking, so that each manual is embedded once and returned to the model as a single unit.

explanation: Hierarchical chunking creates two levels. Small child chunks are embedded and matched, which keeps the vectors precise, and at retrieval time the matched children are replaced by their larger parent chunks, so the model receives the surrounding warnings and prerequisites. It uses no foundation model during ingestion, so it meets all three constraints. Two side effects are worth knowing: `numberOfResults` counts child chunks, and because children that share a parent collapse into one result, fewer results than requested can be returned; and the chunking configuration cannot be edited on an existing data source, so the data source has to be re-created. The option with '2,000-token chunks' does deliver more context, but one embedding then represents a whole section, which blurs matching on a short step and contradicts the wish for small, precise embeddings. The option using 'semantic chunking' groups sentences by meaning using a foundation model, which incurs the extra cost the team wants to avoid, and it still returns only the matched chunk. The option with 'no chunking' treats each manual as one chunk, which is far too coarse for matching and also removes page numbers from citations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-ds-update.html

prompt: A contact-centre company indexes call transcripts in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Each transcript is one JSON file in S3 that holds a list of speaker turns with timestamps. Retrieval quality is poor because the built-in chunkers cut across turns and lose the speaker. The team needs chunks that follow topic segments computed by its own segmentation algorithm, with `speaker_role` and `start_time` stored as metadata on each individual chunk for filtering. Citations must point to the original transcript file, so the files cannot be pre-split into many S3 objects. Which ingestion configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Semantic chunking with a buffer size of 1, plus a `.metadata.json` sidecar per transcript that lists `speaker_role` and `start_time`.
A foundation model parser with a customised prompt that tells the model to emit one chunk per topic segment with speaker labels.
The no-chunking strategy with a custom transformation Lambda function that writes its chunks to an intermediate S3 bucket.
Fixed-size chunking with a small token limit and no overlap, so that each chunk holds about one turn, plus a sidecar metadata file.

explanation: When chunking logic is not natively supported, Knowledge Bases lets you select the no-chunking strategy and specify a custom transformation Lambda function together with an S3 bucket for intermediate storage. Bedrock writes the parsed file to that bucket, the function applies the team's segmentation, writes the chunked content back with per-chunk `contentMetadata`, and returns references for the rest of ingestion. The source document remains the single transcript file, so citations still point to it, and `speaker_role` and `start_time` exist on each chunk; chunk-level metadata overrides file-level metadata on a collision. The option with 'semantic chunking' uses Bedrock's own sentence-similarity boundaries, not the team's algorithm, and a sidecar file describes the whole document, so every chunk would share one speaker and one start time. The option with 'a foundation model parser' confuses parsing with chunking: the parser prompt controls how content is extracted from a file, and the configured chunking strategy still decides the boundaries and adds no per-chunk attributes. The option with 'fixed-size chunking' splits by token count, so it only approximates turns, ignores topic segments, and again offers only file-level metadata. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-custom-transformation.html

prompt: A publisher's Amazon Bedrock knowledge base holds 70 million chunks embedded with Amazon Titan Embeddings G1 - Text as float32 vectors in an OpenSearch Service managed domain on engine version 2.17. Memory-optimized data nodes are the largest line in the bill. An evaluation shows that binary embeddings give acceptable recall for this corpus when a reranker is applied, and the team wants to move to binary vectors to reduce memory and storage while staying on the same domain. Which actions are required to make this change? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Call `UpdateKnowledgeBase` on the existing knowledge base to change the embedding data type, and then start a sync.
Keep Titan Embeddings G1 - Text as the model, and set the embedding data type of the knowledge base to `BINARY`.
Create a new knowledge base that uses Titan Text Embeddings V2 with the `BINARY` embedding data type, and ingest again.
Move the vectors into an S3 vector index, which stores binary embeddings at a lower cost than the domain does.
Create a vector index whose vector field uses the binary data type and the Hamming space type on the faiss engine.

explanation: Titan Embeddings G1 - Text produces floating-point vectors only, whereas Titan Text Embeddings V2 (and the Cohere Embed models) support binary output, so the embedding model has to change. The embedding model and its configuration belong to the knowledge base configuration, which cannot be modified after creation, so a new knowledge base is needed and every document must be embedded again; vectors from different models are not comparable in any case. On the store side, an OpenSearch managed cluster supports binary vectors for Knowledge Bases from engine version 2.16, and the index must declare the vector field with `data_type` binary and the Hamming space type on the faiss engine. The option that calls '`UpdateKnowledgeBase`' fails because that operation cannot change the `knowledgeBaseConfiguration` or `storageConfiguration` fields; they must be resubmitted unchanged. The option that will 'keep Titan Embeddings G1 - Text' relies on a capability that model lacks. The option that moves to 'an S3 vector index' fails twice: S3 Vectors supports only floating-point embeddings, and the team wants to stay on the domain. Only OpenSearch Serverless and OpenSearch managed clusters can store binary vectors for a knowledge base. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-supported.html

prompt: A training company wants a RAG assistant over 4,000 hours of recorded instructor-led courses (.mp4), audio recordings of support calls (.mp3), and slide decks exported to PDF with many diagrams. Learners will type questions such as 'what did the instructor say about rollback strategies' and expect generated answers with citations from `RetrieveAndGenerate`. Nobody will search by uploading an image. The files are in Amazon S3, and the team wants a managed ingestion path with no transcription pipeline of its own. Which knowledge base configuration should the team choose?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as the parser, a text embedding model, and a multimodal storage destination in S3.
Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings as the embedding model, the default parser, and a multimodal storage destination in S3.
A foundation model parser that uses a vision-capable model, a text embedding model, and a multimodal storage destination in S3.
Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 as the embedding model, the default parser, and an S3 content bucket.

explanation: The decisive facts are that the valuable content is speech and that users ask text questions and want generated answers. Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) converts multimedia to text, producing speech transcripts and visual descriptions for video, transcripts for audio, and extracted text and figures for PDFs, and that text is then chunked and embedded normally. AWS documents this path as having full `RetrieveAndGenerate` support and recommends it for meeting recordings, calls and training videos. A multimodal storage destination is needed for non-text input. The option with 'Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings' embeds media natively for visual similarity and image queries, but AWS states it cannot process speech content meaningfully and that `RetrieveAndGenerate` is limited to text content, so the instructor's spoken words would not be searchable. The option with 'a foundation model parser' handles images and PDF figures but not audio or video, leaving the recordings unindexed. The option with 'Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1' is aimed at image search with the default parser and likewise does nothing with speech. The cost of the BDA path is longer ingestion time and per-page or per-image parsing charges, including for PDFs that contain only text. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-multimodal-choose-approach.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-advanced-parsing.html

prompt: A company already runs Amazon OpenSearch Service for product search: a managed domain on engine version 2.11, deployed inside a VPC, whose k-NN indexes use the nmslib engine. The search team wants a managed domain to be the vector store for a new Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, embedding with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 as float32 vectors, so that the company keeps one search technology and the team can set HNSW parameters itself. Which conditions must the vector store meet before the knowledge base can be created on it? (Select THREE.)

options.text: The domain stays in the VPC, and an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon Bedrock lets the service reach it.
The domain uses public network access, preferably protected with fine-grained access control.
The domain runs engine version 2.13 or later, which is needed to create the k-NN index.
The vector field is declared with the binary data type so that float32 vectors are stored compactly.
The existing nmslib index is reused, with its space type changed to cosine similarity.
The vector index is created with the faiss engine and the HNSW method.

explanation: For OpenSearch Service managed clusters, Bedrock Knowledge Bases documents three hard requirements that the current domain does not meet. Network: public access must be chosen, because domains behind a VPC are not supported for a knowledge base; AWS recommends fine-grained access control to restrict what the knowledge base service role can do. Version: engine version 2.13 or higher is required to create the k-NN index (2.16 or later only if binary embeddings are used). Engine: the vector field must use faiss, and nmslib is not supported; the sample mapping uses the HNSW method with `m` and `ef_construction` parameters, which is where the team does its tuning. The option in which 'the domain stays in the VPC' with an interface endpoint assumes a connectivity path that Knowledge Bases does not offer for managed domains. The option declaring 'the binary data type' misunderstands that setting: it is for binary embeddings with the Hamming space type, and the stem says the team embeds float32 vectors, which use the l2 space type. The option in which 'the existing nmslib index is reused' fails because nmslib indexes cannot back a knowledge base, whatever space type they use. If private connectivity were mandatory, an OpenSearch Serverless collection with a VPC endpoint would be the alternative. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-osm-permissions-prereq.html

prompt: A software vendor's support assistant uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on OpenSearch Serverless. The application calls `Retrieve` with `numberOfResults` set to 5 and then the Converse API. Evaluation shows two problems. First, questions that quote exact identifiers, such as error code `E-4471` or a CLI flag, often miss the one article that contains that string. Second, for conceptual questions the best article frequently sits between positions 6 and 20 of the similarity ranking, so it never reaches the model. The team will not send more than five chunks to the model because of token cost. Which changes address these problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Raise `numberOfResults` to 50, and pass every returned chunk to the model so that the right article is always in context.
Set `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID` so that the raw chunk text is searched together with the vector embeddings.
Keep `numberOfResults` at 5, and add a reranking configuration with `numberOfRerankedResults` set to 25.
Raise `numberOfResults` to 25, and add a reranking configuration that returns the 5 highest-scoring chunks.
Call the `Rerank` API on the user question before `Retrieve` so that the question is rewritten as ranked keywords.

explanation: The two symptoms have different causes. Exact identifiers are a keyword-matching problem: hybrid search, which OpenSearch Serverless supports when the text field is filterable, queries the raw text as well as the embeddings, so a literal string such as `E-4471` can match. The ranking problem is solved by placing a reranker after retrieval: fetch a wider candidate set (25) and let a reranker model score each chunk against the query and return only the top 5, which keeps the token budget while pulling the best article up from positions 6 to 20. The option that will 'pass every returned chunk to the model' breaks the five-chunk limit and adds noise. The option that keeps '`numberOfResults` at 5' with 25 reranked results has the numbers the wrong way round: the reranker sees only the candidates that were retrieved, and when `numberOfRerankedResults` is greater than `numberOfResults` the response is capped at `numberOfResults`, so an article at position 12 is still never considered. The option that calls '`Rerank` API on the user question' misuses the model: a reranker orders supplied documents by relevance to a query, it does not rewrite queries, and it needs retrieved documents as input. Reranking in Bedrock applies to text only. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-retrieve.html

prompt: A team created its own vector index in an OpenSearch Serverless collection and attached it to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. In the index, the vector field uses the faiss engine, the text chunk field was added with the filterable setting turned off, and the Bedrock-managed metadata field is also not filterable. Ingestion succeeds and semantic retrieval works. To improve matching on SKU codes, a developer sets `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID` in `Retrieve` requests. The calls succeed without errors, but the results and scores are identical to those returned for `SEMANTIC`, and SKU lookups still fail. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: Hybrid search is applied only by `RetrieveAndGenerate`, and `Retrieve` always runs a semantic search.
Hybrid search on OpenSearch Serverless needs a reranker model to merge the keyword and vector scores.
The faiss engine answers vector queries only, and hybrid search requires an index built with nmslib.
The text field is not filterable, so the knowledge base falls back to semantic search for the query.

explanation: Hybrid search is supported only for Amazon RDS (Aurora), OpenSearch Serverless and MongoDB vector stores that contain a filterable text field. The documentation states that if the store is a different type or its text field is not filterable, the query uses semantic search. That explains the symptoms: no error, and results identical to `SEMANTIC`. AWS's own setup instructions map the text chunk field as filterable (true) and the Bedrock-managed metadata field as not filterable (false), so this index has the text field set the wrong way. The fix is to create an index with a filterable text field and point a knowledge base at it. The option claiming hybrid search is applied 'only by `RetrieveAndGenerate`' is wrong, because `overrideSearchType` sits in the retrieval configuration used by both operations. The option requiring 'a reranker model' confuses two independent features; reranking is an optional step after retrieval and is not needed for hybrid search. The option requiring 'an index built with nmslib' has it backwards: Knowledge Bases requires the faiss engine on OpenSearch Serverless and directs you to create a new faiss index if yours uses nmslib. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: An electronics retailer's assistant calls `RetrieveAndGenerate` on a customer-managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base stored in OpenSearch Serverless. Simple questions are answered well. Compound questions such as 'Is the X200 or the X300 cheaper to repair out of warranty, and which has the longer battery warranty?' produce answers that cover only one product, because the top results all come from a single product's documents. Logs show one search per question. The team wants to fix this with the LEAST development effort and without adding orchestration components. What should the team do?

options.text: Set the query transformation type to `QUERY_DECOMPOSITION` in the orchestration configuration of the request.
Add a reranker model to the retrieval configuration so that chunks about both products are ranked highest.
Build a Step Functions workflow in which a Lambda function splits the question and calls `Retrieve` for each part.
Change the data source to hierarchical chunking so that each result returns a larger passage about a product.

explanation: Query decomposition is a built-in option of `RetrieveAndGenerate`: setting `orchestrationConfiguration.queryTransformationConfiguration.type` to `QUERY_DECOMPOSITION` makes the knowledge base break a complex question into sub-queries, run a search for each, and generate the answer from the combined results. A question about two products becomes separate searches for each product, which fixes the one-search-per-question limitation with a request parameter and no new components. The option that adds 'a reranker model' cannot help, because a reranker only reorders chunks that the single search already returned; if no X300 chunks were retrieved there is nothing to promote. The option that builds 'a Step Functions workflow' implements the same idea by hand and would work, but it adds the orchestration components and development effort the team wants to avoid. The option that changes to 'hierarchical chunking' returns larger parent passages for the matched chunks, which are still about the one product that dominated the similarity ranking, and it requires re-creating the data source. For managed knowledge bases, agentic retrieval offers iterative multi-query retrieval through a separate API, but this knowledge base is customer-managed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A fintech's assistant is built on the Converse API with a carefully tuned system prompt, a guardrail, streaming output, and three existing tools for account lookups. The team now wants answers grounded in a policy knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock. The requirements are that the model decides on each turn whether a policy search is needed (greetings and balance questions must not trigger retrieval), that the existing system prompt and citation format stay under the application's control, and that only one model generation produces the final answer. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Call `RetrieveAndGenerate` for every user message, and pass its generated answer to Converse as additional context for the reply.
Add a tool whose handler calls `RetrieveAndGenerate`, and return the generated answer to the model as the tool result for that turn.
Add a policy-search tool to `toolConfig`, and when the model requests it, call `Retrieve` and return the chunks as the result.
Call `Retrieve` with every user message before Converse, and prepend the returned chunks to the system prompt.

explanation: Exposing retrieval as a tool (function calling) gives the model a consistent interface: the application adds a tool definition to `toolConfig`, the model decides when the tool is needed, and the application code executes it and returns the result. Implementing the handler with `Retrieve` returns raw chunks and their source metadata without generating anything, so the single Converse generation, under the existing system prompt and guardrail, writes the answer and formats citations the way the application wants. Greetings and balance questions simply never produce a tool request. The option that calls '`RetrieveAndGenerate` for every user message' retrieves on every turn and generates twice. The option whose handler calls '`RetrieveAndGenerate`' lets the model choose when to search, but each search runs a second generation with the knowledge base's own prompt template, so the answer is produced by two generations and the citation format is no longer the application's. The option that calls '`Retrieve` with every user message' keeps one generation but searches on every turn, which the requirement excludes. The same tool can be published to other agents over MCP; for managed knowledge bases, AgentCore Gateway exposes `Retrieve` as an MCP tool without custom code. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/tool-use.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-retrieve.html

prompt: A bank's platform team owns a customer-service prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. It defines the assistant's role in a system instruction, the model and the inference parameters, and it has `{{customer_tier}}` and `{{question}}` variables. Compliance has approved version 4. Application teams must run exactly the approved role definition and parameters without being able to alter them per request, further edits to the working draft must not change production behaviour, and moving to a newly approved version must not require redeploying application code. How should the applications invoke the prompt?

options.text: Call `GetPrompt` for the working draft at start-up, fill in the variables in code, and send the text to Converse with a local system prompt.
Call Converse with the ARN of prompt version 4 as the model ID and the values in `promptVariables`, reading the ARN from AWS AppConfig.
Call Converse with the ARN of prompt version 4, and pass `system` and `inferenceConfig` in each request to restate the approved settings.
Keep one prompt variant per application in the prompt, and have each application select its variant by name in the Converse request.

explanation: A prompt version is a snapshot of the draft at a point in time, so pinning the application to the ARN of version 4 isolates production from later edits to the working draft. The Converse API accepts the ARN of a prompt version in `modelId` and fills the template from `promptVariables`. When a managed prompt is used this way, the request cannot include `system`, `inferenceConfig`, `toolConfig` or `additionalModelRequestFields`; those must be defined in Prompt Management, which is what enforces the approved role definition and parameters. Reading the ARN from AWS AppConfig lets the team move to version 5 by changing configuration, with no redeployment. The option that calls '`GetPrompt` for the working draft' reads a mutable draft and sends a locally defined system prompt, so neither the approval nor the role definition is enforced. The option that passes '`system` and `inferenceConfig` in each request' is rejected by the API for a managed prompt, and if it were allowed it would defeat central control. The option that keeps 'one prompt variant per application' misuses variants, which are alternative configurations compared while testing; the Converse request has no field for choosing a variant, and saving a comparison as the draft discards the others. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-test.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Converse.html

prompt: A utilities company is building a service-request assistant. An Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API invokes stateless Lambda functions that call the Converse API. Conversations span many turns and can resume from another device, so history must be loaded by session ID with millisecond latency and must be removed automatically some time after the session ends, without scheduled clean-up jobs. When a request is ambiguous, for example a missing meter number, the workflow must send the customer a clarifying question by SMS, pause for up to 48 hours, and resume exactly where it stopped when the reply arrives. Which design choices meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store each turn in a DynamoDB table keyed by session ID and turn timestamp, with TTL on a Number attribute that holds an epoch-seconds expiry.
Store each turn in a DynamoDB table keyed by session ID and turn timestamp, with TTL on a String attribute that holds an ISO 8601 expiry timestamp.
Run each request as a Step Functions Standard workflow that sends the question with a task token and waits for the callback.
Run each request as a Step Functions Express workflow that sends the question with `.waitForTaskToken` and waits for the callback.
Keep the history in a module-level variable of the Lambda function so that warm invocations reuse it across turns.

explanation: Conversation history for stateless compute belongs in a low-latency key-value store. A DynamoDB table with the session ID as partition key and a turn timestamp as sort key returns a session's turns in order with one query, from any device. DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items automatically without consuming write throughput, but the TTL attribute must be a Number holding Unix epoch time in seconds. For the clarification step, the Step Functions callback pattern pauses a task until a task token is returned with `SendTaskSuccess` or `SendTaskFailure`; the SMS reply handler returns the token and the execution resumes at the same state. This pattern is available in Standard workflows, which can wait far longer than 48 hours. The option with 'a String attribute that holds an ISO 8601 expiry' fails because items whose TTL attribute is not a Number are ignored by the TTL process, so history would never be removed. The option using an 'Express workflow' fails because Express Workflows support only request-response integrations, not `.waitForTaskToken`. The option with 'a module-level variable' keeps state inside one execution environment, which is not shared with other environments and disappears when it is recycled, so another device or a cold start loses the conversation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/TTL.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html

prompt: A healthcare company manages production prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management in a dedicated production account. After an incident in which an engineer edited a prompt and published a new version directly, the security team sets two requirements. First, there must be a durable record of who created, modified or versioned each prompt, and when. Second, no person may change or publish a prompt in production directly; a version may be created only after a reviewer has approved the change. Engineers keep read access to prompts for debugging. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, and query the logs for the identity that changed each prompt.
Create a CloudTrail trail that delivers management events to S3, which records `UpdatePrompt` and `CreatePromptVersion` calls.
Add CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::Prompt` resource type, and use them as the record of prompt edits.
Publish a CloudWatch dashboard of invocation metrics for each prompt, and review it for unexpected changes in behaviour.
Allow `UpdatePrompt` and `CreatePromptVersion` in IAM only for a pipeline role that runs after a CodePipeline manual approval.

explanation: Changes to prompts are control-plane API calls (`CreatePrompt`, `UpdatePrompt`, `CreatePromptVersion`, `DeletePrompt`), which CloudTrail records as management events with the caller identity, time and request details. Event history shows only recent events, so a trail that delivers to S3 provides the durable record. Prevention is an IAM matter: engineers get read actions such as `GetPrompt` and `ListPrompts`, while the write actions are granted only to a deployment role assumed by a pipeline that has a manual approval action before the stage that calls `CreatePromptVersion`. Prompt Management supplies versions and variables; the approval workflow itself is built with IAM and a pipeline. The option that enables 'model invocation logging' captures the inputs and outputs of model invocations, not edits to prompt resources. The option that adds 'data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::Prompt` resource type' records `RenderPrompt`, the permission-only action that fires when a managed prompt is rendered for inference; that tracks usage, whereas edits are management events, which are logged by default. The option with 'a CloudWatch dashboard of invocation metrics' shows counts and latency without identities, and observing behaviour afterwards neither records who changed a prompt nor stops a direct change. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-prereq.html

prompt: A travel company keeps its itinerary-summary prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management and releases new versions through AWS CodePipeline. Twice, a wording change fixed one complaint but broke date formatting for multi-city trips, and nobody noticed until customers reported it. The team has a golden dataset of 400 inputs with expected properties (required JSON fields, date format, no invented flights), including known edge cases. Every candidate version must be checked against the whole dataset within a few minutes before release, the pass rate must be tracked over time, and the release must stop when the rate drops. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Compare the candidate with the current prompt as variants in the prompt builder on several sample inputs, and publish the candidate version if the outputs look right.
Release the candidate version, and create CloudWatch alarms on model invocation errors and latency that trigger a rollback of the release.
Attach a guardrail with contextual grounding checks to the application, so that summaries with invented flights are blocked at run time.
Add a pipeline stage that runs a Step Functions Map state over the dataset, where Lambda checks each output and publishes a CloudWatch pass-rate metric.

explanation: Prompt regression testing means re-running a fixed set of cases against every candidate and comparing the results with expectations before release. A Step Functions Map state fans the 400 cases out in parallel, so the run finishes in minutes; a Lambda function invokes the candidate prompt version for each case and verifies the expected properties, including the edge cases; and publishing the pass rate as a CloudWatch metric gives a history over time and a threshold that the pipeline stage can use to fail the release. This is the pattern the exam guide names for this skill: Lambda to verify expected output, Step Functions to test edge cases, CloudWatch to track prompt regression. The option that will 'compare the candidate with the current prompt as variants' is a useful authoring aid, but it is manual, the builder compares up to three variants on test values entered by hand, and it does not cover the dataset or block a release. The option that will 'release the candidate version' and alarm on errors and latency acts after customers are exposed, and a wrongly formatted date is a successful invocation, so those metrics do not move. The option that attaches 'a guardrail' is a run-time safety control; it does not test JSON fields or date formats and gives no pre-release signal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-create.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-deploy.html

prompt: An insurer moves a claims-extraction workload to a different foundation model because the model it used is being retired. The 700-token prompt, kept in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, was hand-tuned for the old model. On the new model the output misses fields and the format varies between runs. The team has about 30 representative claim texts to test with, but no labelled dataset and no evaluation pipeline yet. It wants a quick improvement now and a repeatable way to compare each revision with the original before promoting it. What should the team do FIRST?

options.text: Fine-tune the new model on the 30 claim texts so that it learns the field layout expected by the old prompt.
Run prompt optimization for the new model, compare the result with the original as variants, and save a version.
Enable prompt caching on the system instruction of the prompt so that the model sees a stable prefix on each call.
Raise the temperature and top-p values in the prompt configuration so that the model explores more candidate outputs.

explanation: Prompts are model-specific, so the first step after a model change is to rewrite the prompt for the new model and compare it against the original. Simple prompt optimization in Amazon Bedrock performs a fast rewrite of a single short prompt for one chosen model, works best for prompts of about 1,000 tokens or less, and needs no evaluation data, which matches a 700-token prompt and a team without labelled data. In the prompt builder the team can then compare the optimized text and the original side by side as variants on the 30 claim texts, keep the better one as the draft, and create a version to promote; repeating this for each revision is the feedback loop. The option to 'fine-tune the new model' needs labelled prompt-completion pairs, which the team does not have, and 30 unlabelled texts cannot teach a field layout. The option to 'enable prompt caching' reduces cost and latency for repeated prefixes; it does not change what the model generates. The option to 'raise the temperature and top-p values' increases randomness, which makes the varying format worse; extraction tasks need lower values and an explicit output format. Once an evaluation dataset exists, evaluation-driven optimization becomes possible. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-optimize.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-create.html

prompt: An insurer wants to automate first-line handling of claim emails with Amazon Bedrock Flows (called Prompt Flows in the exam guide). A prompt classifies each email as `new_claim`, `status_query` or `other`. New claims go to an extraction prompt, status queries go to a knowledge base lookup followed by a reply-drafting prompt, and everything else gets a generic reply. The prompts are maintained in Prompt Management. The operations team wants as little custom code as possible and wants to return production to the previous flow definition within minutes without changing the calling application. Which design decisions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Route with a Lambda function node that contains the branching logic and calls the Converse API with the right prompt for each email class.
Connect the classifier prompt node to a condition node whose conditions test the class and whose default leads to the generic reply.
Route with an iterator node that passes the classifier output to each branch in turn and a collector node that keeps the result.
Have the application call `InvokeFlow` on the test alias `TSTALIASID` so that production always runs the latest working draft.
Publish a version of the flow, point an alias at that version, and have the application call `InvokeFlow` on the alias.

explanation: Flows chains prompts declaratively: a prompt node can reference a prompt from Prompt Management, and its output can feed a condition node, which sends data to different downstream nodes according to conditions written with relational and logical operators. Conditions are evaluated in order and a default condition catches everything else, which gives the three-way routing with no code. For deployment, a flow version is an immutable snapshot and an alias points to a version; the application sends `InvokeFlow` requests to the alias, so rolling back means repointing the alias to the previous version, with no application change. The option that routes with 'a Lambda function node' would work but moves the branching and model calls into custom code, which the team wants to minimise. The option that routes with 'an iterator node' misuses that node: an iterator takes an array and emits its items one by one for the same downstream path, and a collector gathers them back into an array; neither chooses between branches. The option that calls the test alias '`TSTALIASID`' runs the mutable working draft, so every edit reaches production immediately and there is no earlier version to return to. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows-nodes.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows-deploy.html

prompt: A research firm built a due-diligence agent with Strands Agents. One investigation is a single session in which an analyst sends many follow-up requests; the agent keeps working files on local disk and in memory between requests, and a session can stay active for up to 5 hours. The security team requires that the compute, memory and filesystem used for one analyst's session are never shared with another session. The platform team has two engineers and does not want to build session routing or manage container lifecycle. Which hosting option meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Package the agent as an AWS Lambda function with a 15-minute timeout and keep the working files in the function's /tmp directory between invocations.
Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and have the client pass the same runtimeSessionId on every request in an investigation.
Run the agent as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer with sticky sessions enabled on the target group.
Start one Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate per investigation from a custom dispatcher that tracks task addresses and stops the idle tasks.

explanation: AgentCore Runtime gives every session its own dedicated microVM with isolated compute, memory and filesystem, preserves context between invocations that carry the same `runtimeSessionId`, and terminates the microVM and sanitizes memory when the session ends. A session can run for up to 8 hours on microVMs, which covers the 5-hour investigation, and the service handles routing and lifecycle, so the two engineers build nothing extra. The idle timeout defaults to 15 minutes and is configurable. The option to 'Package the agent as an AWS Lambda function' fails because Lambda offers no session affinity: consecutive requests can land on different execution environments, so files in /tmp and in-memory state are not reliably there, and an environment is not reserved for one analyst. The 'Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer with sticky sessions' keeps requests on one task, but each task serves many analysts, so compute and filesystem are shared between sessions. The option to 'Start one Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate per investigation' does isolate sessions, but the custom dispatcher, address tracking and idle cleanup are exactly the routing and lifecycle work the team wants to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-sessions.html

prompt: A wealth-management firm hosts an advisor assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime using microVM compute with default lifecycle settings and no session storage. The agent keeps conversation history in a Python list in process memory. Advisors report that when they return to a client conversation the next morning, the agent has forgotten everything. The firm also wants the agent to recall each advisor's stated preferences (report format, risk vocabulary) in new conversations weeks later, and compliance requires that one advisor's preferences are never retrievable for another advisor. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Write each turn to AgentCore Memory with CreateEvent using the advisor's actorId and the conversation's sessionId, and reload the events when a conversation resumes.
Set idleRuntimeSessionTimeout and maxLifetime to 172,800 seconds so that the microVM that holds each conversation stays alive across two full working days.
Add a user preference memory strategy whose namespace is /preferences/ so that the records extracted from all conversations are stored together in one place.
Add a user preference memory strategy whose namespace includes {actorId}, and retrieve records from that advisor's namespace at the start of new conversations.
Serialize the history list to a file under /tmp in the microVM after each turn and read the file back when the same runtimeSessionId is invoked the next time.

explanation: The microVM behind a Runtime session is ephemeral: by default it stops after 15 idle minutes, and anything in process memory or on local disk is lost. AWS directs you to AgentCore Memory for state that must outlive the compute. Short-term memory stores raw turns as events keyed by `actorId` and `sessionId`, so the agent can reload a conversation the next morning. Long-term memory needs a strategy; a user preference strategy extracts preferences asynchronously in the background, and putting `{actorId}` in the strategy namespace scopes the extracted records to one advisor across all of that advisor's sessions. Setting the timeouts 'to 172,800 seconds' is not possible on microVMs, where both lifecycle settings accept at most 28,800 seconds (8 hours), and it would do nothing for recall weeks later. A namespace of '/preferences/' has no actor component, so every advisor's records share one namespace and can be retrieved for anyone, which breaks the compliance rule. The option to 'Serialize the history list to a file under /tmp' fails because local disk lasts only for the compute lifecycle unless session storage is configured, and here it is not. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/memory-organization.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-lifecycle-settings.html

prompt: A health insurer assigns diagnosis codes to clinical notes. It tested three foundation models from different providers on Amazon Bedrock: each is about 91% accurate alone, each takes about 3 seconds per note, and analysis shows that the models mostly make different mistakes from one another, while a single model repeats the same mistake when it is asked again. The claims system allows 6 seconds per note. Auditors want every model's individual output recorded, and notes on which the models disagree must go to a human coder. Which design gives the GREATEST accuracy improvement within these constraints?

options.text: Call the largest of the three models three times per note at a temperature of 0.7 and accept the code that appears most often across the three responses.
Chain the models in an AWS Step Functions workflow so that each model reviews and corrects the previous model's code before the final answer is stored.
Put a classifier in front of the models that predicts which one model is strongest for each note type, and send the note only to that selected model.
Invoke all three models in an AWS Step Functions Parallel state, then apply majority-vote logic in AWS Lambda and flag split votes for review.

explanation: An ensemble helps most when its members make independent errors, which is what the test showed across the three providers. Running the three calls as branches of a Step Functions Parallel state keeps latency near the slowest single call (about 3 seconds), the execution history records each model's output for the auditors, and custom aggregation logic in Lambda takes the majority code and routes split votes to a human coder. The option to 'Call the largest of the three models three times' is a self-consistency vote, but the stem says a single model repeats its own mistakes, so the three votes are correlated and add little; it also records only one model's output. The option to 'Chain the models' runs three 3-second calls in sequence, about 9 seconds, which exceeds the 6-second limit, and later models tend to anchor on the earlier answer. The 'classifier in front of the models' is a model selection framework, not an ensemble: each note still gets one model's answer at roughly 91% accuracy, there is no disagreement signal for human review, and only one output is recorded. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-parallel.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-bedrock.html

prompt: A logistics company runs a dispatch agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. All production clients invoke the runtime with the qualifier DEFAULT. Last week an engineer updated the runtime with a new container image for testing, and production traffic immediately started using the faulty build. The team wants to keep testing new builds on the same runtime without affecting production, promote a build only by an explicit action, and return production to the previous build within seconds without rebuilding or redeploying a container. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a named endpoint pinned to the current good version, point production clients at it, and move it between versions with UpdateAgentRuntimeEndpoint.
Keep production on the DEFAULT endpoint and roll back by editing the configuration of the latest version so that it references the previous container image.
Create a second AgentCore Runtime for testing and promote a build by repeating the same update against the production runtime after the tests have passed.
Keep production on the DEFAULT endpoint and roll back by pushing the previous container image to Amazon ECR under the same tag that the runtime references.

explanation: Every update to an AgentCore Runtime creates a new immutable version, and the `DEFAULT` endpoint automatically moves to the latest version. That is why the test build reached production. Named endpoints do not move on their own: they stay on the version they were given until someone calls `UpdateAgentRuntimeEndpoint`. Pointing production clients at a named endpoint means new builds can be exercised through `DEFAULT` on the same runtime, promotion is an explicit endpoint update, and rollback is another endpoint update back to the earlier version, which still exists unchanged. The option to 'roll back by editing the configuration of the latest version' relies on something the service does not allow, because versions are immutable once created, and `DEFAULT` would still track every new update. The option to 'Create a second AgentCore Runtime for testing' does not use the same runtime, and returning production to an earlier build means redeploying that build as another update. The option to roll back 'by pushing the previous container image to Amazon ECR' requires rebuilding or re-pushing an image, and production on `DEFAULT` would still receive every test build. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agent-runtime-versioning.html

prompt: An enterprise has about 340 internal REST operations described in OpenAPI specifications and 25 AWS Lambda functions that agents should be able to call. Agent teams use different frameworks (Strands Agents and LangGraph) and want one MCP endpoint rather than framework-specific integrations. In a pilot where every tool definition was loaded into the prompt, input tokens per request tripled and the model often selected the wrong tool. The platform team wants to avoid writing and hosting wrapper code for each API. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Build MCP servers with an MCP SDK that wrap each API group, run them on Amazon ECS, and register every server's URL in each agent's configuration.
Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with OpenAPI and Lambda targets, and have each agent call tools/list at startup and bind every tool returned.
Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with semantic search enabled, add OpenAPI and Lambda targets, and have agents use its search tool.
Define the operations as action groups on Amazon Bedrock Agents by using the OpenAPI schemas, and call those agents from the Strands and LangGraph agents.

explanation: AgentCore Gateway turns OpenAPI specifications and Lambda functions into MCP tools without wrapper code and aggregates all MCP targets behind one virtual MCP server that any MCP client library can reach, whatever the agent framework. With semantic search enabled, the gateway adds the built-in `x_amz_bedrock_agentcore_search` tool, so an agent sends a natural-language query and receives only the relevant tools instead of carrying 365 definitions in every prompt. Semantic search can be enabled only when the gateway is created, so it has to be part of the initial design. The option to 'Build MCP servers with an MCP SDK' is the wrapper code and hosting the team wants to avoid, and it produces many endpoints rather than one. The gateway option in which agents 'call tools/list at startup and bind every tool returned' gives one endpoint but repeats the pilot's problem: every definition is in the prompt, so tokens and wrong selections stay high. The option to 'Define the operations as action groups on Amazon Bedrock Agents' does not give the other frameworks an MCP endpoint; it adds an extra agent hop instead. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Agents Classic, and AWS maps action groups to Gateway MCP tools. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-using-mcp-semantic-search.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-create.html

prompt: A consulting firm hosts an assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Employees sign in through the corporate identity provider, and the runtime validates their JWT. The agent uses two tools. The first reads files from the signed-in employee's Google Drive and must only ever see files that employee can see. The second calls an internal inventory API that accepts only registered service clients and is also used by scheduled runs when no user is present. Security policy forbids long-lived secrets in agent code, environment variables or prompts. Which combination of AgentCore Identity configurations meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use an OAuth credential provider with the client credentials grant for Google Drive so that the agent can read files without prompting employees for consent.
Use an OAuth credential provider with the authorization code grant for Google Drive so that each employee consents and tokens are bound to that user.
Use an OAuth credential provider with the authorization code grant for the inventory API so that every call carries the signed-in employee's own identity.
Place a Google refresh token for each employee in the runtime's environment variables and exchange it for an access token inside the Drive tool's code.
Use an OAuth credential provider with the client credentials grant for the inventory API so that the agent authenticates as a registered service client.

explanation: AgentCore Identity separates user-delegated access from machine-to-machine access. For Google Drive the agent must act on behalf of the signed-in employee, which is the authorization code grant (three-legged OAuth, `USER_FEDERATION` in the SDK): the employee consents once, and the token is kept in the token vault bound to the agent's workload identity and that user, so the agent sees only that user's files. For the inventory API there may be no user at all, so the client credentials grant (two-legged OAuth, `M2M`) is the fit; the agent authenticates as the service client. In both cases the credential provider and vault hold the secrets, not the agent. The 'client credentials grant for Google Drive' makes the agent act as an application rather than as the employee, so access is no longer limited to what that employee can see. The 'authorization code grant for the inventory API' needs an interactive user to consent, which fails for scheduled runs, and the API accepts only service clients. The option to 'Place a Google refresh token for each employee in the runtime's environment variables' puts long-lived secrets exactly where the policy forbids them. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/identity-authentication.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-outbound-auth.html

prompt: A retailer's support agents, built by three teams with different frameworks, call a refund tool through one Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway that uses OAuth inbound authorization. Each agent's system prompt says refunds above 500 USD are not allowed, but a red-team exercise used prompt injection to make one agent issue a 2,000 USD refund. The company needs a control that is evaluated on every refund call regardless of what the model generates, is defined once for all three agents, allows larger refunds only when the caller's token carries a supervisor role, and can be observed before it starts blocking traffic. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic for large refunds to each agent's model calls, and review the guardrail trace before enforcing it.
Attach an AgentCore Policy engine to the gateway with Cedar policies on the refund amount and the role claim, starting in LOG_ONLY mode before ENFORCE.
Add a shared validation library to each agent that checks the refund amount and the user's role before the agent's code sends the tool call to the gateway.
Rewrite the three system prompts with explicit refusal examples for large refunds, and add an evaluation suite that replays the red-team prompts on release.

explanation: Policy in AgentCore intercepts every tool call that passes through the gateway and evaluates it against Cedar policies before the tool runs, outside the agent's code and independent of model output. The engine generates a schema from the gateway's tool definitions, so a policy can test the refund tool's amount parameter, and with OAuth inbound authorization the principal carries JWT claims such as role as tags. One engine on the shared gateway covers all three agents, evaluation is default-deny with forbid-wins, decisions are logged, and the `LOG_ONLY` mode lets the team observe decisions before switching to `ENFORCE`.
