The 'Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic' classifies the text of prompts and responses; it does not deterministically evaluate a tool call's numeric parameter or the caller's role, and it must be attached per agent. The 'shared validation library' sits inside each agent's code, so it is three integrations rather than one definition, and an agent that skips or changes it bypasses the rule. The option to 'Rewrite the three system prompts' still depends on the model obeying instructions, which is the control that prompt injection already defeated. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/policy.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/policy-core-concepts.html

prompt: A bank wants a ReAct-style agent for reconciliation breaks. Each iteration asks a model on Amazon Bedrock for a thought and an action, runs the chosen tool as an AWS Lambda function, and feeds the observation into the next iteration. Some tools query slow mainframe gateways, so a run can take up to 40 minutes. Risk officers require that every thought, action and observation is visible step by step in an execution history, and that a run ends when the model returns a final answer or after 8 iterations, whichever comes first. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: A Standard workflow in AWS Step Functions that loops through a Bedrock InvokeModel task, a Choice state that tests the answer and an iteration counter, and a tool task.
An Express workflow in AWS Step Functions that loops through a Bedrock InvokeModel task, a Choice state that tests the answer and an iteration counter, and a tool task.
A single AWS Lambda function that runs the whole loop in code with an iteration counter, calls the tool functions directly, and writes each step to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
A Standard workflow in AWS Step Functions that runs a Map state over 8 planned tool calls in parallel and then asks the model on Amazon Bedrock to summarize the results.

explanation: A ReAct loop maps directly onto a state machine: a task calls the model through the optimized Bedrock `InvokeModel` integration, a Choice state checks whether the model returned a final answer or the iteration counter in the state has reached 8, a task runs the chosen tool, and the flow returns to the model. The Choice state is the stopping condition. A Standard workflow can run for up to one year and records every state's input and output in its execution history, which gives the risk officers the step-by-step record. The 'Express workflow' with the same loop fails on duration alone: Express workflows can run for at most five minutes, and a run here can take 40. The 'single AWS Lambda function' cannot run longer than 900 seconds, so a 40-minute run is impossible, and log lines are not a per-step execution history. The design that 'runs a Map state over 8 planned tool calls in parallel' is not ReAct: each action must be chosen after seeing the previous observation, so the calls cannot be planned up front and run concurrently, and nothing stops early on a final answer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-bedrock.html

prompt: An agent orchestrated by an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow calls a partner pricing API through a tool Lambda function. During a partner outage, each tool call hung until the function's 15-minute timeout, the workflow retried the task, and the model then asked for the same tool again. Hundreds of executions stayed open for hours and model spend spiked. Healthy runs call the tool in under 5 seconds and can legitimately run for 30 minutes overall because of other steps. The team wants to fail fast on a hung call and to stop sending traffic to the API while it is known to be down. Which combination of changes meets these goals? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Raise the reserved concurrency of the tool function so that hung invocations no longer block the tool calls that are made by the other running executions.
Convert the state machine to an Express workflow so that every execution, including a stuck one, is terminated by the service after at most five minutes.
Set a short TimeoutSeconds on the tool task and the function, with a bounded Retry and a Catch that returns an error observation to the model.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model so that the repeated reasoning steps of stuck executions no longer compete for the on-demand quota.
Record repeated tool failures in an Amazon DynamoDB item with a TTL, and check it before the tool task to skip the call while the circuit is open.

explanation: Two safeguards are missing. First, a timeout: a tool that normally answers in 5 seconds should not be allowed to hang for 15 minutes. A short Lambda timeout and `TimeoutSeconds` on the Task state raise `States.Timeout` quickly, a Retry with a small `MaxAttempts` and backoff bounds the retries, and a Catch turns the failure into an error observation so the model can stop or answer without the tool. Second, a circuit breaker: AWS Prescriptive Guidance describes storing the degraded service's status in DynamoDB with an expiry timestamp removed by TTL; the workflow checks the item first and fails immediately while the circuit is open, so no traffic reaches the API until the record expires. The option to 'Raise the reserved concurrency' lets more invocations hang at once; it neither shortens a hung call nor stops calls to a dead API. The option to 'Convert the state machine to an Express workflow' would also kill healthy runs, which legitimately take up to 30 minutes. The option to 'Purchase Provisioned Throughput' addresses model capacity, not the hung tool, and adds a fixed hourly cost while the wasted reasoning steps continue. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/circuit-breaker.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html

prompt: A company runs an analytics agent whose only tool is an AWS Lambda function that executes model-generated SQL in Amazon Athena. The agent is meant to query the sales_curated database only. A document that a user uploaded contained hidden instructions, and the agent ran a query against the hr_payroll database; the tool's execution role has broad AWS Glue Data Catalog and Amazon S3 read access to the whole data lake. The security team wants a preventive control that holds even if the model is manipulated again and that does not depend on recognizing malicious SQL text. Which change BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Add a system prompt rule and an Amazon Bedrock guardrail denied topic that tell the model never to reference payroll or human resources tables in a query.
Parse each generated statement in the tool function and reject it when a regular expression finds a database name other than sales_curated in the text.
Enable AWS CloudTrail data events on the payroll bucket and alert the security team through Amazon EventBridge whenever the tool's role reads an object.
Scope the tool function's execution role to the sales_curated catalog resources, its S3 prefix and a dedicated Athena workgroup, and nothing else.

explanation: The reliable boundary for an agent is what its tools are permitted to touch, not what the model is told. The tool runs with the Lambda function's execution role, and Athena checks that role's access to the AWS Glue Data Catalog database and tables and to the underlying S3 objects. If the role's identity-based policy allows only the sales_curated catalog resources, its S3 prefix and one workgroup, a query against hr_payroll fails with an access error no matter how the SQL was produced. This is preventive and does not involve inspecting the SQL. The 'system prompt rule and an Amazon Bedrock guardrail denied topic' are model-level, probabilistic controls; the incident was itself a case of the model being manipulated past its instructions. The option to 'Parse each generated statement' with a regular expression is useful parameter validation, but it depends on recognizing malicious SQL text, which the requirement rules out, and it can be evaded through views, quoting or comments. The option to 'Enable AWS CloudTrail data events' and alert is a detective control: it reports the read after the payroll data has already been returned. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/fine-grained-access-to-glue-resources.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-intro-execution-role.html

prompt: A legal-tech company uses an agent in an AWS Step Functions workflow to draft contract amendments. Before an amendment is sent to a counterparty, a lawyer must approve or reject it from a link in an email. Lawyers usually respond within hours but may take up to 3 business days, and the workflow must continue as soon as a decision arrives. If nobody decides within 5 days, the amendment must be escalated to a partner. The company does not want compute or state transitions spent on polling while the workflow waits. Which combination of design elements meets these requirements? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Run the process as a Standard workflow whose approval step is a task that uses the .waitForTaskToken integration pattern to send the token with the review link.
Run the process as an Express workflow whose approval step is a task that uses the .waitForTaskToken integration pattern to send the token with the review link.
Expose the approve and reject links through Amazon API Gateway backed by a Lambda function that calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with the token.
Set HeartbeatSeconds to 300 on the approval task so that the workflow detects quickly when a lawyer has opened the email but has not yet made a decision.
Add a Wait state of 3 days after the email is sent, followed by a task that reads the lawyer's decision from an Amazon DynamoDB table and then branches.
Set TimeoutSeconds on the approval task to 5 days and add a Catch for States.Timeout that routes the execution to a partner escalation step.

explanation: The callback pattern fits human approval. A task that uses `.waitForTaskToken` passes a task token to the notification step and then pauses, with no polling, until the token comes back; a Standard workflow can wait this way for up to one year. The email links call API Gateway, and a Lambda function behind it calls `SendTaskSuccess` or `SendTaskFailure` with the token, so the workflow resumes the moment the lawyer decides. Without a limit the task would wait indefinitely, so `TimeoutSeconds` of 5 days plus a Catch on `States.Timeout` provides the escalation path. The 'Express workflow' version fails because Express workflows do not support the callback pattern and run for at most five minutes. Setting 'HeartbeatSeconds to 300' would break the design: nothing in this flow sends `SendTaskHeartbeat`, so the task would time out five minutes after the email is sent; a heartbeat does not detect an opened email. The 'Wait state of 3 days' holds every amendment for the full 3 days even when the lawyer approves within an hour, so the workflow does not continue as soon as a decision arrives. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html

prompt: A subscription business has an existing Amazon Bedrock agent with an action group whose cancelSubscription action is fulfilled by an AWS Lambda function that contains the billing logic. After several accidental cancellations, the product team requires that the mobile app shows the customer a yes/no prompt with the exact action and parameters before the cancellation runs, and that a refusal is reported back to the agent so that it can continue the conversation. The billing logic must stay in the existing Lambda function, and the team wants the smallest change. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Change the action group executor to return control, and have the mobile app perform the cancellation and send its result in returnControlInvocationResults.
Add an instruction to the agent that it must always ask the customer to type YES before it calls cancelSubscription, and test this with sample dialogues.
Enable user confirmation on the action, and have the mobile app read invocationInputs and reply with a confirmationState of CONFIRM or DENY.
Have the Lambda function start an AWS Step Functions execution that waits for a task token, and return that token to the agent as the action's result.

explanation: User confirmation is a per-action setting on an action group. When the agent decides to call the action, the `InvokeAgent` response returns the action and its elicited parameters in `invocationInputs` instead of running it. The app shows the prompt and sends the answer back in `sessionState.returnControlInvocationResults` with `confirmationState` set to `CONFIRM` or `DENY`. On confirm, the agent invokes the existing Lambda function; on deny, the agent is told and carries on. Only the action setting and the app's response handling change. The option to 'Change the action group executor to return control' also pauses the agent, but return of control hands fulfillment to the application in place of the Lambda function, so the app would have to carry out the cancellation itself. The option to 'Add an instruction to the agent' depends on the model following it every time and gives the app no structured action and parameters to display. The Step Functions option that 'waits for a task token' requires rewriting the function and building separate approval plumbing, which is a far larger change. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Agents Classic in maintenance mode; existing agents and these APIs continue to work. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-userconfirmation.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-returncontrol.html

prompt: A retailer's Strands agent uses a model on Amazon Bedrock with two Lambda-backed tools, get_order_status and get_order_history. Both tool descriptions read 'Gets order information', and order_id is declared as a plain string. Traces show the model passing values such as 'order #12345' or a customer email as order_id; the function then raises an unhandled exception and the customer receives a generic failure. In other traces the model calls get_order_history when the customer asked where a parcel is. Order IDs are always 10 digits. Which combination of changes MOST improves the reliability of these tool calls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Catch every exception in the function and return an empty result with a success status so that the agent loop always continues through to a final answer.
Validate order_id in the function and return a tool result with an error status and a message that states the expected format so that the model can retry.
Wrap the tool invocation in automatic retries with exponential backoff so that the same call is repeated three times whenever the function raises an error.
Rewrite each tool description to say when to use it and what it returns, and constrain order_id in the input schema with a 10-digit pattern.
Raise the model's temperature and maximum output tokens so that it considers more candidate tool calls before it commits to one of the two tools.

explanation: Two things are wrong: the tool definitions and the error path. The model chooses a tool and fills its parameters from the name, description and input schema. Identical vague descriptions give it no basis for choosing between the two tools, and a bare string type says nothing about the format. Descriptions that state when to use each tool and what it returns, plus a schema that constrains order_id to 10 digits, fix selection and reduce malformed arguments. For the arguments that still arrive malformed, the function should validate them and return a tool result marked as an error (the Converse API `toolResult` block has a `status` of `success` or `error`) with a message the model can act on, so it corrects the value or asks the customer. The option to 'return an empty result with a success status' hides the failure: the model concludes that no order exists and answers wrongly. The 'automatic retries with exponential backoff' repeat a deterministic validation failure with the same bad input, which adds latency and never succeeds. The option to 'Raise the model's temperature' makes tool selection and argument formatting less consistent, not more. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_ToolResultBlock.html

prompt: A media company is exposing two sets of tools to its agents through MCP. The first set performs quick lookups against Amazon DynamoDB; each call finishes in under a second, keeps no state between calls, and traffic is bursty with hours of no requests. The second set drives headless browser sessions to render and compare web pages: a single tool call can run for 25 minutes, streams progress notifications, and relies on a browser process kept in memory across calls in the same MCP session. The company wants the MOST cost-effective hosting that meets the technical needs of both sets. Which approach should it choose?

options.text: Host both sets as stateless MCP servers on AWS Lambda functions behind function URLs, and store the browser session data in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Host both sets as MCP servers in one Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer with a minimum of two running tasks.
Host the lookup tools on Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate and the browser tools on AWS Lambda with the timeout and memory set to their maximum values.
Host the lookup tools as a stateless MCP server on AWS Lambda and the browser tools as an MCP server on Amazon ECS with session affinity.

explanation: The two tool sets have opposite profiles. The lookups are short, stateless and bursty, which suits a stateless MCP server on Lambda: it scales to zero during the idle hours and bills per request. The browser tools are long-running and stateful: a call can last 25 minutes and depends on a live browser process in memory across calls in a session, which needs a long-lived container such as an ECS task with requests for a session routed to the same task. Agents reach both through the same MCP client library, so the split is invisible to them. Hosting 'both sets as stateless MCP servers on AWS Lambda' fails for the browser tools: a Lambda invocation cannot exceed 900 seconds, and a running browser process cannot be parked in a DynamoDB table between invocations. Hosting 'both sets as MCP servers in one Amazon ECS service' works technically but keeps tasks running through hours of no lookup traffic, so it is not the most cost-effective choice. The option that puts 'the browser tools on AWS Lambda' has the assignment backwards: the maximum Lambda timeout is still 15 minutes, and the lightweight lookups would pay for idle containers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-mcp-protocol-contract.html

prompt: An insurer is building a claims system with Strands Agents. An intake agent extracts claim data, then a fraud agent scores the claim. Claims with a high score go to an investigator agent and all others go to an adjuster agent. If the adjuster finds a missing document, the claim returns to the intake agent and the sequence repeats. Regulators require that the possible transitions between agents are defined by developers in advance and that claims with the same intermediate results follow the same path. Which multi-agent pattern BEST fits these requirements?

options.text: A Graph in which the agents are nodes and developers define conditional edges, including an edge from the adjuster agent back to the intake agent.
A Swarm in which the four agents share context and each agent decides when to hand the claim off to whichever agent it judges to be most suitable.
An orchestrator agent that is given the four specialist agents as tools and decides at run time which specialist to call next for each claim.
A Workflow tool in which the four agents are tasks in a dependency graph and independent tasks are executed in parallel wherever possible.

explanation: The Strands documentation describes Graph as a structured, developer-defined flowchart: developers define all nodes and edges in advance, and it is the pattern to use for a process that needs conditional logic, branching or loops with a deterministic execution flow. The claims process is exactly that: a conditional branch on the fraud score and a loop from the adjuster back to intake, with the allowed transitions fixed in code, so the same intermediate results always lead down the same path. In a 'Swarm' the developer supplies a pool of agents and the agents themselves decide the path through autonomous handoffs; the route is emergent, which conflicts with transitions defined in advance. The 'orchestrator agent that is given the four specialist agents as tools' (agents as tools) leaves the choice of the next specialist to the orchestrator's model at run time, so the order is not fixed by developers. The 'Workflow tool' runs a pre-defined task graph that is a DAG; its flow is fixed by dependencies, so it cannot express the loop back to intake or choose a branch from the fraud score. AWS Prescriptive Guidance lists Swarm, Graph and Workflow as the built-in Strands coordination models. Read more: https://strandsagents.com/docs/user-guide/sdk/multi-agent/multi-agent-patterns/ https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/agentic-ai-frameworks/strands-agents.html

prompt: A claims processor runs a document-extraction pipeline on an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock, invoked by AWS Lambda functions with the model ID in one AWS Region. The model supports Provisioned Throughput. Volume is steady around the clock and has stayed within 5% of the same tokens per minute for a year. The pipeline now receives ThrottlingException errors at its on-demand quota, and a further quota increase was declined. Contracts require that prompts are processed only in that Region, and the validated prompts must keep using this model. Finance has confirmed the workload will run unchanged for at least 6 months and wants the lowest cost that guarantees the throughput. Which option meets these requirements?

options.text: Switch the Lambda functions to a cross-Region inference profile for the same model so that requests can draw on capacity in other Regions.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model with no commitment so that the capacity can be deleted at any time if the volume changes.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model with a 6-month commitment and invoke the provisioned model ARN from the Lambda functions.
Deploy an open-weight model of similar size to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint in the Region and route the pipeline to it.

explanation: Provisioned Throughput buys model units that deliver a fixed level of throughput for one model in one Region, billed hourly, so it removes the dependence on shared on-demand quota while keeping processing in the Region. AWS offers no commitment, 1-month and 6-month terms, and the hourly price is more discounted the longer the commitment. With a flat, year-long load profile and a confirmed 6-month horizon, the 6-month term is the cheapest way to guarantee the throughput. The functions then pass the provisioned model ARN as the model ID. The 'cross-Region inference profile' may relieve throttling, but it routes requests to other Regions, which breaks the contractual residency rule, and it is still on-demand capacity rather than a guarantee. Provisioned Throughput 'with no commitment' meets the throughput need but at a higher hourly price; its flexibility has no value when the workload is fixed for 6 months. The option to 'Deploy an open-weight model' to SageMaker AI changes the model, which the validated prompts do not allow, and adds endpoint operations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: A law firm fine-tuned an open-weight LLM and hosts it itself on Amazon SageMaker AI because the weights must stay in the firm's account. The model summarizes deposition transcripts: request payloads are up to 300 MB, and one summary takes 10 to 25 minutes on a GPU instance. About 40 transcripts arrive per day in bursts during business hours and none overnight or at weekends. Paralegals need each summary within about an hour of upload and want to be notified when it is ready. The firm wants the lowest cost that meets these needs. Which deployment should it use?

options.text: A real-time endpoint with target tracking auto scaling on invocations per instance and a minimum of one GPU instance.
An Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero instances on queue backlog and publishes results through Amazon SNS.
A Serverless Inference endpoint with the maximum memory size and provisioned concurrency during business hours only.
A nightly batch transform job that reads the day's transcripts from Amazon S3 and writes all summaries before morning.

explanation: SageMaker AI Asynchronous Inference queues requests, reads the payload from Amazon S3 and writes the result to S3. It supports payloads up to 1 GB and processing times up to one hour, can notify through Amazon SNS on success or error, and can scale the instance count to zero when the queue is empty, with scaling driven by the backlog metric. That covers the 300 MB transcripts, the 25-minute runs, the notification and the idle nights and weekends, and requests that arrive at zero instances are queued until capacity starts, which fits the one-hour expectation. The 'real-time endpoint' is limited to 25 MB payloads and 60 seconds of processing for regular responses, so these requests cannot run on it, and one GPU instance would be billed all night. The 'Serverless Inference endpoint' allows 4 MB payloads and 60 seconds, offers at most 6 GB of memory and does not support GPUs. The 'nightly batch transform job' handles the size and duration but delivers summaries the next morning, not within about an hour of upload. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/async-inference.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model-options.html

prompt: A team is deploying a 70-billion-parameter open-weight LLM to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on a multi-GPU instance, using a large model inference (LMI) container. The model artifacts are a single 140 GB model.tar.gz object in Amazon S3. Endpoint creation runs for a long time and then fails. Amazon CloudWatch Logs show the artifact still being downloaded and extracted, followed by a health check timeout; the same container deploys a 7-billion-parameter model successfully. Which combination of changes will MOST likely allow the endpoint to reach InService? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Upload the artifacts uncompressed under an S3 prefix and reference them through ModelDataSource with CompressionType set to None.
Raise the initial instance count of the production variant to four so that the model download is spread across several instances.
Increase ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds and ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds on the production variant.
Deploy the model to a Serverless Inference endpoint with the maximum memory size so that SageMaker AI manages model loading.
Increase the read timeout and retry count of the SDK client that calls InvokeEndpoint so that slow first responses succeed.

explanation: The symptoms point to model load time, a problem specific to very large models: the container is healthy for a small model, but 140 GB cannot be downloaded, extracted and loaded onto the GPUs before the default timeouts expire. AWS recommends deploying large models uncompressed, because compressing and then decompressing a model with billions of parameters takes significant time; the artifacts go under an S3 prefix and are referenced with `ModelDataSource` (`S3DataType` of `S3Prefix`, `CompressionType` of `None`). AWS also documents raising `ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds` for large models and `ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds` when logs show a health check timeout on a correctly configured container. Raising 'the initial instance count of the production variant to four' does not split the work: every instance must download and load the full model, so each one hits the same timeout. A 'Serverless Inference endpoint' offers at most 6 GB of memory and no GPUs, so it cannot host this model. Increasing 'the read timeout and retry count of the SDK client' affects calls to an endpoint that is already InService; this endpoint fails during creation, before any invocation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/large-model-inference-hosting.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/large-model-inference-uncompressed.html

prompt: A company hosts three fine-tuned 7-billion-parameter models for internal tools, each on its own Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with one ml.g5.12xlarge instance (4 GPUs). Each model fits on a single GPU, average GPU utilization is below 15%, and the tools are used only during business hours. Users have agreed that the first requests after an idle period may fail and be retried for a few minutes while capacity starts. The company wants the LARGEST reduction in hosting cost without changing the models. Which combination of actions should it take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move each model to a Serverless Inference endpoint so that the company pays only for the compute used during each inference request.
Keep the three endpoints and register each production variant with Application Auto Scaling using a minimum capacity of zero instances.
Replace each endpoint's instance with an ml.g5.48xlarge instance so that every model can serve more concurrent requests per instance.
Deploy the three models as inference components on one endpoint, with each component reserving one accelerator on shared instances.
Set the endpoint's managed instance scaling minimum to zero and add a step scaling policy on a CloudWatch alarm to scale out from zero.

explanation: Two sources of waste exist: twelve GPUs for three models that need one each, and instances running all night. Inference components let several models share one endpoint's instances, with each component declaring the accelerators and memory it needs, so three single-GPU models pack onto one 4-GPU instance instead of three. An endpoint that hosts inference components can also scale in to zero instances: managed instance scaling is set with `MinInstanceCount` of 0, component copies scale to zero, and a step scaling policy attached to a CloudWatch alarm scales back out when requests arrive. AWS notes that provisioning takes several minutes and invocations fail during that time, which the users have accepted. A 'Serverless Inference endpoint' does not support GPUs and offers at most 6 GB of memory, so it cannot host these models. Registering each existing variant with 'a minimum capacity of zero instances' is not possible: an endpoint can scale to and from zero instances only if it hosts inference components. Moving to 'an ml.g5.48xlarge instance' per endpoint adds GPUs to endpoints that already use under 15% of what they have, which raises cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/endpoint-auto-scaling-zero-instances.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/realtime-endpoints-deploy-models.html

prompt: A company serves a self-hosted LLM for a chat product from an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with response streaming. Requests generate anywhere from 50 to 4,000 output tokens, so one request can occupy a GPU for 1 to 60 seconds. Auto scaling uses target tracking on SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance. During unpredictable traffic spikes, time to first token degrades for several minutes before new instances are added, even though invocations per minute rise only moderately. GPU instances take a few minutes to become ready, so the scaling signal must fire as early as possible. Which change BEST addresses the problem?

options.text: Lower the target value for SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance so that the existing policy adds instances at a smaller request count.
Replace the policy with target tracking on the CPUUtilization metric of the endpoint's instances, with a target value of 50 percent.
Add scheduled scaling actions that raise the minimum instance count during the hours of the day when spikes have been seen before.
Use target tracking on the high-resolution SageMakerVariantConcurrentRequestsPerModelHighResolution predefined metric.

explanation: For LLMs the load on an instance is set by how many requests are in flight and for how long, not by how many arrive per minute. A burst of long generations saturates the GPUs while the invocation count barely moves, so a policy on invocations per instance reacts late. SageMaker AI provides the `ConcurrentRequestsPerModel` metric (and `ConcurrentRequestsPerCopy` for inference components) as high-resolution metrics that are emitted more frequently than standard CloudWatch metrics, so a target tracking policy on the corresponding predefined metric scales out much more quickly. That gives the earliest signal, which matters when GPU instances need minutes to start. The option to 'Lower the target value' keeps a one-minute request count that cannot tell a 1-second request from a 60-second one; it over-provisions in quiet periods and still lags when long generations pile up. Target tracking on 'the CPUUtilization metric' watches the wrong resource, because token generation is bound by the GPU and CPU can stay low while requests queue. The 'scheduled scaling actions' assume the spikes recur at known hours, but the stem says they are unpredictable. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/endpoint-auto-scaling-add-code-define.html

prompt: A telecom's support assistant sends every question to a large model on Amazon Bedrock. Analysis of 200,000 conversations shows that about 85% are routine (plan details, password resets) and 15% need multi-step reasoning over policy. The company must cut inference cost substantially and improve p95 latency for routine questions, while answer quality on the complex questions must not drop. It has no labeled training data and no ML engineers, and a much smaller, cheaper model is already available to it through the same API. Which approach BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Send each question to the small model first and escalate to the large model only when its structured output flags low confidence.
Send each question to both models in parallel and return the large model's answer whenever the two answers differ from each other.
Fine-tune the small model on past conversations so that it can replace the large model for both the routine and the complex questions.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the large model so that the price per token falls and response latency becomes more consistent.

explanation: This is API-based model cascading. The small model handles every question first; because about 85% are routine, most traffic is answered at the small model's lower price and lower latency. The small model is prompted to return a structured result that includes an escalation or confidence flag, and the application calls the large model only for flagged questions, so the complex 15% still get the large model's quality at the cost of one extra short call. No training data or ML expertise is needed, only orchestration code and a threshold tuned on sample conversations. Sending 'each question to both models in parallel' pays for the large model on every request, so cost goes up rather than down. The option to 'Fine-tune the small model' needs labeled data and ML skills the company does not have, and removing the large model puts quality on the multi-step questions at risk. The option to 'Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the large model' still sends routine questions to the slowest, most expensive model; it is a capacity commitment billed hourly, not a way to make routine answers faster. The Well-Architected Generative AI Lens recommends right-sizing model selection to the task for cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/gencost01-bp01.html

prompt: A startup fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B in an Amazon SageMaker AI training job; the weights are in Amazon S3 in Hugging Face safetensors format. Its application already calls Amazon Bedrock models through InvokeModel. Traffic to the fine-tuned model is a few hundred requests per day in unpredictable clusters with idle gaps of several hours. The two-person team does not want to manage endpoints, instances or scaling policies, does not want to pay for an always-on instance, and accepts that the first request after an idle period may need client retries. Which deployment option BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on one GPU instance and call it from the application through InvokeEndpoint.
Import the weights with Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import and invoke the model on demand, retrying on ModelNotReadyException.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint with the maximum memory size and call it through InvokeEndpoint.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero, and exchange requests and results through S3.

explanation: Custom Model Import brings a model customized elsewhere, such as in SageMaker AI, into Amazon Bedrock from S3; Llama 3.1 is a supported architecture. The imported model is invoked with `InvokeModel` or `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` on demand, so the application keeps its existing Bedrock integration and the team manages no endpoint, instance or scaling policy. Bedrock adjusts the number of running model copies with demand and bills for running copies in 5-minute windows from the first successful call. When a model that has been removed is invoked again, Bedrock restores it and the call can return `ModelNotReadyException`, which AWS says to handle with retries; the team has accepted that. The 'real-time endpoint on one GPU instance' bills for the instance through every idle gap and must be operated by the team. The 'Serverless Inference endpoint' offers at most 6 GB of memory and no GPUs, which is not workable for an 8-billion-parameter LLM. The 'Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero' avoids idle cost, but the team would own an endpoint and its scaling policies and would have to rework the application around S3 request and result objects. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-import-model.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/invoke-imported-model.html

prompt: A logistics company runs a legacy order-management system that already publishes an OrderDelayed event to a custom Amazon EventBridge event bus. Three other teams consume the event through their own rules. A new team must draft a customer apology for every delayed order by calling an Amazon Bedrock model; each call takes about 40 seconds. During storms the legacy system emits 1,500 events within a few minutes, and the account's Bedrock quota supports about 10 concurrent invocations of the model. Every draft must be ready within 3 hours, no event may be lost, failed events must be kept for inspection, and neither the legacy system nor the existing consumers may be changed. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a rule that sends the event to an Amazon SQS FIFO queue using one message group ID, and process the queue with an AWS Lambda function.
Change the legacy system to also write each event to an Amazon SQS queue, and process the queue with a Lambda function that its event source mapping limits to 10 concurrent executions.
Add a rule that targets an Amazon SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue, consumed by a Lambda event source mapping with maximum concurrency 10.
Add a rule that invokes a Lambda function directly, and wrap the Bedrock call in SDK retries with a long exponential backoff.

explanation: Adding a new rule on the existing bus leaves the legacy publisher and the other consumers untouched, which is the point of event-driven loose coupling. The SQS standard queue absorbs the burst durably, the dead-letter queue keeps events that keep failing, and the maximum concurrency setting on the Lambda event source mapping caps the number of concurrent function instances at 10, so the Bedrock quota is respected. At 10 parallel 40-second calls, 1,500 events finish in about 100 minutes, inside the 3-hour limit. The option that uses 'an Amazon SQS FIFO queue using one message group ID' fails the deadline: for FIFO queues concurrency is capped by the number of message group IDs, so one group means one call at a time, roughly 16 hours of work. The option to 'change the legacy system' violates the rule that the legacy system must not be modified. The option that 'invokes a Lambda function directly' has no buffer and no concurrency cap: hundreds of concurrent executions hit the model at once, sit in retries, and events whose asynchronous retries are exhausted are dropped unless extra failure handling is added. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-sqs-scaling.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-targets.html

prompt: A SaaS ticketing platform calls a company's webhook for every new ticket and expects an HTTP 200 within 3 seconds; otherwise it retries and eventually disables the webhook. The company wants to enrich each ticket with a summary and a suggested priority from an Amazon Bedrock model (8 to 25 seconds per call) and write the result back through the SaaS REST API. That API requires OAuth client-credentials authentication and accepts at most 20 requests per second, while ticket bursts reach 200 per second during incidents. The security team forbids fetching or handling the OAuth client secret in function code. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an Amazon API Gateway Lambda proxy integration with the maximum integration timeout; the function calls Bedrock, posts the result to the SaaS API, and then returns 200.
Have a webhook Lambda function put the ticket on an EventBridge bus and return 200; an enrichment function's result event goes to an API destination with an OAuth connection and a rate limit of 20.

Have a webhook Lambda function send the ticket to an SQS queue and return 200; a consumer function calls Bedrock, reads the client secret from AWS Secrets Manager, obtains a token, and posts the result to the SaaS API.
Have a webhook Lambda function start a Step Functions Express workflow and return 200; the workflow invokes Bedrock and posts the result with an HTTP Task that uses an EventBridge connection.

explanation: Acknowledging the webhook immediately and doing the slow model call asynchronously satisfies the 3-second rule. An EventBridge API destination delivers the result to the SaaS HTTPS endpoint; its connection holds the OAuth client-credentials configuration, which EventBridge stores in AWS Secrets Manager and uses on its own, so no function code touches the secret. The API destination's invocation rate limit per second holds delivery at 20 requests per second and EventBridge retries the backlog (a dead-letter queue is advisable for long incidents). The design with 'the maximum integration timeout' keeps the webhook waiting for the 8 to 25 second model call, so the SaaS platform never gets its 200 in time. The design where the consumer 'reads the client secret from AWS Secrets Manager, obtains a token' is exactly the credential handling in code that security forbids. The design with 'an HTTP Task that uses an EventBridge connection' does keep the secret out of code, because an HTTP Task also authenticates through an EventBridge connection, but nothing in it limits the write-back rate, so a 200-per-second burst exceeds the SaaS limit of 20. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-api-destinations.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-target-connection.html

prompt: A bank's platform team must let developers and one application role use a single Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock from eu-central-1 through the EU geographic cross-Region inference profile. The security policy states that principals must not be able to invoke any other model, must not be able to call the foundation model directly and bypass the inference profile, and that developers must sign in with the corporate identity provider and never hold long-lived credentials. A first test with a policy that allows bedrock:InvokeModel only on the inference profile ARN returns AccessDeniedException. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Allow the foundation-model ARN in each Region of the profile, conditioned on bedrock:InferenceProfileArn matching the profile ARN.
Allow the foundation-model ARN in eu-central-1 only, because requests made through the profile are always authorized in the source Region.
Allow arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/* so that the profile can route to whichever Region has capacity for the request.
Federate the identity provider with IAM Identity Center and assign developers a permission set that carries the scoped policy.
Issue each developer a long-term Amazon Bedrock API key with a 90-day expiry and rotate the keys through a shared vault.

explanation: Invoking through an inference profile needs permission on the profile and on the underlying foundation model in each Region the profile can route to; the documentation states that when you specify an inference profile you must also specify the foundation model in each Region associated with it. Scoping those foundation-model statements with the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key means the model can be invoked only through that profile, so a direct single-Region call is denied, and no other model is granted. Federating the corporate identity provider with IAM Identity Center gives developers temporary role credentials from a permission set, which meets the no long-lived credentials rule. Allowing the model 'in eu-central-1 only' still fails with AccessDenied when the profile routes to another EU Region, and without the condition it permits direct invocation. Allowing the wildcard foundation-model ARN fixes the error but grants every model, breaking least privilege. Issuing 'a long-term Amazon Bedrock API key' creates a long-lived credential backed by an IAM user, which the policy prohibits; AWS positions long-term keys for exploration only. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles-prereq.html

prompt: A healthcare SaaS company signs users in to its web application through an Amazon Cognito user pool that is federated with each customer's SAML identity provider. For low-latency streaming, the browser calls Amazon Bedrock directly with temporary AWS credentials. Users in the clinician group may invoke a large model and a small model; users in the front-desk group may invoke only the small model. The access decision must be enforced by AWS rather than by front-end code, a user must not be able to raise their own privileges by changing anything they can edit, and the company does not want to add a backend proxy in front of Bedrock. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use one authenticated IAM role that allows both models, and have the application read the cognito:groups claim to hide the large model from front-desk users.
Use identity pool rule-based role mapping on a custom:role user attribute that users can update on their profile page in the application.
Route calls through Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda authorizer that checks the group claim before a Lambda function invokes Bedrock.
Attach an IAM role to each user pool group, and configure the Cognito identity pool to choose the role from the token; scope each role to its model ARNs.

explanation: When IAM roles are attached to user pool groups, the ID token carries the cognito:roles and cognito:preferred_role claims, and an identity pool set to choose the role from the token issues temporary credentials for that role. Each role's policy allows bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream only on the permitted model ARNs, so IAM enforces the difference on every direct call from the browser, group membership is controlled by administrators, and no proxy is needed. The option with 'one authenticated IAM role that allows both models' enforces the rule only in front-end code; a front-desk user holding those credentials can call the large model directly. The option that maps on 'a custom:role user attribute that users can update' violates the privilege requirement: Cognito's guidance warns that if a mapped claim can be modified by the end user, any user can assume the role. The option that routes 'through Amazon API Gateway with a Lambda authorizer' would enforce access correctly, but it introduces the backend proxy the company ruled out. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/role-based-access-control.html

prompt: A hospital group operates in a country that has no AWS Region. National law requires patient records and scanned documents to remain physically in the group's own data centre. The regulator accepts that de-identified text excerpts are processed by a foundation model in an AWS Region in the EU, provided that this traffic never crosses the public internet and that only model-invocation actions can be reached over the path. The group already has an AWS Outposts rack in its data centre, connected to eu-central-1 over private connectivity, and wants to use AWS APIs for storage and for the de-identification service. Which architecture meets these requirements?

options.text: Store documents in Amazon S3 on Outposts, de-identify them on Outposts compute, and call Bedrock through an interface VPC endpoint with a restrictive endpoint policy.
Store documents in an Amazon S3 bucket in eu-central-1 encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, and build an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on that bucket.
Store documents in Amazon S3 on Outposts, de-identify them on Outposts compute, and call the public Bedrock endpoint over the data centre's internet link using TLS and SigV4.
Deploy the storage and de-identification service in an AWS Wavelength Zone in the country, and call Bedrock from there over the carrier gateway.

explanation: With Amazon S3 on Outposts, object data is always stored on the Outpost and never in an AWS Region, so the records stay physically in the data centre while the team still uses S3 APIs. De-identification runs on Outposts compute next to the data, and only the excerpts leave. Calling Bedrock through an interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime keeps the traffic on AWS PrivateLink and the private connection instead of the internet, and an endpoint policy can restrict the path to actions such as bedrock:InvokeModel. The design with 'an Amazon S3 bucket in eu-central-1' moves the source documents out of the country, which encryption does not cure. The design that calls 'the public Bedrock endpoint over the data centre's internet link' keeps data local but sends prompts across the public internet, which the regulator excludes even with TLS. The design in 'an AWS Wavelength Zone' places data in a telecommunications carrier's facility rather than the group's own data centre; Wavelength exists to give low latency to mobile and edge users, not on-premises residency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/s3-outposts/S3onOutposts.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html

prompt: A team ships a RAG assistant (Lambda code, prompt templates and infrastructure templates) through AWS CodePipeline with the stages Source, Build, DeployStaging and DeployProd. Three incidents occurred last quarter: a prompt change that lowered groundedness reached production, a release contained a hardcoded API key, and a faulty production deployment stayed live for two hours until someone redeployed the previous version. The team now requires that a release is blocked when its score on a 200-question golden dataset is below a threshold, that secrets and vulnerable dependencies are detected before any deployment, and that production returns to the last good release automatically when the stage fails or its error alarm fires, with no manual steps. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a manual approval action before DeployProd so that a QA lead reviews the evaluation report and the scan findings for each release candidate before it goes live.
Add AWS CodeBuild actions that run secret and dependency scans in Build and score the golden dataset against staging, exiting non-zero on findings or a low score.
Enable automatic retry on stage failure for DeployProd so that a failed production deployment is attempted again without an operator.
Enable model invocation logging in production and alarm on a groundedness metric that notifies the on-call engineer through Amazon SNS.
Configure DeployProd for automatic rollback on failure, and add an On Success condition with a CloudWatchAlarm rule whose result is Rollback.

explanation: A CodeBuild action fails the pipeline when its build exits with a non-zero code, so running secret and dependency scanners in the Build stage and an evaluation script against the staging deployment creates automated security and quality gates: a release with findings or a golden-dataset score below the threshold never reaches DeployProd. For recovery, a CodePipeline stage can be configured for automatic rollback on failure, which returns the stage to its most recent successful execution, and an On Success condition with a CloudWatchAlarm rule and a Rollback result rolls the stage back when the production alarm fires after deployment. The 'manual approval action' could catch problems but breaks the no-manual-steps requirement. 'Automatic retry on stage failure' re-runs the same faulty revision instead of restoring the last good one. 'Model invocation logging in production' with an alarm that only notifies an engineer detects a regression after users see it and neither blocks the release nor restores the previous one. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/stage-rollback-auto.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/stage-conditions.html

prompt: A platform team operates a central GenAI gateway for 14 product teams that share one AWS account. Every model call goes through Amazon API Gateway to a Lambda function that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with the function's own execution role. Callers already authenticate with IAM (SigV4) using their corporate federated roles, and that must remain the access control. The team must now give each product team its own request rate limit and monthly request quota so that one team cannot starve the others, and finance must see each team's monthly Bedrock spend in AWS Cost Explorer without anyone parsing logs. The platform team wants managed features rather than a custom metering store. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use a REST API with one API key and usage plan per team for throttling and quotas, and keep IAM authorization on the methods.
Move to an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, and set route-level throttling values that correspond to each product team's limits.
Create an application inference profile per team with a cost allocation tag, and have the gateway invoke the model through the caller's team profile.
Remove IAM authorization and use each team's API key as its credential so that identity, throttling and quotas come from one mechanism.
Enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3 and schedule a monthly Amazon Athena query that groups input and output token counts by identity.arn for finance.

explanation: API Gateway REST APIs support usage plans: an API key identifies each team and the plan applies a per-key throttle rate, burst and quota, while IAM authorization continues to decide who may call the API. AWS states that API keys are for identifying clients and must not be used for authentication or authorization, and that usage plan limits are applied on a best-effort basis, which is acceptable for fairness between internal teams. For cost, an application inference profile is a user-created profile for tracking cost and usage; tagging one per team and invoking the model through it makes the on-demand spend appear under that cost allocation tag in Cost Explorer. Moving 'to an HTTP API' fails because HTTP APIs have no API keys, usage plans or per-client throttling, and route throttling applies to all callers together. Using 'each team's API key as its credential' removes the required IAM access control and contradicts AWS guidance. The option that groups 'token counts by identity.arn' requires log parsing, which is excluded, and every call is made by the same Lambda execution role, so the grouping cannot separate teams. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-api-usage-plans.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles.html

prompt: An insurer summarises claims asynchronously. Uploads place messages on an Amazon SQS standard queue (visibility timeout 1,800 seconds, redrive policy with maxReceiveCount 3 to a dead-letter queue). A Lambda function with a 300-second timeout receives batches of 10 and calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API once per message. During morning peaks Lambda scales to several hundred concurrent executions, Bedrock returns ThrottlingException for some calls, and the function raises the exception. The team observes that claims that were already summarised are summarised again two or three times, and that valid claims end up in the dead-letter queue. Which combination of changes resolves these problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Convert the queue to a FIFO queue with content-based deduplication so that a claim that was summarised once is not delivered again.
Increase the batch size to 100 with a batching window so that fewer invocations compete for the model's tokens-per-minute quota.
Set maximum concurrency on the event source mapping to a value that the model's Bedrock quota can sustain during the peak.
Lower maxReceiveCount to 1 so that a message whose batch failed is moved aside immediately instead of being processed again.
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures, catch errors per message, and return only the failed message IDs in batchItemFailures.

explanation: Two separate faults are visible. First, nothing limits how far the event source mapping scales, so hundreds of concurrent functions exceed the model quota; the maximum concurrency setting on an SQS event source mapping caps the number of concurrent function instances the queue can invoke, which removes most throttling at the source while the queue holds the backlog. Second, by default when a function raises an error the whole batch becomes visible again, including messages that were processed successfully, which explains the repeated summaries and why healthy messages reach maxReceiveCount and move to the dead-letter queue. With ReportBatchItemFailures the function returns only the failed message IDs and the rest are deleted. 'Content-based deduplication' on a FIFO queue deduplicates messages that are sent twice within the deduplication interval; it does not stop redelivery of a message that was received but not deleted. A 'batch size to 100' makes each failure re-drive ten times more successful work. Lowering 'maxReceiveCount to 1' sends valid claims to the dead-letter queue after a single throttled batch; AWS recommends at least 5. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-sqs-errorhandling.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-sqs-scaling.html

prompt: A company exposes a text-generation endpoint to partners through an Amazon API Gateway REST API with a Lambda proxy integration that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. About 18% of partner requests are malformed: the messages array is missing, maxTokens is sent as a string, or required headers are absent. Each of these requests still invokes the Lambda function, and some reach Bedrock and come back as ValidationException. The company wants malformed requests rejected with HTTP 400 before any compute runs, wants the request contract to live in the API definition that partners export as OpenAPI, and wants the LEAST operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a schema-validation library to the Lambda function and return HTTP 400 at the start of the handler when the payload is invalid.
Define a JSON schema model for the request body and assign a request validator for body and parameters to the method.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the stage and write rules that inspect the JSON body for the required keys and block other requests.
Migrate the endpoint to an HTTP API and use parameter mapping to drop requests whose body does not match the expected shape.

explanation: API Gateway REST APIs offer basic request validation. A request validator assigned to a method checks that required URI, query string and header parameters are present and that the payload adheres to the JSON schema model configured for the method. When validation fails, API Gateway immediately returns a 400 response, publishes the result to CloudWatch Logs and does not call the integration, so neither Lambda nor Bedrock is invoked. The model and validator are part of the API definition and can be included in the exported OpenAPI document, so the contract is visible to partners with nothing extra to run. Adding 'a schema-validation library to the Lambda function' still invokes compute for every malformed request, which is what the company wants to avoid. Using 'an AWS WAF web ACL' can block some requests before the backend, but WAF rules do not validate types against a schema and the contract would live outside the API definition, adding rules to maintain. Migrating 'to an HTTP API' fails because HTTP APIs do not support request validation; parameter mapping only transforms requests. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-method-request-validation.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/http-api-vs-rest.html

prompt: A company's support assistant is a single-page application that calls a Regional Amazon API Gateway REST API. The API uses a Cognito user pool authorizer, an AWS WAF web ACL and usage plans, and invokes a Node.js Lambda function that calls Amazon Bedrock. Answers take 20 to 70 seconds; the user sees nothing until the answer is complete, and longer answers fail at the 29-second integration timeout. The company wants text to appear as it is generated, wants to keep the existing authorizer, web ACL and usage plans, and wants the browser to keep using ordinary HTTPS requests rather than a new connection protocol. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST change?

options.text: Create an API Gateway WebSocket API, and have the function push each chunk to the client through the connection management callback URL.
Expose the function through a Lambda function URL in RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode, and have the application call that URL directly.
Move the route to an API Gateway HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, and return chunks from the function as it reads ConverseStream.
Have the function write ConverseStream output to its response stream, and set the proxy integration's response transfer mode to STREAM.

explanation: API Gateway REST APIs can stream the response of a Lambda proxy (AWS_PROXY) integration when the integration's response transfer mode is changed from the default BUFFERED to STREAM. The function reads events from ConverseStream and writes them to its response stream, API Gateway forwards them as they arrive, and a streamed response may run for up to 15 minutes, so the 29-second limit no longer ends long answers. The authorizer, web ACL and usage plans stay where they are, and the browser still makes a normal HTTPS request and reads the body incrementally. The 'WebSocket API' option delivers incremental text but requires the client to adopt a new connection protocol and the backend to manage connections. The 'Lambda function URL' option streams, but calling it directly bypasses the REST API, so the Cognito authorizer, the web ACL and the usage plans no longer apply. The 'HTTP API' option fails because response streaming is supported only for REST APIs, and HTTP APIs also lack AWS WAF integration and usage plans. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/response-transfer-mode.html

prompt: A team enabled response streaming (response transfer mode STREAM) on an edge-optimized Amazon API Gateway REST API. The Lambda proxy integration calls ConverseStream on Amazon Bedrock and forwards text as it arrives. Answers that produce text continuously complete correctly, including some that stream for three minutes. However, when the model calls an inventory tool that takes 35 to 50 seconds to respond, during which the function sends no bytes, the browser reports that the connection was closed. Lambda logs show that the function kept running and finished normally afterwards. There are no throttling errors, and every response is far smaller than 1 MB. Which change resolves the problem?

options.text: Change the API to a Regional endpoint, which allows a streamed response to be idle for up to 5 minutes rather than 30 seconds.
Request an increase to the integration timeout quota so that the integration may run for longer than the default limit of 29 seconds.
Increase the Lambda function's timeout and memory so that the tool call finishes before the invocation is terminated.
Return the response in BUFFERED transfer mode so that the tool delay is absorbed before any bytes are sent to the client.

explanation: Streamed responses in API Gateway are subject to an idle timeout that depends on the endpoint type: 5 minutes for Regional or private endpoints but only 30 seconds for edge-optimized endpoints. A 35 to 50 second silence while the tool runs exceeds the edge-optimized limit, so the connection is closed even though the total duration is well under the 15-minute streaming maximum and Lambda keeps executing. Moving to a Regional endpoint raises the idle allowance to 5 minutes; the documentation adds that a Regional API behind your own CloudFront distribution can get more than 30 seconds by raising the distribution's response timeout. Sending periodic keep-alive bytes would also avoid idleness, but it is not among the options. The option to increase 'the integration timeout quota' addresses the 29-second limit, which streaming mode already lifts, as the three-minute answers show. The option to increase 'the Lambda function's timeout and memory' does not help because the function was never terminated. The option to use 'BUFFERED transfer mode' brings back the 29-second integration timeout and removes incremental output, so long answers fail again. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/response-transfer-mode.html

prompt: A shared inference service on Amazon ECS uses one long-lived AWS SDK client for the Amazon Bedrock runtime to serve 30 tenants and to call four different models. After ThrottlingException errors appeared on the most popular model, an engineer set the client's retry mode to adaptive with 10 maximum attempts. Since then, whenever that model is throttled, p95 latency for the other three models rises from 2 seconds to more than 20 seconds, although Amazon CloudWatch shows no throttles for them and they are far below their quotas. During a recent Regional disruption, requests also hung for over a minute before failing. Which change is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Keep adaptive mode and raise the maximum attempts to 20 so that throttled requests to the popular model eventually succeed.
Set maximum attempts to 1 and add an application loop that waits 2 seconds between attempts for every error that the service returns.
Use standard retry mode with the default maximum attempts, and send a request to a fallback model when its retries are exhausted.
Keep adaptive mode and purchase Provisioned Throughput for the three models whose latency increased during throttling.

explanation: Adaptive retry mode adds a client-side rate limiter that works per SDK client instance and can delay even the initial request. AWS advises against it when one client talks to multiple resources or serves multiple tenants, because throttling on one resource slows every request from that client; that is why calls to three healthy models became slow. Standard mode, the recommended default, never delays the initial request: it retries only failed calls using exponential backoff with jitter, and it has a retry quota that makes the client fail fast during a widespread disruption. (The updated SDK retry behaviour, which is opt-in through AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026=true until it becomes the default, additionally uses a longer base delay for throttling errors than for transient errors.) With the default of 3 attempts the added latency is bounded, and a fallback model gives graceful degradation once retries are exhausted. Raising 'the maximum attempts to 20' in adaptive mode lengthens the hangs and keeps the cross-model slowdown. Replacing SDK retries with 'an application loop that waits 2 seconds' removes backoff and jitter, so clients retry in step, and it retries errors that are not retryable. Buying 'Provisioned Throughput for the three models' addresses a capacity problem they do not have; the delay is created inside the client. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/feature-retry-behavior.html

prompt: A B2B writing assistant exposes an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Each partner sends an API key and is authorized by a Lambda authorizer; a Lambda function then calls an Amazon Bedrock model with on-demand throughput in one Region. One partner's bulk script now sends 50 requests per second, which consumes the account's tokens-per-minute quota for the model. Other partners receive HTTP 500 because the function surfaces ThrottlingException after the SDK's retries. The company requires that no partner can use more than its contracted share of requests, that users receive a slightly lower-quality answer instead of an error while the primary model is throttled, and that no new always-on cost is introduced. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Lower the stage's default method throttling to 20 requests per second so that total traffic stays within the model's token quota.
Associate each partner's API key with a usage plan that sets that partner's throttle rate, burst and request quota.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a six-month commitment sized for the peak load of all partners combined.
Catch throttling errors once SDK retries are exhausted and invoke a smaller fallback model, flagging the answer as degraded.
Raise the SDK's maximum attempts to 15 and the function timeout to 15 minutes so that throttled calls eventually succeed.

explanation: Per-client limits in API Gateway come from usage plans: each partner's API key is associated with a plan whose throttle rate, burst and quota apply to that key, so the bulk script receives 429 responses when it exceeds its share while other partners are unaffected. Authorization stays with the Lambda authorizer; the key only identifies the client. For graceful degradation, the function lets the SDK retry with backoff and, when throttling persists, calls a fallback such as a smaller model that has its own quota and returns that answer marked as degraded. Both measures are pay-per-use. Lowering 'the stage's default method throttling' limits all partners collectively, so the noisy partner still takes most of the 20 requests per second and the others are rejected. 'Provisioned Throughput with a six-month commitment' adds exactly the always-on cost that is excluded and does not enforce contracted shares. Raising 'the SDK's maximum attempts to 15' makes calls wait far beyond API Gateway's 29-second integration timeout, so users still receive errors and never a degraded answer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-request-throttling.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-api-error-codes.html

prompt: A travel company's English-language support assistant sends every question to the larger of two models in one provider's family on Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API. An analysis of transcripts shows that about 70% of questions, such as baggage allowances and check-in times, are answered equally well by the smaller model in the same family, which costs much less per token. The company wants to reduce cost without a noticeable loss of answer quality on the harder questions, wants to state how much quality difference justifies using the larger model, wants the application to keep calling a single endpoint, and does not want to build or maintain a classifier. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Add an AWS Step Functions Express workflow in which the smaller model rates each question's complexity and a Choice state selects the model.
Create a configured prompt router with the two models, a fallback model and a response quality difference, and call the router's ARN.
Store keyword and intent rules in AWS AppConfig, and have the application choose the model for each question from the matching rule.
Send all questions to the smaller model through a cross-Region inference profile so that capacity is available for the extra volume.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing provides a single serverless endpoint that predicts, for each request, the response quality of the models behind the router and sends the request to the model with the best balance of quality and cost. A configured prompt router is created with exactly two models from the same family, a fallback model and a routing criterion expressed as a response quality difference, which is the quality tolerance the company wants to state. The application keeps using Converse and passes the router ARN as the model ID. The feature is optimized for English prompts, which fits this workload. The 'Step Functions Express workflow' option is a self-built classifier: it adds a model call per request plus workflow logic to maintain. The 'AWS AppConfig' rules option is static routing that the team must keep curating, and keyword rules misjudge unfamiliar questions. Sending 'all questions to the smaller model' lowers cost but gives up quality on the 30% of harder questions; a cross-Region inference profile adds capacity, not answer quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-routing.html

prompt: A document-intake service receives scanned invoices, long legal contracts and source-code files through one API. Each kind must be processed by a different specialised foundation model on Amazon Bedrock: a multimodal model, a large-context model and a code model, from three providers. The kind must be determined by inspecting the content with an inexpensive classifier model, because client-supplied type fields have proved unreliable. If a specialised model still fails after retries, the item must go to a general-purpose fallback model. Compliance needs a record of every routing decision and every step of each item, retrievable for 90 days, without the team building its own audit logging. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock prompt router across the three specialised models, and let intelligent prompt routing select a model for each item.
Use an Amazon API Gateway mapping template that reads the documentType field of the request and selects the integration for that model.
Write one AWS Lambda function that classifies the item, calls the matching model in an if/else block, and writes audit items to Amazon DynamoDB.
Use an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow: a Bedrock task classifies the item and a Choice state routes to model tasks with Retry and Catch.

explanation: Step Functions provides dynamic, content-based routing with built-in control flow. A task that uses the optimized Amazon Bedrock integration invokes the classifier model, a Choice state branches on its output to the task for the matching specialised model, and Retry and Catch on those tasks send persistent failures to a fallback-model task. Standard workflows record every state transition with its input and output, and the execution history can be retrieved through the Step Functions API for up to 90 days after an execution completes, which gives compliance its per-item record with no custom logging. The 'prompt router' option relies on a capability the feature does not have: intelligent prompt routing works with exactly two models from the same family and chooses by predicted response quality, not by document kind across three providers. The 'mapping template' option can route on a request field, but it depends on the client-supplied documentType that is known to be unreliable and cannot inspect content with a model. The 'one AWS Lambda function' option can route correctly, but writing audit items to DynamoDB is precisely the self-built audit logging the team wants to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-bedrock.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html

prompt: A reporting service uses a Python Lambda function with a 15-minute timeout, invoked asynchronously, to generate 20-page reports. The function calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API (not streaming) on an Anthropic Claude model with extended thinking, using a boto3 client with default configuration; one generation takes 3 to 6 minutes. The function log shows a ReadTimeoutError about 60 seconds after each call, followed by further attempts, and the invocation finally fails. Model invocation logs show that Bedrock completed every one of those requests successfully, and token charges are several times higher than expected. No throttling metrics are recorded. Which change fixes the root cause?

options.text: Increase the Lambda function's memory and move it to provisioned concurrency so that each model call is processed faster.
Request a tokens-per-minute quota increase for the model so that the long requests are no longer interrupted.
Create the Bedrock runtime client with a botocore Config whose read_timeout covers the longest expected generation.
Reduce maxTokens in the inference configuration so that each response is returned within the first 60 seconds.

explanation: AWS SDK clients time out after 1 minute by default.
