Have the pipeline store intended use, risk rating and metric values as custom metadata properties on each model package version, and build a reporting dashboard for auditors.
Have the pipeline create a SageMaker model card for each version with the SageMaker Python SDK, reference the Clarify report in S3, and export the card to PDF.
Have the pipeline tag each training job and model package with governance tags, and present AWS Config configuration history to auditors as the record of changes.

explanation: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards are built for this record. A card has fields for intended uses, a risk rating of unknown, low, medium or high, training details and evaluation results, and it can parse evaluation metrics automatically from a SageMaker Clarify JSON report in S3. Any edit other than an approval status change creates a new card version, which gives the immutable history, and a card can be exported to PDF. Cards can be created programmatically with the SageMaker Python SDK or the low-level APIs, and they integrate with Model Registry, so the pipeline needs little code. "write a JSON governance record to an S3 bucket" could satisfy the regulator, but the team would have to design the schema, parse the Clarify output and build the PDF rendering itself, which is the most custom development. "custom metadata properties on each model package version" fails because it provides neither a versioned document of edits nor a PDF export. "tag each training job and model package" fails because AWS Config history describes resource configuration, not intended uses, limitations or evaluation results. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/model-cards.html

prompt: An insurer has an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over policy PDFs that five business units store in Amazon S3. The assistant calls RetrieveAndGenerate and currently shows only the S3 URI of each cited document. Compliance now requires every answer to display the owning business unit, the document version and the effective date for each source that was used. The same attributes must also restrict retrieval to the business unit of the signed-in user. The displayed attributes must come from stored data, not from model-generated text. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Upload a .metadata.json file with the three attributes beside each PDF, sync the data source, filter on business unit, and render each retrieved reference's metadata.
Add the three attributes as S3 object tags, call GetObjectTagging for every cited S3 URI after each response, and render the returned tag values beside the citation.
Insert a header line with the three attributes at the top of each PDF, sync the data source, and instruct the model in the prompt template to repeat the header per source.
Register each PDF in an AWS Glue Data Catalog table that holds the three attributes, and query the table with Amazon Athena for every cited S3 URI after each response.

explanation: Knowledge base document metadata serves both needs with one mechanism. A file named after the source file with `.metadata.json` appended carries the attributes; after a sync they are stored with every chunk of that document. A metadata filter in the retrieval configuration restricts results to the user's business unit, and each retrieved reference in the `citations` of the RetrieveAndGenerate response returns the `metadata` map and `location` of its source, so the application displays stored values rather than generated text. "Add the three attributes as S3 object tags" can display the attributes, but S3 tags are not available to knowledge base filters, so retrieval is not restricted, and it adds an S3 call per citation. "Insert a header line" fails because the header lands only in the first chunk of each document and the displayed values would be model-generated. "Register each PDF in an AWS Glue Data Catalog table" is a sound way to catalog sources, but the catalog is not consulted during retrieval, so it cannot filter results, and an Athena query per citation adds latency and operations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/s3-data-source-connector.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_agent-runtime_RetrievedReference.html

prompt: A company runs a public assistant on Amazon Bedrock with a versioned guardrail that includes a denied topic for legal advice. Model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs is the company's regulated response log. A safety audit sets two controls. First, the on-call engineer must be notified within minutes when denied-topic interventions by the guardrail rise sharply, because this has previously signalled coordinated misuse. Second, if anyone removes the invocation logging configuration, it must be restored automatically and the security team must be notified. Which combination of actions implements both controls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationsIntervened metric in the AWS/Bedrock/Guardrails namespace for the TopicPolicy policy type, with an SNS action.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationClientErrors metric in the AWS/Bedrock namespace for the production model ID, with an SNS action.
Add CloudTrail data event selectors for the AWS::Bedrock::Model resource type so that changes to the logging configuration are recorded and can be matched.
Create an EventBridge rule for the DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration CloudTrail event that invokes a Lambda function to restore logging and notify.
Schedule a daily Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job with the Builtin.Harmfulness metric on sampled responses, and alarm when the average score rises.

explanation: Guardrails publish runtime metrics in the `AWS/Bedrock/Guardrails` namespace. `InvocationsIntervened` counts invocations where the guardrail intervened, and the `GuardrailPolicyType` dimension separates `TopicPolicy` from the other policy types, so an alarm on it with an SNS action notifies within minutes of a spike in denied-topic interventions. The logging configuration is changed through control plane operations such as `DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration`, which CloudTrail records as management events. An EventBridge rule can match that event and invoke a Lambda function that calls `PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration` again and publishes to SNS, which is detection plus automated remediation. "InvocationClientErrors" fails because it counts invocations that end in client-side errors, and a guardrail intervention is a successful response, so the metric does not track denied-topic interventions. "Add CloudTrail data event selectors" fails because the logging configuration operations are management events; that data event type covers bidirectional streaming and async invoke calls. "Schedule a daily Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job" fails because a daily batch score cannot notify within minutes and measures harmfulness of responses, not denied-topic interventions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-guardrails-cw-metrics.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html

prompt: A health insurer builds the corpus for an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with AWS Glue. Glue Spark jobs join raw claims tables, remove identifiers and write curated tables that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog; a final job exports the curated text to the S3 data source. Auditors ask the team to show, for any curated table, which upstream tables and which job runs produced it, and how that has changed over time. The team already uses an Amazon DataZone domain, surfaced through Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, as its business data catalog. Lineage must be captured automatically as jobs run and must not be maintained by hand. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail data events on the raw and curated S3 buckets, and reconstruct the upstream tables for each curated table from the object-level read and write events.
Enable job bookmarks on every Glue job, and use the bookmark state of each job run as the record of which upstream data produced each curated table.
Add a source_tables parameter to each curated table in the Data Catalog, and have every job overwrite it with the list of tables that it read during the run.
Add the Glue databases to the domain as a data source with lineage enabled, and configure the Glue Spark jobs to send their lineage events to the domain.

explanation: Data lineage in Amazon DataZone (also available in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio) is OpenLineage-compatible. Lineage can be captured automatically for AWS Glue Data Catalog tables when the databases are added to the domain as a data source, and Spark ETL job runs on AWS Glue 5.0 and later can be configured to send lineage events to the domain. The result is a graph of dataset and job-run nodes that auditors can walk upstream from a curated table, and because lineage is versioned with each event, they can also see how it looked at an earlier point in time. "Enable CloudTrail data events" fails because object-level API events show which principal read or wrote which object, not which tables a transformation derived a table from, and the team would have to build the reconstruction. "Enable job bookmarks" fails because bookmarks only persist state about data a job has already processed so that reruns skip it. "Add a source_tables parameter" fails because it is a hand-built convention in job code, and overwriting the value on each run discards the history. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datazone/latest/userguide/datazone-data-lineage.html

prompt: A law firm's research assistant calls RetrieveAndGenerate on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The firm's transparency policy requires every answer to show the passages it relies on, and the UI renders them from the citations in the API response. To enforce a house writing style, a developer replaced the default knowledge base prompt template with a custom one. Since that release, answers are still accurate and clearly drawn from the firm's documents, and the Retrieve API returns the expected passages for the same queries, but responses no longer contain citations, so the UI shows no sources. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The custom template omits the $search_results$ placeholder, so the retrieved passages are no longer passed to the model that generates the answer.
The documents have no .metadata.json files, so the knowledge base cannot return a source location for the passages that the model used.
The custom template omits the $output_format_instructions$ placeholder, so the model no longer receives the instructions for formatting citations.
The number of retrieved results is set too low, so the response generator has too few passages available to attribute its statements to.

explanation: Knowledge base prompt templates use placeholders that Amazon Bedrock fills at run time. The documentation notes that `$output_format_instructions$` is required for citations to be displayed in the response; it carries the underlying instructions for formatting the response and its citations, and without it the response will not contain citations. A developer who writes their own formatting instructions and drops the placeholder gets exactly this symptom: grounded answers with no citations. Restoring the placeholder, or building attribution in the application from the Retrieve results, fixes it. The option about "the $search_results$ placeholder" does not fit because without the retrieved passages the answers would stop being drawn from the firm's documents, and the scenario says they still are. The option about ".metadata.json files" does not fit because metadata files only add custom attributes; the source location of a retrieved passage is returned without them. "The number of retrieved results is set too low" does not fit because nothing changed in the retrieval configuration, Retrieve returns the expected passages, and fewer results would reduce the number of citations rather than remove them. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A public agency uses an Amazon Bedrock agent to pre-assess benefit applications. The agent calls two action groups and queries a knowledge base of eligibility rules. Under the agency's responsible AI policy, the caseworker who receives each assessment must see in the case-management UI, together with that response, which rules were looked up, which actions were called with which inputs, and the agent's reasoning at each step. The explanation must reflect what the agent actually did rather than an account written afterwards, and it must not add further model invocations. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add an instruction that tells the agent to end every answer with a step-by-step account of the rules, actions and reasoning it used, and display that section in the UI.
Set enableTrace on each InvokeAgent request, and render the rationale, invocation inputs and observations from the orchestration trace in the UI.
Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, and have the UI run a Logs Insights query for the prompts of the session after each response.
Log InvokeAgent data events in CloudTrail for the agent alias, and have the UI display the event record that belongs to each caseworker request.

explanation: When the trace is enabled, each chunk of the InvokeAgent response is accompanied by a trace part. The orchestration trace contains the rationale, which is the agent's reasoning for the next step, the invocation input sent to an action group or knowledge base, and the observation that came back. This is a record of the steps the agent actually executed, it arrives with the response, and it needs no extra model call, so the UI can show it to the caseworker directly. "Add an instruction that tells the agent to end every answer with a step-by-step account" fails because that text is generated by the model after the fact and is not guaranteed to match the steps that ran. "Enable model invocation logging" fails because the logs hold raw request and response bodies of model calls in a separate store, not a structured step record returned with the response. "Log InvokeAgent data events in CloudTrail" fails because the event shows who called the agent and when, not its reasoning or tool inputs. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Agents Classic; agents built on AgentCore expose the same kind of step record through OpenTelemetry traces. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/trace-events.html

prompt: An HR software company uses an Amazon Bedrock model to draft interview feedback. Before each release, the responsible AI team must test whether drafts differ in stereotyped content when only a candidate's name or gender changes. The team has 900 paired prompts that differ only in those attributes. It needs a score with an explanation for every response so that pairs can be compared, and it needs the company's own HR specialists to rate the lowest-scoring pairs. The process must be repeatable for every release without building evaluation infrastructure. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run a model evaluation job that uses a judge model with the Builtin.Stereotyping metric on the paired prompt dataset.
Attach a guardrail with the hate and insults filters at high strength, and use the intervention count as the fairness score.
Run a model evaluation job that uses human workers, with the HR specialists as the work team, on the flagged pairs.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with the context relevance metric on the paired prompt dataset.
Attach a SageMaker Model Monitor bias drift schedule to the Amazon Bedrock model that generates the drafts.

explanation: A model evaluation job that uses a judge model scores every response on the selected metrics and returns an explanation with each score. `Builtin.Stereotyping` evaluates whether a response contains stereotypes of any kind, so running it over the counterfactual pairs lets the team compare the two members of each pair, and 900 prompts fit in a single job. A custom metric can be added if the team needs a rubric of its own. For expert review, a model evaluation job that uses human workers sends responses to a work team that the company manages, here the HR specialists. Both job types are managed and can be rerun for each release. "Attach a guardrail with the hate and insults filters" fails because those filters block overtly harmful content; an intervention count says nothing about subtle differences between paired responses. "retrieve-only RAG evaluation" fails because it measures the quality of retrieved passages, not model responses. "SageMaker Model Monitor bias drift" fails because it monitors predictions of models hosted on SageMaker AI endpoints, not an Amazon Bedrock model, and it is no longer open to new customers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-metrics.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-type-human.html

prompt: A bank's assistant uses a prompt stored in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Version 4 is in production. A fairness review found that answers to loan questions take a more cautious tone for some customer groups, and an engineer created version 5 to correct this. Before production changes, the team must compare versions 4 and 5 on the same 600 counterfactual prompts, obtain a score with an explanation for each response, and be able to attribute every result to an immutable prompt version. No customer may receive a version 5 response during the test. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Open the prompt in Prompt builder, add the two prompt texts as variants in Compare variants, and review the outputs side by side for each test input.
Route 10% of production requests to version 5, tag each call with request metadata, and compare guardrail intervention rates per version after a week.
Edit the working draft to match version 5, run the 600 prompts against the draft and against version 4, and compare the two sets of outputs with a text diff.
Invoke each version by its versioned prompt ARN over the 600 prompts, then score both response sets in judge-based evaluation jobs with the same metrics.

explanation: A prompt version is an immutable snapshot, and a managed prompt can be invoked by passing its ARN with the version as `modelId` and the test values in `promptVariables`. Running both version ARNs over the same 600 inputs offline produces two response sets that are each tied to a fixed version and that no customer sees. A judge-based model evaluation job accepts your own inference responses in the prompt dataset, skips the invoke step and scores them, returning a score and an explanation per response, so the same metrics, for example `Builtin.Stereotyping` and a custom tone metric, apply to both sets. "Compare variants" in Prompt builder is useful while authoring, but it is a manual side-by-side view of draft variants for one set of test values at a time and produces no scores. "Route 10% of production requests to version 5" fails because customers would receive version 5 responses, and intervention rates are not a fairness score. "Edit the working draft to match version 5" fails because a draft is mutable, so results cannot be attributed to an immutable version, and a text diff gives no score or explanation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-test.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-prompt-datasets-judge.html

prompt: An insurer serves customers through two models: an Amazon Bedrock model called with the Converse API, and a fine-tuned model hosted on a SageMaker AI endpoint. The company's AI policy forbids investment advice and requires personal data to be masked in every response. The compliance team wants one policy definition that it can version and update centrally and that is applied identically to the outputs of both models. The check must run in the existing Lambda post-processing step and must not require another foundation model invocation. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Define one versioned guardrail with a denied topic and a sensitive information filter, and call ApplyGuardrail with source OUTPUT from the Lambda function for both models.
Define one versioned guardrail and pass it in guardrailConfig on the Converse calls, and add the same policy wording to the system prompt of the model on the SageMaker AI endpoint.
Call Amazon Comprehend PII detection from the Lambda function for both models, and match responses against a keyword list of investment terms that is stored in AWS AppConfig.
Send each response from the Lambda function to a small Amazon Bedrock model with a policy-review prompt, and release only the responses that the reviewing model approves.

explanation: The `ApplyGuardrail` API assesses any text against a configured guardrail without invoking a foundation model, and the `source` field is set to `OUTPUT` when model output is being checked. One versioned guardrail with a denied topic for investment advice and a sensitive information filter that masks personal data therefore becomes the single policy definition, and the Lambda step applies it in the same way to text from the Amazon Bedrock model and from the SageMaker AI endpoint. Updating the policy means publishing a new guardrail version. "pass it in guardrailConfig on the Converse calls" covers only the Amazon Bedrock model; a system prompt on the other model is an instruction, not an enforced check, so the two outputs are not treated identically. "Call Amazon Comprehend PII detection" handles the masking, but a keyword list does not recognise investment advice that avoids the listed terms, and the policy is split across two mechanisms. "Send each response ... to a small Amazon Bedrock model" fails because it adds another foundation model invocation for every response. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-use-independent-api.html

prompt: A hospital network uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize clinical guidelines for nurses. Each request passes the guideline text as the grounding source, and a guardrail with a contextual grounding check blocks summaries that score below a grounding threshold of 0.75. The responsible AI committee asks for two additions. Nurses must see the evidence behind each summary and a caution banner when confidence is marginal, and the committee wants a weekly view of how grounding confidence is distributed over time, not just how many summaries were blocked. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Raise the grounding threshold to 1.0 so that only fully grounded summaries are returned and no caution banner is needed for the nurses.
Read the grounding score from each response's guardrail trace, publish it as a custom CloudWatch metric, and show the banner for marginal scores.
Chart the InvocationsIntervened guardrail metric for the contextual grounding policy type as the weekly distribution of grounding confidence.
Display the guideline passages that were supplied as the grounding source beside each summary so that nurses can check each statement.
Set temperature to 0 so that summaries are deterministic, and present the repeatable output to the nurses as a high-confidence result.

explanation: A contextual grounding check produces a confidence score for grounding and for relevance on every response it processes. With the guardrail trace enabled, the assessment in the response lists each contextual grounding filter with its `score`, its `threshold` and the action taken. The application can read that score, publish it as a custom CloudWatch metric to chart the distribution week by week, and show a caution banner when a summary passes but sits close to 0.75. Presenting the guideline passages that were used as the grounding source next to the summary gives nurses the evidence to verify statements themselves. "Raise the grounding threshold to 1.0" fails because valid thresholds run from 0 to 0.99; a threshold of 1 is invalid because it would block all content. "Chart the InvocationsIntervened guardrail metric" fails because it counts interventions, which is exactly the blocked-only view the committee said is insufficient; it carries no scores. "Set temperature to 0" fails because repeatable output is not evidence that the output is grounded, so labelling it high confidence would mislead users. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Converse.html

prompt: A team is about to change the retrieval configuration of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base: more results per query and a reranking model. The team has 300 test questions, each with the passages that a correct answer needs. Before release, a CI stage must show whether the retrieved passages are relevant to each question, detect when required passages are no longer retrieved, and confirm that p95 retrieval latency stays under 800 ms. The results must not be influenced by the model that writes the final answer. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with context relevance and context coverage, using the passages as ground truth, and time the Retrieve calls in the test harness.
Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job with correctness and faithfulness, using reference answers as ground truth, and take retrieval latency from the job report.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with context relevance on the questions without ground truth, and time the Retrieve calls in the test harness with AWS X-Ray.
Run a judge-based model evaluation job with the Builtin.Relevance metric on the questions, and read the InvocationLatency metric for the model from Amazon CloudWatch.

explanation: A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job scores what the knowledge base returns, without a response generator, so the result is not influenced by the answering model. Its two built-in metrics map to the first two requirements: `Builtin.ContextRelevance` measures how relevant the retrieved texts are to the questions, and `Builtin.ContextCoverage` measures how much of the ground truth the retrieved texts cover, which is what reveals that a required passage has dropped out. Coverage needs ground truth in the prompt dataset, which the team has. Latency is not an evaluation metric, so the harness has to time the `Retrieve` calls itself and compute p95. "retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job with correctness and faithfulness" fails because those metrics judge the generated answer, so the generator influences the result, and the report does not provide retrieval latency. "context relevance on the questions without ground truth" measures relevance and latency but cannot detect missing required passages, because coverage needs ground truth. "judge-based model evaluation job with the Builtin.Relevance metric" fails because it scores a model's response to a prompt, not retrieval, and `InvocationLatency` describes model invocations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-evaluation-metrics.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A retailer runs a refund agent built with Strands Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with observability enabled. For a refund request the agent must call verify_identity, then lookup_order, then issue_refund, in that order. Additional read-only lookups between those calls are acceptable. A regression suite of recorded sessions must fail the build when the required sequence is broken, and this check must be deterministic rather than scored by a judge model. The suite must also assess whether each session satisfied a list of natural-language success statements. Which AgentCore Evaluations configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Builtin.TrajectoryExactOrderMatch with the expected trajectory, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements supplied as assertions.
Builtin.TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch with the expected trajectory, and Builtin.Correctness with the success statements supplied as the expected response.
Builtin.TrajectoryInOrderMatch with the expected trajectory, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements supplied as assertions.
The tool selection accuracy and tool parameter accuracy evaluators on every tool call, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate without any ground truth.

explanation: AgentCore Evaluations accepts ground truth with a session: an `expectedTrajectory` of tool names and a list of `assertions`. The three trajectory evaluators are scored programmatically, with no LLM call, which gives the deterministic check. `Builtin.TrajectoryInOrderMatch` requires all expected tools to appear in order but allows extra tools between them, which matches a required sequence with optional read-only lookups. `Builtin.GoalSuccessRate` is a session-level evaluator that, given assertions, judges whether the agent's behaviour satisfied each natural-language statement. "Builtin.TrajectoryExactOrderMatch" fails because it demands the same tools in the same order with no extras, so sessions with an acceptable extra lookup would break the build. "Builtin.TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch" fails because it ignores order, so issuing a refund before verifying identity would pass, and `Builtin.Correctness` compares one turn's response with an expected answer rather than checking assertions across the session. "tool selection accuracy and tool parameter accuracy" fails because those tool-level evaluators are scored by a judge model for each call and do not compare the sequence with an expected trajectory. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/ground-truth-evaluations.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/prompt-templates-builtin.html

prompt: A travel company's booking agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and emits OpenTelemetry traces through AgentCore Observability. Product leaders want a weekly quality report: goal success and tool selection scores trending over time on roughly 10% of production sessions, shown on a CloudWatch dashboard with an alarm when scores fall. Separately, the support team wants to score the specific sessions named in customer complaints, using the same evaluators, on the day a complaint arrives. The team wants to avoid building its own scoring pipeline. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run a weekly Amazon Bedrock judge-based model evaluation job on a fixed prompt dataset, and chart the scores from the job's S3 output.
Edit the prompt template of the built-in goal success evaluator to add the company's rubric, and use the edited evaluator for both of the needs.
Create an online evaluation configuration with 10% sampling and built-in evaluators, and build the dashboard and alarm on its CloudWatch results.
Log the agent runtime invocations as CloudTrail data events, and chart the count of successful invocations as the goal success score.
Run an on-demand evaluation with the same built-in evaluators, passing the span or trace IDs of each session named in a complaint.

explanation: AgentCore Evaluations offers online evaluation, which continuously scores live production traffic. A configuration names the evaluators and a sampling percentage for sessions; results are written to CloudWatch Logs and the scores are also emitted as CloudWatch metrics, so a dashboard and an alarm can be built without a custom pipeline. On-demand evaluation complements it: you supply the span or trace IDs of chosen interactions and apply the same built-in or custom evaluators, which is the documented way to investigate specific customer interactions. "weekly Amazon Bedrock judge-based model evaluation job on a fixed prompt dataset" fails because it scores a model's responses to dataset prompts, not sampled production agent sessions with their tool calls. "Edit the prompt template of the built-in goal success evaluator" fails because built-in evaluator configurations, including their prompt templates, cannot be modified; a company rubric needs a custom evaluator. "Log the agent runtime invocations as CloudTrail data events" fails because an API call that returned successfully says nothing about whether the user's goal was met or the right tool was chosen. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/evaluations-types.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/results-and-output.html

prompt: A company serves an onboarding workflow through an Amazon Bedrock flow. Client applications call InvokeFlow on the alias named prod, which points to version 7. The team has created version 8 with a rewritten prompt node and a different model. Release policy requires that the exact artifact going to production first passes a suite of synthetic user journeys, with automated checks on answer grounding and output format against thresholds. No customer may be served by version 8 before it passes, clients must not change the identifier they call, and rollback must take seconds. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Run the suite against the working draft through the test alias, and when it passes, create version 9 from the draft and point the prod alias to version 9.
Create a second alias that points to version 8 and run the suite against it, then repoint prod to version 8, and repoint prod to version 7 to roll back.
Repoint the prod alias to version 8 and run the suite against prod, then repoint prod to version 7 if any check in the suite falls below its threshold.
Have the suite, and then the clients, invoke version 8 by its version identifier, and return the clients to the prod alias when a rollback is needed.

explanation: Flow versions are immutable snapshots, and applications invoke a flow through an alias that points to a version. A second alias on version 8 lets the synthetic journeys run through `InvokeFlow` against the exact artifact that will be released, with the trace enabled if the checks need per-node inputs and outputs, while prod keeps serving version 7. When the quality gate passes, updating prod to point to version 8 releases it without any client change, and pointing prod back to version 7 is the rollback. "Run the suite against the working draft" fails because the draft is mutable and is not version 8; what passes the suite is not guaranteed to be the artifact that is later versioned and released. "Repoint the prod alias to version 8 and run the suite against prod" fails because customers are served by version 8 while it is still being validated. "invoke version 8 by its version identifier" fails because clients would have to change what they call, and deployed flows are invoked through an alias. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows-deploy.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows-trace.html

prompt: A team re-created the data source of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base to move from fixed-size chunking with 300-token chunks to hierarchical chunking with 1,500-token parent chunks and 300-token child chunks. The old data source and its vectors were deleted first. The application still calls Retrieve with numberOfResults set to 20 and places all results in the prompt ahead of the task instructions. Since the change, input tokens per request have risen severalfold, the model often ignores the formatting instructions at the end of the prompt, and requests with long questions fail because the input exceeds the model's context window. Retrieval relevance looks good. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The overlap setting copies most of each child chunk into its neighbours, so the 20 results repeat the same passage text several times.
The sync ran incrementally, so the vector store now holds both the 300-token chunks and the hierarchical chunks for every document.
The embedding model truncates each parent chunk at its input limit, so the vector store pads every result to one fixed length.
Retrieved child chunks are replaced by their parent chunks, so each of the results can carry up to 1,500 tokens into the prompt.

explanation: With hierarchical chunking, the knowledge base searches over child chunks but replaces the retrieved children with their broader parent chunks before returning results. `numberOfResults` maps to the number of child chunks to retrieve, so a setting that used to yield 20 passages of about 300 tokens can now yield many parents of up to 1,500 tokens each. That explains the jump in input tokens, the instructions at the end of a very long prompt being neglected, and the context window errors on long questions, while relevance stays good. Lowering `numberOfResults`, reducing the parent size, or enforcing a token budget on the context fixes it. "The overlap setting copies most of each child chunk" does not fit because overlap is a configured number of tokens between consecutive chunks, not most of a chunk, and it would not multiply the input severalfold. "The sync ran incrementally" does not fit because the old data source and its vectors were deleted, and `numberOfResults` still caps what is returned. "The embedding model truncates each parent chunk" does not fit because embeddings affect which chunks match, not the length of the text returned. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A support chatbot stores every turn of a conversation in Amazon DynamoDB and sends the full history on each Converse call. In sessions longer than about 60 turns, latency and cost climb steadily, and the longest sessions end with an error stating that the input is too long for the model. Customers in long sessions often refer back to details that they gave at the start, such as an order number, so early facts must stay available to the model. Which combination of changes addresses the root cause? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Track the inputTokens value in the usage field of each response, and start compacting the history when it crosses a set budget.
Enable prompt caching with a cache checkpoint after the conversation history so that earlier turns no longer count toward the context window.
Replace older turns with a running summary that keeps the key facts, and send the summary together with only the most recent turns.
Raise maxTokens in inferenceConfig to the model's maximum so that long sessions have more room available in the context window.
Send only the 10 most recent turns on each call, and leave all earlier turns out of the request to keep the input small.

explanation: The root cause is unbounded growth of the input: every call resends the whole history until it no longer fits the model's context window. Two changes work together. The Converse response returns a `usage` object with `inputTokens`, so the application can measure how large the prompt has become and trigger compaction at a budget well below the limit. Compaction that replaces older turns with a running summary of key facts, plus the most recent turns verbatim, keeps the input bounded while early details such as the order number remain available. "Enable prompt caching" can lower cost and latency for a repeated prefix, but cached tokens are still part of the prompt and still occupy the context window, so the overflow remains. "Raise maxTokens" fails because that parameter limits the output length; it does not enlarge the window, and a larger output reservation leaves less room for input. "Send only the 10 most recent turns" stops the overflow but drops the early facts that customers refer back to, which violates the stated requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Converse.html

prompt: A claims application in a member account calls Converse from a Lambda function. Its execution role allows bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the model and inference profile that it uses, and the code passes no guardrailConfig. On Monday every call began to fail with AccessDeniedException, and the message refers to a guardrail ARN in the organization's management account. Nothing was deployed in the member account over the weekend. The security team confirms that on Sunday it attached an Amazon Bedrock policy in AWS Organizations to the application's OU, and that no SCP was changed. Calls from an administrator role in the same account succeed. Which action resolves the error?

options.text: Allow bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on the management account's guardrail ARN in the policy of the Lambda execution role.
Add guardrailConfig with the management account's guardrail ARN and its version to each Converse request.
Create a guardrail with the same configuration in the member account and reference that guardrail in each Converse request.
Request a higher guardrail text unit quota for the member account and add retries with backoff to the function.

explanation: The symptoms point to organization-level guardrail enforcement. Once an Amazon Bedrock policy naming a guardrail is attached to the OU, that guardrail is applied automatically to InvokeModel and Converse calls from the member accounts. The setup guide requires that roles in member accounts have `bedrock:ApplyGuardrail` permission on the management account's guardrail, and it notes that AccessDenied errors indicate an IAM permission configuration issue. The Lambda role allows only the invoke actions, so it fails, while the administrator role, which has broad Bedrock permissions, succeeds. Adding `bedrock:ApplyGuardrail` on that guardrail ARN to the role fixes it. "Add guardrailConfig with the management account's guardrail ARN" fails because naming the guardrail in the request does not grant the missing permission. "Create a guardrail with the same configuration in the member account" fails because the enforced guardrail is still applied in addition to any request-level guardrail, so the denied permission is still needed. "Request a higher guardrail text unit quota" fails because quota exhaustion produces throttling errors, not an access denied error that an administrator role in the same account does not see. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-enforcements.html

prompt: A nightly job summarizes support tickets with on-demand Converse calls to one model in one Region. Many calls fail with ThrottlingException (HTTP 429) even after SDK retries. CloudWatch shows that the sum of InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount per minute peaks at about 30% of the model's tokens-per-minute quota, and requests per minute peak at about 20% of the request quota. Each request sends roughly 3,000 input tokens and sets maxTokens to 32,000, the model's maximum, although summaries average 300 tokens. No ServiceUnavailableException errors are recorded. Which change is MOST likely to stop the throttling without reducing throughput?

options.text: Request a higher requests-per-minute quota for the model, because 429 errors are returned when the request rate limit is exceeded.
Turn off model invocation logging for the job, because the logged request and response bodies count toward the token quota.
Set maxTokens near the real summary length, because input tokens plus maxTokens are deducted from the quota at request start.
Raise the SDK retry count and add jitter, because the unused quota shows that the errors come from brief bursts of requests.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock deducts total input tokens plus `max_tokens` from the tokens-per-minute quota at the start of each request and throttles the request if that would exceed the quota. The deduction is adjusted periodically during processing, and any unused tokens are replenished when the request ends. Here each request reserves about 35,000 tokens at the start while its final consumption is only a few thousand (about 3,300 at a 1:1 output burndown rate; some models count each output token several times), so concurrent requests exhaust the quota even though the measured token counts stay near 30%. The documentation advises reducing `max_tokens` to approximate the size of your completions when you hit TPM limits earlier than expected, and it warns that usage estimates differ from the reservation that drives throttling. Setting maxTokens to a few hundred tokens above the real summary length removes the over-reservation without slowing the job. "Request a higher requests-per-minute quota" fails because the request rate peaks at 20% of its quota. "Turn off model invocation logging" fails because logging has no effect on token quotas. "Raise the SDK retry count and add jitter" may let more calls eventually succeed, but it lengthens the job and leaves the over-reservation in place. A 503 ServiceUnavailableException, not a 429, is the error that signals capacity constraints unrelated to account quotas. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-api-error-codes.html

prompt: A contracts team extracts clause data with an Anthropic Claude model through InvokeModel on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. Requests include a JSON schema in output_config.format, and the downstream parser has received valid JSON for months. To show reviewers where each value came from, a developer enabled citations on the document content blocks in the same request. Since that deployment, every request returns HTTP 400. The schema, model ID, inference profile and IAM policy are unchanged, and requests succeed again when the citations setting is removed. What is the cause, and what should the team do?

options.text: The cached grammar for the schema expired after 24 hours and has to be compiled again; retry each failed request with exponential backoff.
Structured outputs cannot be combined with citations for these models; request citations and the schema-constrained JSON separately.
Citations are supported only through the Converse API; move the request to Converse and pass the schema in outputConfig.textFormat.
The schema uses constraints that structured outputs do not support; remove the numeric and string length constraints from the schema.

explanation: The structured outputs documentation states that structured outputs is incompatible with citations for Anthropic models: if citations are enabled while structured outputs is in use, the model returns a 400 error. That matches the evidence exactly, because the only change is the citations setting and removing it restores success. The team has to separate the two needs, for example one request that returns the schema-constrained JSON and another that returns cited passages, or a schema field that carries a supporting quote for each value. "The cached grammar for the schema expired" does not fit because compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from first access and a new compilation only adds latency; it does not return a 400 on every request. "Citations are supported only through the Converse API" does not fit because the incompatibility is between the two features, not the API, so the Converse request would fail in the same way. "The schema uses constraints that structured outputs do not support" does not fit because an unsupported schema is rejected immediately with a 400, and this unchanged schema has worked for months. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/structured-output.html

prompt: A team moved its hand-built prompt into Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. The managed prompt contains the system instructions and a user message with a {{ticket}} variable. The application now calls Converse with the prompt version ARN as modelId and passes promptVariables. To limit the change, a developer left the old code path in place, so each request also sends a messages array that contains the previously rendered user message. After release, input tokens per call roughly doubled, and the model sometimes answers the ticket twice or remarks that the request was repeated. Running the old prompt text and the managed version side by side in the console with test values gives identical, correct outputs. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The promptVariables values are ignored when modelId is a prompt ARN, so the model receives the template with its variable left unfilled.
The prompt version ARN resolves to the working draft at run time, and the draft still holds an earlier copy of the instructions.
Prompt caching on the managed prompt replays the cached prefix as additional input tokens on every request that the application sends.
Messages sent in the request are appended after the messages defined in the prompt, so the ticket text reaches the model twice.

explanation: When a Prompt Management prompt is invoked through Converse by passing its ARN as `modelId`, the messages and system instructions come from the prompt template and the caller only supplies `promptVariables`. The documentation adds that if the request includes the `messages` field, those messages are appended after the messages defined in the prompt. The leftover code path therefore sends the rendered ticket a second time: the input roughly doubles and the model sees the same request twice, while the console comparison, which has no extra messages, looks correct. Version comparison isolates the fault to the calling code rather than the prompt text; removing the `messages` array fixes it. "The promptVariables values are ignored" does not fit because passing variables with a prompt ARN is the documented way to fill the template, and an unfilled template would not double the tokens. "resolves to the working draft" does not fit because a version ARN identifies an immutable snapshot. "Prompt caching ... replays the cached prefix" does not fit because caching reuses a processed prefix and does not add content to the request. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-test.html

prompt: A team added department and year attributes to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base so that queries can be filtered. For each document, such as claims-guide.pdf, it uploaded a sidecar file named claims-guide.metadata.json to the same S3 prefix and ran a sync that completed without failed documents. The vector store is an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless index that the team created by hand two years ago. Unfiltered Retrieve calls return good results, but any call with a filter such as department equals claims returns nothing, and the results of unfiltered calls show none of the custom attributes. Which causes should the team investigate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Metadata filters are evaluated only by RetrieveAndGenerate, so a Retrieve call ignores the filter expression in its request.
The sidecar files are not named after the full source file name, which would be claims-guide.pdf.metadata.json.
Metadata attributes become filterable only when includeForEmbedding is set to true for each attribute in the file.
The vector index was created with the nmslib engine instead of faiss, which causes the metadata files to be ignored.
The embedding model has to be replaced with one that supports metadata before the attributes can be stored.

explanation: The symptoms say the metadata never reached the index: unfiltered results carry no custom attributes, so a filter on them matches nothing. The sync documentation lists two conditions to check so that metadata files are not ignored. First, each `.metadata.json` file must share the same file name and extension as its source file, so the sidecar for claims-guide.pdf must be claims-guide.pdf.metadata.json. Second, when the vector index is in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, it must be configured with the faiss engine; with nmslib, the fix is a new index created with faiss and a new knowledge base that uses it. An index made by hand two years ago is worth checking. "Metadata filters are evaluated only by RetrieveAndGenerate" is wrong because filters are part of the retrieval configuration for both Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate. "includeForEmbedding is set to true" is wrong because that flag only controls whether an attribute is added to the embedded text; with false the metadata is still stored and available for filtering. "The embedding model has to be replaced" is wrong because metadata is stored alongside the vectors and does not depend on the embedding model. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-data-source-sync-ingest.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/s3-data-source-connector.html

prompt: A team traces its GenAI API with AWS X-Ray. Each Lambda function wraps the Amazon Bedrock call in a subsegment and records the prompt template ID, the template version and a schema_valid flag from its JSON Schema check as X-Ray metadata on that subsegment. After a template update, downstream parsing failures rose, and the team wants to pull only the traces where template version 12 produced output that failed schema validation, then compare their latency with version 11. In the trace console, filter expressions on these keys return no traces, although the values are visible when a single trace is opened. What should the team change?

options.text: Record the template ID, version and schema_valid flag as annotations, because annotations are indexed for filtering and metadata is not.
Raise the X-Ray sampling rate to 100 percent, because traces that are sampled out are excluded from filter expressions on custom keys.
Enable active tracing on the Lambda functions, because subsegment data is searchable only when the Lambda service creates the segment.
Move the three values into the Bedrock requestMetadata field, because X-Ray reads custom keys from the model invocation log records.

explanation: X-Ray distinguishes two kinds of custom data on segments and subsegments. Annotations are simple key-value pairs that are indexed for use with filter expressions, so traces can be grouped and searched by them. Metadata can hold values of any type but is not indexed; it is stored with the trace and visible in the trace details, which is exactly what the team observes. Recording the template ID, version and schema_valid flag as annotations lets the team filter for version 12 with failed validation and compare latency against version 11. X-Ray indexes up to 50 annotations per trace, so three keys fit comfortably. "Raise the X-Ray sampling rate" would record more traces, but the recorded ones still could not be filtered on unindexed metadata. "Enable active tracing" does not fit because the subsegments are already recorded and visible; the gap is indexing, not who creates the segment. "Move the three values into the Bedrock requestMetadata field" would put the values into model invocation logs, which is useful for CloudWatch Logs Insights queries, but X-Ray does not read filter keys from those logs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts.html

prompt: A retailer runs two workloads on one Amazon Bedrock model in a single account, both through the Converse API. A checkout assistant is customer-facing, and its p95 response time degrades during two daily two-hour demand peaks. A nightly evaluation harness replays 40,000 multi-turn agent conversations in which the model calls tools and each request depends on the previous response; it has a nine-hour window and no latency target. Finance will not sign any capacity commitment and wants the lowest total inference spend. The model supports every Bedrock service tier. Which design BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity on the Reserved tier for the checkout assistant, and send the evaluation harness on the Flex tier.
Send checkout requests on the Priority tier during the peaks, and move the evaluation harness to a nightly batch inference job with Amazon S3 input and output.
Send checkout requests on the Priority tier during the peaks and on the Standard tier otherwise, and send the evaluation harness on the Flex tier.
Keep checkout requests on the Standard tier, and send the evaluation harness on the Flex tier so that it draws on a separate Flex quota and frees capacity.

explanation: The Priority tier gives the fastest responses for a price premium and needs no reservation, so paying the premium only in the two peak windows fixes checkout latency without a commitment. The Flex tier gives a pricing discount to workloads that tolerate longer processing, and AWS names model evaluations and agentic workflows as examples; the harness keeps its synchronous, multi-turn tool loop and simply runs cheaper. The tier is chosen per request with the `serviceTier` field in Converse (`service_tier` in the request body of other APIs). "Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity" fails the no-commitment rule: the Reserved tier is a 1-month or 3-month reservation with minimums of 100,000 input and 10,000 output TPM, billed around the clock for a four-hour daily need. "Move the evaluation harness to a nightly batch inference job" fails because batch inference does not support tool calling and processes each record independently without multi-turn interaction. "Draws on a separate Flex quota" is wrong on the mechanics, since the on-demand quota is shared across the priority, default and flex tiers, and it leaves checkout latency untouched. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/batch-inference.html

prompt: A SaaS company fronts Amazon Bedrock with an LLM gateway on Amazon ECS. The gateway calls the Converse API on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint for 300 tenants using one shared task role, so all spend appears under a single principal. Finance needs invoice-accurate dollars per tenant in AWS Cost Explorer. Product managers need token usage for each individual request, sliced by the feature that made the call; the feature changes from one call to the next inside the same tenant session. Model invocation logging is already delivered to CloudWatch Logs. The team does not want to create a Bedrock resource per tenant. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Have the gateway assume its Bedrock role once per tenant with session tags, cache those credentials, and activate the tags as cost allocation tags.
Pass the tenant in `requestMetadata` on every call, and activate that metadata key as a cost allocation tag so that it appears in Cost Explorer.
Pass the feature as an STS session tag when the gateway assumes the role, and group the invocation log records by that session tag.
Pass the feature in `requestMetadata` on every call, and aggregate the token counts in the invocation logs by that metadata key.
Route all tenants through one application inference profile that is tagged per feature, and split its cost by tenant in Cost Explorer.

explanation: IAM principal attribution records the caller identity of every inference request and delivers billed dollars to Cost Explorer and CUR 2.0. Behind a gateway, AWS recommends assuming the Bedrock role per user or tenant with session tags (the trust policy must allow `sts:TagSession`), caching the credentials, and activating the tags as cost allocation tags; that gives per-tenant dollars with no per-tenant Bedrock resource. Per-request metadata tagging is the mechanism for per-call detail: `requestMetadata` is written to the model invocation log record beside the token counts, and it can change on every call. "Activate that metadata key as a cost allocation tag" fails because request metadata lands in invocation logs only and never appears in Cost Explorer or CUR. "Group the invocation log records by that session tag" fails because session tags are bound when the role is assumed, stay constant for the session, and are not written to invocation logs, which carry `identity.arn` instead. "One application inference profile that is tagged per feature" fails because a profile's tags are fixed on the resource, so one profile cannot separate tenants or vary by call. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-management.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-mgmt-iam-principal-tracking.html

prompt: A legal-tech company is planning on-demand capacity for a contract-review assistant that calls an Anthropic Claude model through the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. The model's documented output-token burndown rate is 5x. At steady state the assistant sends 300 requests per minute. Each request reads a 10,000-token clause library from the prompt cache, adds 2,000 uncached input tokens, writes nothing new to the cache, and returns 800 output tokens; `max_tokens` is set to 1,000. The team wants to know whether its 2,000,000 tokens-per-minute quota is enough before launch. Approximately how much of the tokens-per-minute quota does this workload consume once responses complete?

options.text: About 840,000 tokens per minute, because quota usage equals the uncached input tokens plus the output tokens that are billed.
About 1,800,000 tokens per minute, because cache reads are excluded and each output token is counted five times.
About 3,840,000 tokens per minute, because cached and uncached input both count and each output token is counted once.
About 4,800,000 tokens per minute, because cached and uncached input both count and each output token is counted five times.

explanation: For models on `bedrock-runtime`, the quota consumed by a completed request is InputTokenCount plus CacheWriteInputTokenCount plus OutputTokenCount multiplied by the burndown rate; CacheReadInputTokenCount is not counted. Here that is 2,000 + 0 + (800 x 5) = 6,000 quota tokens per request, or 1,800,000 per minute at 300 requests, which is 90 percent of the quota and leaves little headroom. At the start of each request the service deducts input tokens plus `max_tokens` (3,000 here), then adjusts to the final figure, so the modest `max_tokens` value does not inflate the reservation. "About 840,000" confuses quota with billing: you are billed only for actual tokens, but output burns quota at five times its count. "About 3,840,000" wrongly adds the 10,000 tokens read from cache and ignores the burndown rate. "About 4,800,000" applies the burndown rate correctly but still counts cache reads, which the documentation excludes from the quota. Burndown rates are model-specific (5x, 10x or 15x for different Claude generations, 1:1 for most other models), so check the rate for the exact model before sizing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html

prompt: A travel company streams chat answers with `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` and applies an Amazon Bedrock guardrail that uses content filters and denied topics only; it performs no masking of sensitive information. Users complain that the first words take too long to appear. Profiling shows that the model starts generating quickly, but chunks are held until the guardrail has scanned them. The risk team accepts that a few chunks of an answer might be displayed before a violation is detected, provided that the rest of the answer is blocked. The budget does not allow a higher per-token price. Which change MOST reduces the time until users see the first text?

options.text: Send the requests on the Priority service tier so that the model and the guardrail scan are both served ahead of Standard traffic.
Remove the guardrail from the request, and call `ApplyGuardrail` on the complete answer once the stream has finished.
Switch from `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` to `InvokeModel`, and apply the same guardrail to the complete response before returning it.
Set `streamProcessingMode` to `ASYNCHRONOUS` in the guardrail configuration of the streaming request so that chunks are not held.

explanation: With a streaming response, guardrails run in synchronous mode by default: chunks are buffered and scanned before they are sent, which adds latency to every chunk. Asynchronous mode sends chunks as soon as they are available and applies the policies in the background; when a violation is found, subsequent chunks are blocked. That is exactly the trade-off the risk team accepted, it costs nothing extra, and it is permitted here because the guardrail does no sensitive-information masking, which asynchronous mode does not support. "Send the requests on the Priority service tier" breaks the budget rule, because Priority carries a price premium, and it does not remove the buffering that profiling identified. "Call `ApplyGuardrail` on the complete answer once the stream has finished" shows the whole unmoderated answer first, so nothing remains to block. "Switch from `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` to `InvokeModel`" gives up streaming, so the first text appears only after the full generation and scan. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-streaming.html

prompt: A wealth-management portal shows each client a generated portfolio summary on the landing page. Positions for all 60,000 accounts are refreshed once a day by a load that finishes at 02:00, and the summary depends only on that data. Most clients sign in between 08:00 and 09:00, when the current design calls Converse on demand, takes 6 to 9 seconds per summary, and is occasionally throttled. The product owner requires the complete summary to be visible within 500 ms of page load and wants the lowest inference cost. The summaries do not use tool calling. Which design BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: After the 02:00 load, run a batch inference job for all accounts, store the results in DynamoDB, and read them at sign-in.
Switch the landing page to ConverseStream so that the first tokens of each summary are rendered as soon as they are generated.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput sized for the 08:00 peak so that every sign-in request has dedicated model capacity available.
Cache the shared system prompt with a one-hour TTL so that each sign-in request processes only the account's own positions.

explanation: The input is fixed for the day once the 02:00 load completes, so the query is predictable and can be pre-computed. A batch inference job (`CreateModelInvocationJob`) reads the prompts from Amazon S3 and writes the responses to S3 asynchronously; six hours is ample, the work moves off the on-demand quota that is throttling the morning peak, and batch has its own pricing, which the Amazon Bedrock pricing page lists below on-demand. Serving the stored text from DynamoDB is a key lookup that fits a 500 ms budget. Batch fits because the summaries need no tool calling, which batch does not support. "Switch the landing page to ConverseStream" improves time to first token only; the complete summary still takes seconds, and the calls still land in the peak. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput" removes throttling but not the 6 to 9 seconds of generation, and it bills hourly for capacity used one hour a day. "Cache the shared system prompt" trims input processing, but each account's positions are unique and the output still has to be generated at sign-in. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/batch-inference.html

prompt: An industrial distributor uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base backed by an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector index that includes a filterable text field. Technicians ask questions that contain exact part numbers such as `XR-4471-B`. The Retrieve API returns chunks about similar parts, and the chunk that literally contains the part number is often missing from the five results. The application's latency budget has no room for another model invocation in the query path, and the team cannot re-ingest the 2 million documents this quarter. Which change should the team make FIRST to improve retrieval relevance?

options.text: Add a reranker model to the Retrieve request, and raise `numberOfResults` so that more candidate chunks are scored.
Set `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID` in the vector search configuration of the Retrieve request.
Enable query decomposition so that each technician question is broken into sub-queries before retrieval takes place.
Switch the knowledge base to an embedding model that produces vectors with more dimensions for finer similarity.

explanation: Semantic search compares embeddings, which place similar part numbers close together and do not reward a literal token match. Hybrid search combines the vector search with a search through the raw text, so a chunk that contains `XR-4471-B` verbatim is scored on that match. It is a request-level setting (`retrievalConfiguration.vectorSearchConfiguration.overrideSearchType`), it needs no extra model call and no re-ingestion, and it is supported here because hybrid search works with Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon RDS (Aurora) and MongoDB vector stores that contain a filterable text field. "Add a reranker model" inserts a model invocation into the query path, which the latency budget forbids, and it can only reorder candidates that the semantic search already found. "Enable query decomposition" also adds a model call; it is configured on RetrieveAndGenerate and targets multi-part questions, not exact identifiers. "Switch the knowledge base to an embedding model" requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and denser vectors still do not guarantee exact-string matching. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A claims processor calls an Anthropic Claude model on demand through Converse on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. Every request repeats the same 9,000-token policy instructions, adds about 1,500 tokens of claim data, sets `maxTokens` to 16,000, and receives about 400 output tokens. At 80 requests per minute the application receives `ThrottlingException`. The model's quota is 2,000,000 tokens per minute, its requests-per-minute quota is far above 80, and the tokens actually billed per minute are under half of the token quota. A quota increase will take weeks to approve. Which changes let more requests be admitted under the existing quota? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Send the requests on the Flex service tier, which is metered against an on-demand quota of its own.
Lower `maxTokens` to a value just above the largest response that the application expects.
Switch to ConverseStream so that tokens are deducted from the quota only as they are generated.
Send the requests on the Priority service tier, which is admitted ahead of the token quota.
Add a cache checkpoint after the policy instructions so that they are read from the prompt cache.

explanation: At the start of each request Amazon Bedrock deducts the input tokens plus `max_tokens` from the tokens-per-minute quota and throttles if the quota is exceeded; unused tokens are replenished only when the request ends. Here each request reserves about 10,500 + 16,000 = 26,500 tokens, so 80 requests reserve about 2.1 million and breach the quota even though real usage is far lower. Setting `maxTokens` close to the real 400-token completions shrinks the reservation by more than half. Caching the 9,000-token instructions helps again: tokens read from the prompt cache do not count toward the quota (cache writes do), so steady traffic counts only the claim data as input. "The Flex service tier, which is metered against an on-demand quota of its own" is false, because the on-demand quota is shared across the priority, default and flex tiers. "The Priority service tier, which is admitted ahead of the token quota" fails for the same reason; Priority changes scheduling and price, not the quota. "Switch to ConverseStream" changes how the response is delivered; the reservation of input plus `max_tokens` is made at the start either way. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html

prompt: A marketing team generates product descriptions with an Anthropic Claude model through the Converse API and wants to A/B test sampling settings on live traffic. Variant A uses temperature 0.7. Variant B uses temperature 0.4 and also sets the model's `top_k` parameter to 50. Both variants use the same model ID, model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs is enabled, and reviewers will score a sample of outputs for each variant. The application already splits traffic. The team wants to compare token usage and outputs per variant with the LEAST additional infrastructure. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Set `temperature` and `topK` together in `inferenceConfig` for variant B, and tag every call with a `requestMetadata` variant key for analysis in the invocation logs.
Invoke a Prompt management prompt ARN through Converse for both variants, and pass each variant's `inferenceConfig` and `additionalModelRequestFields` in the request.
Set `temperature` in `inferenceConfig` and `top_k` in `additionalModelRequestFields` for variant B, and tag every call with a `requestMetadata` variant key.
Send variant B through InvokeModel with a native request body, and compare the two variants by using the `AWS/Bedrock` CloudWatch metrics for the model ID.

explanation: Converse separates parameters that are common to all models from model-specific ones. `inferenceConfig` holds the base set (`maxTokens`, `temperature`, `topP`, `stopSequences`); a parameter such as Claude's `top_k` is passed as JSON in `additionalModelRequestFields`. `requestMetadata` attaches key-value tags to a call, and they are written to the model invocation log record next to the request body, the response body and the token counts, so a CloudWatch Logs Insights query can group usage by variant and pull samples for the reviewers with no new infrastructure. "Set `temperature` and `topK` together in `inferenceConfig`" fails because `topK` is not a base inference parameter of Converse. "Invoke a Prompt management prompt ARN" fails because when a Prompt management prompt is used with Converse the request cannot include `inferenceConfig` or `additionalModelRequestFields`; the settings would have to live in the prompt itself. "Compare the two variants by using the `AWS/Bedrock` CloudWatch metrics" fails because runtime metrics are dimensioned by model ID, which both variants share, and metrics hold no outputs to score. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/conversation-inference.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-mgmt-request-metadata.html

prompt: A research institute hosts a fine-tuned open-weights LLM on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that is used only during working hours. To stop paying for idle GPU instances, the team deployed the model as an inference component, set `MinInstanceCount` to 0 in the variant's managed instance scaling, registered the inference component as a scalable target with a minimum capacity of 0, and attached a target tracking policy on invocations per copy. The endpoint now scales in to zero overnight as intended. Each morning, however, the first requests fail and the endpoint does not provision an instance until an engineer intervenes. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: No step scaling policy is attached to a CloudWatch alarm on the `NoCapacityInvocationFailures` metric to add the first copy.
Inference components cannot run on an endpoint whose `MinInstanceCount` is 0, so the configuration is rejected at the first request.
The target tracking policy's scale-out cooldown of 300 seconds is longer than the client timeout of the first requests.
The target tracking policy tracks invocations per copy instead of a concurrency metric with high-resolution data points.

explanation: The SageMaker AI procedure for scaling to zero has two halves. Scaling in needs an endpoint that hosts inference components, `MinInstanceCount` 0 in managed instance scaling, a scalable target with minimum capacity 0 and a target tracking policy; the team did all of that. Scaling out from zero is separate: once there are no instances the endpoint cannot respond, so you create a step scaling policy on the inference component's desired copy count and assign it to a CloudWatch alarm on `NoCapacityInvocationFailures`, the metric SageMaker AI emits when a request arrives and no instance can serve it. Without that pair nothing triggers provisioning. Even with it, provisioning takes several minutes and invocations return errors meanwhile, so clients need retries or a pre-warm schedule. "Inference components cannot run on an endpoint whose `MinInstanceCount` is 0" is the reverse of the rule; inference components are the prerequisite for zero. "Scale-out cooldown of 300 seconds" would delay a scale-out, not prevent one indefinitely. "Instead of a concurrency metric" changes the scale-in and steady-state signal, but no per-copy metric can trigger scaling when zero copies exist. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/endpoint-auto-scaling-zero-instances.html

prompt: A consultancy generates long reports with an Anthropic Claude 4 model on Amazon Bedrock. A Python AWS Lambda function with a 15-minute timeout calls `InvokeModel` through a boto3 client created with default settings; a typical report takes about three minutes to generate. Profiling with AWS X-Ray shows that a single Lambda invocation contains up to five Bedrock runtime subsegments, each ending in a read timeout error after roughly 60 seconds, and most invocations finally fail. The `InvocationThrottles` metric is zero, and the model invocation logs show several complete generations for the same report. What is the MOST likely cause of this call pattern?

options.text: Lambda retries the function after each failed asynchronous invocation, so every retry issues a new model request.
The on-demand tokens-per-minute quota is exceeded, so the SDK retries each throttled request with backoff.
Amazon Bedrock ends non-streaming Claude inference calls after 60 seconds, so each long generation is cut off.
The SDK client's default read timeout expires before the response arrives, so the SDK resends the request.

explanation: AWS documents that the timeout period for inference calls to Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Claude 4 models is 60 minutes, but that AWS SDK clients time out after 1 minute by default, and recommends raising the client's read timeout (for example `read_timeout` in `botocore.config` to at least 3600). A three-minute non-streaming generation returns nothing within the first 60 seconds, so the client gives up and its retry logic submits the same request again; each attempt starts a fresh generation, which matches the repeated subsegments inside one Lambda invocation and the duplicate generations in the logs. The fix is a longer read timeout, optionally with streaming so that bytes arrive early. "Lambda retries the function" does not fit, because the repeats occur inside a single invocation.
