"The on-demand tokens-per-minute quota is exceeded" contradicts the zero `InvocationThrottles` value and the read timeout errors. "Amazon Bedrock ends non-streaming Claude inference calls after 60 seconds" is contradicted by the logs showing complete generations and by the documented 60-minute service-side limit. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-parameters-anthropic-claude-messages.html

prompt: A logistics company runs a Strands agent in containers on Amazon EKS; it does not use AgentCore Runtime. The agent calls Amazon Bedrock models and several internal tools. The operations team wants each session's traces and spans, including model and tool calls, to appear in the Amazon CloudWatch generative AI observability experience, with the least custom telemetry code and without operating additional telemetry infrastructure. The AWS account has never used CloudWatch Application Signals or Transaction Search. Which steps are required? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploy the ADOT Collector as a DaemonSet, and point the agent's OTLP exporter at the collector's endpoint in the cluster.
Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs so that each model call is recorded as a span of the session.
Enable CloudWatch Transaction Search once for the account so that spans are ingested into CloudWatch Logs.
Enable the Tracing toggle for the agent on the runtime agents page of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console.
Add the ADOT SDK to the agent image, start the agent with `opentelemetry-instrument`, and set the documented OTEL environment variables.

explanation: AgentCore Observability supports agents hosted outside AgentCore Runtime. The documented setup is a one-time enablement of CloudWatch Transaction Search, which lets spans be ingested as structured logs, followed by adding the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK (`aws-opentelemetry-distro`) to the agent, running it under `opentelemetry-instrument`, creating an agent log group, and setting environment variables such as `AGENT_OBSERVABILITY_ENABLED=true` and the OTLP headers. Strands already emits OpenTelemetry GenAI spans, so no custom tracing code is needed; the session ID is propagated through OTEL baggage. "Deploy the ADOT Collector as a DaemonSet" fails because the documentation states that the ADOT Collector is not supported for agent observability (use the SDK or the Lambda layer), and it is extra infrastructure. "Enable model invocation logging" records request and response bodies of model calls, not spans, and says nothing about tool calls. "Enable the Tracing toggle" applies to agents hosted in AgentCore Runtime, which this agent is not. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability-configure.html

prompt: A media company serves a RAG assistant through ConverseStream. An alarm on p90 `InvocationLatency` fired repeatedly last month; each time the cause was a release that produced longer answers or added more retrieved context, not a service problem. The on-call team wants an alarm that fires only when the model itself generates tokens more slowly, and that stays quiet when prompts or answers simply grow. Traffic follows a strong daily pattern, and three months of metric history exist in the `AWS/Bedrock` namespace. Which alarm BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: An anomaly detection alarm on p90 `InvocationLatency` that fires when the value rises above the expected band.
A metric math alarm on `OutputTokenCount` / (`InvocationLatency` - `TimeToFirstToken`) that fires on a drop.
A static alarm on p90 `TimeToFirstToken` that fires when the value exceeds the baseline measured before the releases.
A composite alarm that fires when `InvocationLatency` is high and `InvocationThrottles` is greater than zero.

explanation: `InvocationLatency` is wall-clock time to the last token, so it rises both when the service slows down and when a request simply has more to do. AWS documents output tokens per second (OTPS) to separate the two: OTPS = OutputTokenCount / (InvocationLatency - TimeToFirstToken) x 1000, built as a CloudWatch metric math expression. Subtracting time to first token removes the prefill stage, which scales with input length, and dividing by output tokens removes answer length, leaving decode throughput. A stable OTPS with high latency means the workload changed; a drop means model-side degradation, so the alarm fires on lower-than-threshold or below an anomaly band. `TimeToFirstToken` is published only for the streaming operations, which this workload uses. "An anomaly detection alarm on p90 `InvocationLatency`" adapts to the daily pattern but still fires when answers get longer. "A static alarm on p90 `TimeToFirstToken`" tracks prefill, so more retrieved context trips it and slower token generation does not. "`InvocationThrottles` is greater than zero" detects quota pressure; throttled requests are rejected, not generated slowly. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-runtime-otps.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-runtime-metrics.html

prompt: A company that uses AWS Organizations runs 14 generative AI applications in one shared member account. Each application invokes Amazon Bedrock through its own application inference profile tagged with an `app` key, and that key is activated as a cost allocation tag. Last month one application's spend tripled for four days and nobody noticed, because total Bedrock spend in the account moved only slightly. FinOps wants to be alerted when any single application's spend deviates from its own pattern, without setting thresholds, and wants applications that are added later to be covered automatically. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: In the management account, create an AWS managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor on the `app` tag key, with an alert subscription.
In the member account, create a Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for AWS services, with an alert subscription that covers Amazon Bedrock spend.
In the member account, create a customer managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor that lists the 14 current values of the `app` tag.
In the management account, create an AWS Budgets cost budget for each `app` tag value, with an alert at 120 percent of last month's spend.

explanation: Application inference profile tags flow to billing as cost allocation tags, so spend can be separated per application. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection offers AWS managed monitors by dimension; a managed monitor on a cost allocation tag key tracks every value of that key independently, learns each one's pattern without thresholds, and automatically includes new tag values as they appear. Monitors for cost allocation tags, linked accounts and cost categories can be created only in the management account. "A Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for AWS services" evaluates Amazon Bedrock as one service, which is the aggregate view that already hid the incident. "A customer managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor that lists the 14 current values" fails because tag monitors cannot be created in a member account; a customer managed tag monitor is also limited to 10 selected values, aggregates them, and would not pick up new applications. "An AWS Budgets cost budget for each `app` tag value" relies on fixed thresholds and needs a new budget for every new application. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/getting-started-ad.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-management.html

prompt: A bank runs Amazon Bedrock workloads in 20 accounts that call InvokeModel and Converse on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. After an incident, auditors require two capabilities: an organization-wide record of which principal invoked which model and when, protected against tampering, and the full prompt and response of any individual request, so that an investigator can reconstruct what the model was asked and what it returned. All evidence must be consolidated in a central audit account. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use an organization CloudTrail trail with log file validation, relying on management events to record the model invocation calls.
Add CloudTrail advanced event selectors for Amazon Bedrock data events so that prompt and response bodies are recorded in the trail.
Enable model invocation logging to an S3 bucket in each workload account and Region, and replicate it to the audit account.
Configure model invocation logging in every workload account to deliver directly to a single S3 bucket in the audit account.
Share the `AWS/Bedrock` CloudWatch metrics with the audit account through cross-account observability, and retain them there.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock logs InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, Converse and ConverseStream to CloudTrail as management events, which are recorded by default with the caller identity, time, source IP and model ID. An organization trail delivers them to a central bucket, and log file validation provides tamper evidence; that covers the who, what and when. CloudTrail does not contain prompts or responses. Those come from model invocation logging, which records the request body, response body, token counts and `identity.arn` for each call. Its destinations must be in the same account and Region as the logging configuration, so each account logs locally and S3 replication consolidates the objects. "Add CloudTrail advanced event selectors for Amazon Bedrock data events" fails because data events cover operations such as InvokeAgent, Retrieve, InvokeFlow and ApplyGuardrail, and no CloudTrail event carries the prompt or response body. "Deliver directly to a single S3 bucket in the audit account" violates the same-account, same-Region destination rule. "Share the `AWS/Bedrock` CloudWatch metrics" gives aggregate counts and latency per model, with no principal and no content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime call 14 tools through one AgentCore Gateway; some targets are AWS Lambda functions and others are OpenAPI endpoints. Users report slow answers, and last week one agent looped on a single tool several thousand times before anyone noticed. The platform team needs to tell, for each tool, whether slow calls are caused by the target or by the gateway itself, and to be alerted when the call volume of any tool departs from its normal pattern, without maintaining static thresholds. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda targets, and compare the function durations across the 14 tools.
Compare `TargetExecutionTime` with `Duration` for each tool name in the `AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore` metric namespace.
Create a CloudWatch alarm with a fixed threshold on the gateway `Throttles` metric for each tool name.
Create CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms on the gateway `Invocations` metric for each tool name.
Count the `toolUse` blocks for each tool in the model invocation logs, and chart the totals on a dashboard.

explanation: AgentCore Gateway publishes invocation metrics to CloudWatch in the `AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore` namespace with dimensions that include `Name`, the tool name. `Duration` is the total time from receiving the request to sending the final response, and `TargetExecutionTime` is the time spent executing the target (Lambda, OpenAPI and so on), documented as the way to determine the target's contribution; the difference is gateway overhead, and it works for every target type. `Invocations` per tool is the call-pattern signal, and a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm learns each tool's baseline and fires on departures such as a loop, with no static threshold. "Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda targets" covers only the Lambda targets and shows nothing about the OpenAPI targets or the gateway's own time. "A fixed threshold on the gateway `Throttles` metric" is a static threshold on rejected requests, not a baseline of call volume. "Count the `toolUse` blocks" shows what the model requested, carries no gateway timing, and a dashboard chart alerts nobody. Gateway spans and vended logs add per-call detail when a specific failure must be investigated. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability-gateway-metrics.html

prompt: A company stores RAG embeddings in an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain that uses approximate k-NN indexes. The corpus grows every night. This week the ingestion job reported that new documents with `knn_vector` fields were rejected, while searches against existing data kept working. CloudWatch shows `KNNCircuitBreakerTriggered` at 1 and `KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage` at 100 on the data nodes; `FreeStorageSpace` and `JVMMemoryPressure` are within their normal ranges. The team wants earlier warning of this condition and a remediation that addresses its cause. Which approach should the team take?

options.text: Alarm on low `FreeStorageSpace`, and increase the EBS volume size of the data nodes before the next nightly ingestion run.
Alarm on high `JVMMemoryPressure`, and move the data nodes to a configuration that provides a larger JVM heap for indexing.
Alarm on rising `KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage`, and add data node memory or reduce the memory footprint of the vectors.
Alarm on `ThreadpoolWriteRejected`, and add replica shards so that the indexing load is spread across more data nodes.

explanation: `KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage` is the percentage of native memory used for k-NN graphs relative to the circuit breaker limit (`knn.memory.circuit_breaker.limit`). The metric description states that when it reaches 100 percent the circuit breaker triggers and new `knn_vector` indexing is rejected, which is the symptom here, and `KNNCircuitBreakerTriggered` confirms it. An alarm on the Maximum statistic at a level below 100 gives early warning, and the cause is addressed by giving the graphs more memory (larger or more data nodes) or by making them smaller (fewer dimensions, quantization, or disk-optimized vector storage). "Alarm on low `FreeStorageSpace`" targets disk, which is healthy; the limit that was hit is memory. "Alarm on high `JVMMemoryPressure`" watches the Java heap, but the graphs are held in native memory outside the heap, and the heap metric is normal. "Add replica shards" makes things worse, because every replica needs its own graphs in memory, and write thread pool rejections are a different failure from the k-NN circuit breaker. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/managedomains-cloudwatchmetrics.html

prompt: A support organization syncs an Amazon S3 data source into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base every hour. Ingestion jobs finish with status COMPLETE, but agents keep finding recently uploaded manuals that the assistant cannot cite. The job statistics show nonzero counts of failed and skipped documents and nothing more. For every future sync the team wants a queryable record that names each document that was ignored or that failed during embedding or indexing, together with the reason, and an alarm when that happens, with the LEAST custom code. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable model invocation logging, and search the embedding model's log records for the object keys of the manuals that are missing.
Enable CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase` resource type, and query the recorded events in CloudTrail Lake.
Run a scheduled Lambda function that calls `GetIngestionJob` after each sync and publishes the statistics as custom CloudWatch metrics.
Configure delivery of the knowledge base's `APPLICATION_LOGS` to CloudWatch Logs, and add a metric filter on the failure statuses.

explanation: Knowledge base logging is a vended log delivery (log type `APPLICATION_LOGS`) to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3 or Amazon Data Firehose that tracks the status of each file during an ingestion job. Resource-level records carry the document location, a `status` such as `RESOURCE_IGNORED`, `EMBEDDING_FAILED` or `INDEXING_FAILED`, the `status_reasons`, and chunk statistics, so CloudWatch Logs Insights can list the affected manuals and a metric filter with an alarm covers every future sync without code. It is not on by default; you add a log delivery to the knowledge base. "Enable model invocation logging" records model calls, not ingestion outcomes; a document that is ignored before embedding produces no model call, and no record states why indexing failed. "Enable CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase` resource type" captures Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate calls, which are query-time operations. "Calls `GetIngestionJob` after each sync and publishes the statistics" needs custom code and still yields only the counters the team already has, such as `numberOfDocumentsFailed`, without naming documents. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-bases-logging.html

prompt: An insurer uses Amazon Bedrock Agents with multi-agent collaboration: a supervisor agent routes work to a policy-lookup collaborator that queries a knowledge base and to a claims collaborator that calls an action group. A nightly regression suite replays a golden dataset of 200 questions with known answers through `InvokeAgent`. Six answers are now wrong, and the final text alone does not show whether the supervisor misrouted the request, the knowledge base returned the wrong passage, or the claims collaborator passed wrong parameters to its action group. Which approach identifies where each error entered with the LEAST additional instrumentation?

options.text: Enable model invocation logging, and reconstruct each agent's steps by correlating the raw prompts of the six sessions by timestamp.
Set `enableTrace` on the `InvokeAgent` calls, store the trace, and inspect each step's rationale, invocation input and observation.
Enable CloudTrail data events for the agent aliases, and review the `InvokeAgent` events that were recorded for the six sessions.
Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the action group's Lambda function, and inspect the segments of the six failing runs.

explanation: When trace is enabled, each chunk of the `InvokeAgent` response is accompanied by a trace part that records the agent's step-by-step reasoning. The orchestration trace holds the rationale (the agent's reasoning), the invocation input (which collaborator, action group and parameters, or which knowledge base query, was chosen) and the observation (what the collaborator, action group or knowledge base returned). With multi-agent collaboration the trace part also names the collaborator and the caller chain, and a routing classifier trace shows the supervisor's routing decision. Storing these for the golden-dataset run lets the suite diff a failing run against a passing one and pin the faulty step, with only a request flag and no new instrumentation. "Enable model invocation logging" yields raw prompts and completions that must be stitched together by hand, without the structured step and collaborator attribution. "Enable CloudTrail data events for the agent aliases" records that `InvokeAgent` was called, not the reasoning. "Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the action group's Lambda function" covers one tool and misses routing and retrieval. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now named Agents Classic and is in maintenance mode; its APIs and trace are unchanged. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/trace-events.html
